World.title: The Midwest braces for more heavy flooding, as Indiana seeks federal aid
World.content:
The Midwest braces for more heavy flooding, as Indiana seeks federal aid

toggle caption Indianapolis Fire Department via AP/Indianapolis Fire Department

A relentless stretch of thunderstorms has brought devastating flooding across the Midwest, with additional bouts of heavy rainfall expected through at least Sunday, the National Weather Service said.

The NWS is predicting widespread storms this weekend through the Ohio Valley, Midwest and central Appalachians, bringing additional precipitation to already saturated areas that had just started to see floodwater recede. At least three people have died and more than 150,000 were without power as of Saturday afternoon.

Indiana and Ohio have been among the hardest-hit states, with rainfall totaling more than 11 inches in some areas over the past week. The White River in Anderson, Ind., rose to a record 24.9 feet, surpassing a flood mark that has stood since 1913.

Sponsor Message

Flash flood and flood warnings were in effect across central Illinois and central Indiana, the NWS said Saturday, and flood watches were in effect from Iowa and Missouri eastward to central West Virginia.

"I will do everything in my power to protect Hoosier lives and livelihoods as we respond to this historic severe weather," said Indiana Gov. Mike Braun, who has requested a presidential emergency declaration through FEMA for federal funding and resources. "I have mobilized state and local resources, declared a Statewide Disaster Emergency and deployed the Indiana National Guard."

In addition to the deluge of rain, parts of Indiana have also endured periodic tornadoes and a derecho over the past several days.

Cyndee Gillmore, who owns and operates the Cornerstone Campground and Retreat Center in New Castle, Ind., said 5 feet of water swept across the property flooding the kitchen, banquet hall, youth center and all the center's mobile campers.

"I'm standing in my house right now and it smells to high heaven, but it's just stuff," Gillmore said. "Everybody is pitching in and the community is supporting one another and it's beautiful to see. We're going to keep our focus on God."

Still, she said, she worries about how the area will recover. Neither she nor most of her neighbors have flood insurance, and property insurance does not cover flooding.

Sponsor Message

"My heart breaks, Gillmore said. "Nobody has the money to fix all of this. I don't know how people will make it."

For Gillmore and thousands of other homeowners caught in this week's flooding, the financial damage could be devastating, especially without insurance.

The vast majority of flood insurance is managed by the federal government through FEMA. The agency maps out which homeowners are at risk and requires them to carry flood insurance if they have a federally backed mortgage.

But for decades, an NPR investigation found, those maps have failed to take rainfall and flash flooding into account, relying instead on risk data from coastal storm surges and large river flooding, even as climate change is supercharging rainfall intensity.

First Street, a climate risk modeling company in New York City, discovered more than twice as many Americans live in dangerous flood-prone areas than FEMA's maps suggest, leaving many homeowners and even local officials unaware of the risk.

The result has been that many properties affected by disasters are turning up outside FEMA's floodplains. When Hurricane Helene struck western North Carolina in 2024, 98% of the damaged homes were not included in FEMA's maps. Because flood insurance wasn't required in those areas, most homeowners had no coverage to claim.

In the days ahead, many property owners in the Midwest could find themselves in the same situation. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has predicted minor to major flooding in some areas, while the National Weather Service rain gauges recorded almost 10 inches of rain at the Washington Municipal Airport in Iowa, almost 8 inches of rain in Glouster, Ohio, and more than 6 inches in Elkhorn Creek, Ky.

As that rainfall makes its way into creeks and rivers, the flooding risk to all the areas downstream increases, especially with more storms forecast in the days ahead.

World.title: Families of USS Lincoln crew say Trump should be 'ashamed' of conditions on board
World.content:
Families of USS Lincoln crew say Trump should be 'ashamed' of conditions on board

toggle caption Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

WASHINGTON — Families of sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln are condemning President Trump's comments on the ship's record deployment.

A U.S. defense official not authorized to speak publicly told NPR the USS George Washington is en route to relieve the USS Lincoln, which has been at sea for nearly nine months

Trump was asked by reporters Friday whether the USS Lincoln's deployment had gone on too long.

"No, not nearly long enough," Trump said.

His comments come amid reports of food shortages, plumbing problems and declining mental health among crew members. There have even been some reports — which NPR has not been able to independently confirm — that sailors have attempted to jump overboard.

Sponsor Message

Karen Bramlett's grandson is on the ship. She asked NPR not to use his name for fears he could face repercussions or harassment from the military.

Bramlett said she is able to communicate with her grandson via Instagram about once a week.

"He's saying he's good mentally and physically, thank God," Bramlett said. "But he's just depressed. With the conditions over there you really can't blame him."

Bramlett said her grandson enlisted in the Navy about two years ago. She said it was a dream for him.

"But now he's like, he just can't wait to be done," Bramlett said. "Those dreams have been shattered."

"Donald Trump needs to be ashamed of himself to let them suffer the way that they're doing," she continued. "They're over there fighting for our country. And this is the thanks they get? They can't even get help from him or his administration."

Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said in a statement Friday that the USS Lincoln's mission was extended because the conflict with Iran demanded it.

"It is also true— a small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life," Cao said. "Meal plans were adjusted when fresh resupply was unavailable, without a single meal being missed. Calls home were limited when the operational threat was too high."

Sponsor Message

Cao said those aboard the USS Lincoln are the "epitome of American strength and resilience."

"There is no question our young men and women have been pushed to their limits—but they have never broken," Cao said. "They are rightly tired—but have never been out of the fight."

Democrats demand investigation

Democrats are calling for the Pentagon to investigate and take accountability over the conditions.

Speaking to NPR's Morning Edition Friday, Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) accused the Trump administration of not having a plan.

"They're just kind of winging it right now," he said, adding he felt that the Pentagon's handling of the deployment itself was "not proper leadership."

Gallego also said he had spoken to some of the crew aboard the ship.

"We are able to talk to a lot of these sailors," Gallego said. "We are able to talk to their spouses. And this is why I think it's important they allow us a bipartisan group of members of the House and the Senate to go and visit these sailors - something that has happened before - to make sure that we know that they're doing well and that the secretary of defense is not lying to us."

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said media reports about the conditions on the ship are "misrepresented" and said the U.S. can indefinitely maintain a naval blockade on Iran.

Speaking to NPR's All Things Considered, Julie Roland, a former Navy helicopter pilot, said there needs to be care given to the roughly 5,000 sailors returning to the U.S. from the USS Lincoln.

"I don't think anybody wants to be stuck in their office for 200 days without being able to see their friends or family no matter how good your job is," Roland said. "Some people do really struggle with the mental health of just transitioning from life on board to coming back home. When they return, we have to embrace them and take care of whatever might be the residual effects of having gone through this."

World.title: They own 2 excavators in Gaza and can't keep up with demand as families dig for remains
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the heart of Gaza City, several members of the Al-Drimli family dig for the remains of their friend and neighbour in the rubble of their former home, using only shovels, buckets, a wheelbarrow and their hands.

It's the middle of the day on Monday and the sun's rays are strong. The men work in silence, their heads covered by orange towels or the hoods of sweatshirts. The sounds of shovels clanging in rubble and the buzz of an electric saw fill the air.

The men fill the dusty wheelbarrow with rubble and wheel it to a nearby pile — it barely puts a dent in the mounds of broken cinder block and metal rebar remaining from the six-storey residential building that was hit by an airstrike in November 2023.

Because there are so few excavators available in Gaza, many Palestinians, like this family in Gaza City, have resorted to using their hands, shovels and wheelbarrows as they search the rubble for the remains of loved ones. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

The Al-Drimli family had already recovered the remains of their loved ones at the site and is now looking for a neighbour who was sheltering with them when a strike destroyed the building.

The Gaza Health Ministry estimates that there are between 8,000 and 10,000 bodies still under the rubble almost three years after the start of the war between Israel and Hamas.

"We work with our hands because the cost of equipment today is very expensive and unavailable," Ayman Al-Drimli told CBC News freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife.

Officials and heavy equipment operators in Gaza say there are currently only about a dozen barely functioning excavators in the strip. They say the machines, which were frequently targeted by strikes during the war, are difficult to maintain under current conditions, which include a lack of parts for repair as well as oil and fuel shortages.

Excavators in high demand

Samir Sabra and his son, Uday Sabra, run two excavators in the Gaza Strip. He says the oil alone needed to run one excavator costs at least 2,500 shekels (about $1,175 Cdn) — not a price he can easily afford.

"We can't run the equipment like this," he told CBC on Monday. "There is no maintenance, no equipment and no spare parts."

WATCH | Excavator owner in Gaza says he can't keep up with demand: This family runs 2 of about a dozen remaining excavators in Gaza | Duration 1:19 There are currently about a dozen functioning excavators in the Gaza Strip now working to clear roads and retrieve remains from under the rubble. Samir Sabra says the work will take a long time because his machines are on their last legs and require a lot of maintenance.

Later that day, his son was at a different site just off the main road in Gaza City digging for remains with members of the Palestinian Civil Defence, a volunteer organization of first responders who visit strike sites to search for survivors and recover bodies.

"People call us every day," Uday said, noting he and his father can't keep up with the demand for their services. "There isn't enough equipment for the work because there are so many martyrs under the rubble."

He says he's been working at this site for a week and isn't done yet.

"The amount of damage and destruction in this country, one machine or two machines won't do anything."

Equipment targeted during war

Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for the Palestinian Civil Defence, says there still aren't many excavators available in the strip because they were targeted by strikes during the war.

"There was a policy and strategy of the Israeli army to destroy this equipment," he said.

A man uses an electric saw to break down cinder blocks into smaller chunks while clearing rubble in Gaza City on Monday. A spokesperson for Palestinian Civil Defence says without more access to heavy machinery, the search for remains in the strip could take years to complete. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) did not respond to questions from CBC News about strikes targeting heavy machinery in the strip.

Basal says Civil Defence hires out only one excavator at a time to avoid making the situation worse.

“We are working with the International Committee for the Red Cross on this group of victims under the rubble with one digger who works three days and stops for one day for maintenance,” he said at the site in Gaza City where Uday Sabra was working.

Basal says that despite last October's ceasefire agreement, which included a point on allowing more heavy machinery and equipment to clear rubble and roads, there hasn’t been a change on the ground.

"If we remain in this situation in Gaza," he said, "we are talking about long years of … removing the bodies from under the rubble."

Border restrictions

Humanitarian aid groups have stated that Israeli restrictions on fuel, oil and spare parts are hampering efforts to maintain machinery like hospital generators, ambulances, water pumps and water trucks .

The United Nations notes that restrictions on the entry of heavy equipment have slowed the process of reaching and recovering remains, and Civil Defence recently urged the international community to act to get machinery into the strip to help do this.

In a statement to CBC News, the IDF said it fulfils its obligations under international law, noting that the policy for the entry of heavy equipment into the strip is "determined based on security considerations" and "in accordance with directions from the political echelon."

The statement also said "fuel tankers enter Gaza every day via international organizations."

Uday Sabra operates one of the excavators his family owns to dig through rubble in Gaza City on Monday as members of the Palestinian Civil Defence look on. Sabra's father, Samir, says they can't keep up with the demand for their services. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

Back at the site in Gaza City, Uday continued to dig, slowly but surely making a dent in the mounds of rubble.

He says he will keep coming back until he can recover the remains and give the dead some peace.

World.title: How Iowans feel about Trump's tariffs, Canada's treatment as Republicans vie for support
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This weekend, hundreds of thousands of people are attending the Iowa State Fair — a major attraction featuring several days of entertainment, a rodeo and even a life-size butter cow that's been carved every year since 1911.

Much like the Calgary Stampede in Canada, the Iowa State Fair is a crucial stop for politicians to meet voters, making it a hotbed for political debates — especially when U.S. midterms are coming up.

And this year, one of the topics on Iowans' minds is U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war.

"This policy has been very chaotic, and our farmers have struggled to figure out what's going on," said Aaron Lehman, a fifth-generation family farmer and president of the Iowa Farmers Union.

"If we were getting to a situation that meant fairer trade eventually for farmers, I think farmers would understand that sometimes it's necessary to go through some pain. But we're not seeing us getting any closer.

Aaron Lehman, a fifth-generation family farmer and president of the Iowa Farmers Union, says Trump's economic agenda is damaging his relationship with Iowa farmers and families, and it's making the midterm races much more competitive than years prior. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

"We've lost many international customers of ours who no longer see us as reliable trade partners and they're going to countries where they have a more predictable trade policy, more reasonable trade policy."

For farmers like Lehman, that economic pain may reach another level in just a few days. Canada is Iowa's largest export market, accounting for 30 per cent of the state's total goods exports in 2025, according to the U.S. government .

But that key trading relationship could be upended on Aug. 19, if Trump imposes his threatened 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods. The two countries are working over the weekend to secure a trade deal, but it so far remains out of reach .

Lehman told CBC News he's trying to bring his son into his farm's operations, but with so much economic chaos it's difficult to plan any kind of succession. Instead, he's had to hunker down and focus on getting the next crop planted and harvested.

"So it's a scary time for our farm," Lehman said.

Trump 'pushed a lot of people away'

Other farmers who spoke to CBC News in Iowa also expressed concern about Trump's economic agenda, especially toward Canada.

Jack Ploen, who farms about 80 hectares in Avoca, Iowa, said Canada is "our most valuable partner in the world and in the trading sector."

"I'm a Republican, but I think Donald went too far in some of the things he does," Ploen said. "And he's pushed a lot of people away. A lot of countries are standoffish with us because of his policies. I support some of what he does, but not everything."

WATCH | U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on irritants with Canada: 'For decades we have had major trade issues with Canada,' says Greer | Duration 0:51 Speaking in Des Moines, Iowa, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are 'a lot of issues' with Canada, after being asked by a CBC reporter if there were particular areas the two countries couldn't find agreement on. Greer said that for the U.S., the current situation 'is not a trade war,' but if a country retaliates, 'we're obviously not going to tolerate that.'

Lehman said Trump's economic policies are damaging his relationship with Iowa farmers, and it's showing up in political polling ahead of the midterm elections in November.

During the last gubernatorial race in 2022, the Republican candidate Kim Reynolds beat the Democratic challenger by more than 200,000 votes. In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won the state by a similar margin — a huge victory.

But in 2026, polling suggests Democrats are either in the lead or very competitive in key races, such as the ones for Iowa governor or U.S. senator .

"All indications are that conditions are extremely difficult," Lehman said. "Farmers, ordinary families are all struggling to get by, and so our races are very, very competitive for the first time in a number of years."

Trump official in Iowa defends tariff tactics

On Friday, at a manufacturing facility in Iowa, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer touted Trump's economic strategy and said the U.S. government is committed to making American industry competitive with tariffs and tax cuts.

"We're seeing a transition from an economy that was focused on government spending, government jobs, subsidies for all these different programs… to an economy that's focused on American workers," Greer said.

Iowan Republicans serving in the U.S. House and Senate have tried to straddle the line on Trump's tariffs. In February, all four House representatives voted to uphold Trump’s tariff authority, but one of the four — Zach Nunn — said he could see himself breaking ranks on the issue.

Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley, left, speaks with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer during a visit to the Iowa State Fair in Des Moines on Friday. (Kelly Geraldine Malone/The Canadian Press)

Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee in the 2026 U.S. Senate election in Iowa, has previously said the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement should be renewed but some changes should be made for fairer market access.

On Friday, Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley told The Canadian Press that Trump is likely using his tariff threat against Canada as a lever, and the Canadian government should view his moves as a wake-up call to make changes.

Grassley said there's nothing wrong with Canada and the U.S. having tough negotiations, but they can't be allowed to undermine the trilateral trade agreement known as CUSMA.

"These negotiations cannot be used as a way of destroying [CUSMA]," Grassley said.

Where Canada-U.S. talks stand

Despite a flurry of negotiations toward a tariff deal this past week that were expected to stretch into this weekend, sources tell CBC News that Canada and the U.S. remain far apart as Trump's deadline looms.

The sources said the federal government does not believe a tariff deal is imminent because there are still major disagreements between the two sides.

One source with knowledge of the talks said optimism on the Canadian side is eroding and the Americans are not budging from their latest offer.

That offer includes a proposal that could see the sectoral tariffs on autos halved to 12.5 per cent, an offer that the Canadian side believes is not good enough, the source said.

On Friday, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc briefed his provincial and territorial counterparts on the state of the negotiations. He also held a separate briefing with members of the prime minister’s advisory committee on Canada-U.S. economic relations. The sources are familiar with the briefings but were not authorized to speak publicly.

The federal government has told the provinces to be ready as soon as possible to put American alcohol back on the shelves in case a tariff deal is reached, sources said.

WATCH | Former Conservative leader Erin O'Toole on Canada-U.S. trade talks: 'Our success can be their success': Erin O'Toole | Duration 9:58 CBC News learned on Friday that Canada-U.S. trade minister Dominic LeBlanc told the premiers to be ready to get U.S. booze back on the shelves should the two countries reach a trade agreement, although Ottawa believes such a deal is still yet to come. Power & Politics hears from Erin O'Toole, the former leader of the Conservative Party of Canada and a member of the Advisory Committee for Canada-U.S. Economic Relations.

In addition, the federal government has also asked provinces and territories to be prepared to drop retaliatory procurement rules that favour Canadian suppliers in case a deal is made, the sources said.

Trump cited complaints about provincial booze bans, dairy import quotas and the auto tariffs in threatening the new tariffs.

Industry sources previously told CBC News that Canadian negotiators have aggressively made it clear they see the Aug. 19 date as a cliff-type moment, meaning there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the 50 per cent tariffs come into force.

World.title: Tiny, beautiful species are going missing from restored forests and wetlands
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A regrown forest can look tall, lush and green. Restored wetlands can buzz with insects and flutter with birds. But scientists looking more closely are finding that some of their smallest inhabitants — including certain mosses, lichens, algae and fungi — are often still missing.

Restoring habitats such as forests and wetlands can save declining species of animals and plants and help their populations bounce back. But recent research shows they don't all return at the same rate. Some of the smallest, least noticeable inhabitants can remain rare or absent for decades — with potential consequences for other species.

Ellen Macdonald, a University of Alberta botanist, has spent her career studying forests — but not so much the trees. She focuses instead on the tiny flowers, mosses, liverworts and lichens that grow in their shade, among their roots or on the textured surfaces of their bark.

"There's way, way, way, way, way more species there than there is a tree species," said Macdonald.

To the average person, Macdonald said, a regrown forest a few decades after logging might look much like one that had never been cut, full of tall trees, birds and insects.

But Macdonald recalled walking through regrown coniferous boreal forests and sensing that something was not quite right, even if she could not immediately identify what.

"To really notice what was maybe missing, you'd have to be collecting data," she said.

Chiloscyphus pallescens, a liverwort frequently found on rotting logs. (Michael Lüth)

Macdonald did just that, combining her own research with data from around the world to examine how long it takes plants and animals to return as boreal forests regrow after clearcutting.

The study, published recently in the journal Nature Sustainability , found that birch and aspen forests and their inhabitants appeared to recover within 25 years, while conifer forests took far longer. In conifer forests, understory plants — especially lichens, mosses and liverworts — took 85 years or more to return, and in some cases had not recovered during the century of available data.

Linnea borealis (twin flower) and other understory plants in a boreal forest. (E. Macdonald)

'They may not come back easily'

The pattern is not unique to boreal forests. Scientists studying wetlands and other restored habitats have also found that places can look healthy while some of their less visible species remain absent.

Years ago, CBC News spoke with German botanist Michael Melkonian about research into how plants evolved to live on land . He described wetlands near his home in the village of Jexmühle, in southern Germany, that teemed with carnivorous plants, sphagnum mosses, frogs and dragonflies.

The bogs "superficially looked very nice," Melkonian said in a more recent interview. They had been restored and replanted decades after being drained for industrial activities such as logging, providing wildlife habitat and storing carbon to fight climate change.

But beneath the water, Melkonian expected to find hundreds of species of the varied desmid algae he studies. Instead, there were only a handful.

"The diversity of algae was not there," he said.

Sphaceleria, top, Stylonema, bottom left, and Stephanosphaera, bottom right. Some of the diverse algae in different habitats that Michael Melkonian and his colleagues are trying to preserve. (Gerd A. Guenther/Central Collection of Algal Cultures)

Viktoria Wagner, an associate professor in the Department of Biological Sciences at the University of Alberta, describes this kind of decline as "a silent form of loss." Species do not necessarily go extinct entirely, she said, but disappear from many places where they once lived, reducing the number of species found at individual sites.

Wagner describes this as " dark diversity " and has found evidence of it among plants in habitats around the world. Algae are not technically plants, but are related.

Once species disappear from a particular place, Melkonian said, "they may not come back easily." Some may already be locally extinct.

Wagner said while restoring landscapes can be possible, "it's not easy, it's not always guaranteed that it works."

Micrasterias rotata, another kind of freshwater desmid algae. (Gerd A. Guenther/Central Collection of Algal Cultures)

Missing species may slow recovery

Those losses can have consequences that are not immediately visible.

Despite their small size, Melkonian said, algae have an enormous effect on the availability of oxygen and food on the planet.

"It's thought that algae in general are responsible for half of global photosynthesis ," he said.

Wagner said many species have important roles in ecosystems, and when diversity declines "this trickles down" and can negatively affect other species.

In boreal forests, Macdonald said, it's not surprising that many mosses, lichens and other understory plants take decades to recover after a clearcut. They depend on shade and old growth trees for habitat.

"That's all the stuff that's missing in a forest after harvesting and the things that take a really long time to recover," she said. "You know, you can't just get old big trees, except by waiting for trees to grow older."

Lichen on a branch of an old spruce tree in a boreal forest. (E. Macdonald)

Knowing these patterns could show people who manage landscapes like forests how to do it in a way that preserves more species. Macdonald said the research suggests conifer forests might be harvested more selectively or partially rather than clearcut.

An algal 'zoo'

Mekonian said habitats for algae are also under threat around the world, along with the species that live in them.

Many algae look like little more than a smudge of colour on snow or a spot of slime on a rock or in water — forms most people might not recognize as living things.

Melkonian painstakingly collects those specks from different habitats, spooning and pipetting them into vials.

Michael Melkonian at the Central Collection of Algal Cultures in Essen, Germany, in 2025. (Submitted by Michael Melkonian)

The work is part of an effort to preserve them. Melkonian and his colleagues have collected and grow more than 5,000 strains — "an algal zoo, if you wish … that's a way maybe to ensure that we have a repository of these species as living organisms."

For Wagner, the widespread "silent loss" of species shows that preserving biodiversity requires more than protecting isolated pockets of habitat. It means maintaining and restoring enough habitat for species to persist across the landscape.

"Loss happens all the time and it's a continuous process and it needs active interventions."

This is part of a series of articles highlighting the work of scientists looking at disappearing groups of species you may not have thought much about. It's a chance to get to know them and how they impact our lives, and find out what can be done to keep them around.

World.title: Letting go of prized possessions can be tough. Let the professionals help, experts say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The struggles of downsizing and finding new homes for precious items

The Current 19:19 When no one wants your grandmother's best china

When Susan Masi sold her Surrey, B.C., townhouse earlier this year to move in with her son and grandchildren, she knew she’d have to get rid of some things precious to her.

Like the China cabinet her mother gave her when she got married. Or the mahogany dining table she inherited from her great-grandmother that is believed to be at least 126 years old.

Parting ways with items that hold so many memories is difficult, Masi says.

“We sat 12 people around that table. It breaks my heart to let it go, but this is the house I'm living in now. There's no way that it fits,” the 79-year old widow told The Current guest host Rebecca Zandbergen.

Masi says she had to let go of a lot of things like furniture, dinnerware and knickknacks.

“I ended up with hardly any of it. Now I’m in a modern house with two small children,” she said.

Susan Masi had to sell her vintage mahogany dining room table that belonged to her great-grandmother and a China cabinet her mother gifted her when she got married. (Submitted by Susan Masi)

Choosing to give away something you own can be a difficult and emotional decision, says June Cotte. The Western University marketing professor says it can feel like throwing away part of your identity.

“Getting rid of a cherished object is getting rid of what someone thought defined them and was important to them,” said Cotte, who studies consumer behaviour and is a former president of the Association for Consumer Research.

Canada’s aging population means more people could find themselves in a similar position. According to a 2024 Statistics Canada report, about one in four Canadians will be 65 or older by 2030. A RE/MAX survey this spring found that among Canadian respondents aged 65 or older, 16 per cent said they plan to downsize their home within the next 10 years.

Cotte says people usually first turn to family or friends to take their precious items, which can lead to difficult conversations.

Often people hold on to items they could give away because they haven't found a worthy recipient, Cotte says.

“They don't think that anybody will appreciate it, so they hold on and defer the decision until it's actually too late."

Hiring help to clear out

Cotte says some turn to agents to help them find new homes for their objects.

Masi hired Vancouver-based company Estate Sales by Christine Caroline to help her deal with her belongings. The company’s founder, Christine Valk, has been in the business for 15 years.

Together they determined which items were valuable enough to be auctioned off and what needed to be discarded. Masi says the company also made an effort to figure out what could be recycled or donated so those items could get a second life.

Cotte says it’s important to have a strategy for downsizing, especially when it comes to larger items. She recommends people start giving things away while they’re still alive or before a move.

June Cotte, a professor of marketing at Western University in London, Ont., says giving up your possessions can feel like throwing away part of your identity. (Submitted by June Cotte)

Younger generations are set to inherit an unprecedented amount of stuff, but Cotte says older Canadians may be surprised by how little people are willing to pay for their precious items.

It’s one of the challenges some older Canadians face when downsizing, she says.

“I think the younger generations are more aware that spending money on life experiences is probably going to be more happiness than buying more and more stuff,” Cotte said.

The resale market

Yet some of these cherished items will find new owners — it just takes a few steps to connect them with the right buyers, says Christopher Reid, CEO of MaxSold, an online auction platform used for estate sales and downsizing, based in Waterloo, Ont.

He says vintage buyers are interested in things from a different time that have history.

“They might not sell how they would’ve sold when those styles were very prevalent in North America, but they still sell and go on to have another life,” Reid said.

Christopher Reid is the CEO of MaxSold, an online auction platform used for estate sales and downsizing based in Waterloo, Ont. Reid says he has seen unprecedented demand for vintage items. (Submitted by Chris Reid)

For example, Reid pointed to the rising popularity of things like CDs, vinyl records and old school radios.

However, Reid says a lot of people don’t have the time or desire to take steps, such as getting items evaluated and authenticated, preparing auction listings and taking photographs, so they turn to companies like his.

A chance to look back

Masi says she knows some of her possessions will have to be thrown away, but she didn’t have the heart to do so herself.

“This has all been quite traumatic to make this move at this time stage in my life,” she said.

In this undated photo, Susan Masi and her family enjoy a meal. Masi says 12 people could sit around the mahogany wooden table that was at her old home in Surrey, B.C., which she got from her great-grandmother. (Submitted by Susan Masi)

Masi says she’s spent a lot of time deciding what means something to her and what she’s OK to let go. But it’s been almost impossible to figure out which photos — of family gatherings and dinners — to part with.

“I don't know what I'm going to do with them, but I can't let them go,” Masi said.

Despite the emotional toll of the work, Masi says it’s special to be able to look back at 56 years worth of memories.

“I'm blessed really when I think about it and all the people that sat around that table and the fun we had."

World.title: Canadair water-bomber builder feels heat of demand as wildfires rage around the world
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Raging wildfires around the world have put iconic Canadian-made water bombers in such high demand the manufacturer De Havilland can’t keep up. For The National, CBC’s Kyle Bakx breaks down the high demand for the ‘super scooper’ and the push to get more of those aircraft in the sky faster.

As Canada, the United States and Europe grapple with another brutal wildfire season, pressure is building on the manufacturer of the Canadair "Super Scooper" water bombers to increase production, and on the federal government to bulk order the planes.

Calgary-based De Havilland is taking the rare step of reviving production of the Canadair after acquiring the water bomber program. The planes had been built by Bombardier up until 2015.

The world-renowned aircraft are built by hand with the majority of assembly in Calgary, from a supply chain across the country. The revived production line was announced in 2022 and is beginning to produce results as the first two aircraft are taking shape and on schedule to be completed and delivered in early 2028.

Canadian premiers and European leaders are desperate to get their hands on those aircraft amid current shortages and aging fleets.

First produced in the 1960s, the Canadair amphibious firefighting plane was designed for fighting vast fires in the Canadian wilderness. Its unique design allowed it to navigate narrow canyons at low altitude and scoop thousands of litres of water directly from lakes, rivers and oceans in seconds.

A Canadair aircraft collects water from the River Seine in Ivry-sur-Seine as it assists efforts fighting a wildfire in the Fontainebleau forest near Paris on July 14. (Stephane Mahe/Reuters)

The aircraft was purpose-built as a firefighting aircraft, as opposed to other planes and helicopters that are often modified to be able to carry water.

The latest version of the Super Scooper will be remarkably similar to past Canadair aircraft, with high wings spanning 30 metres, a 6,100-litre water tank, and the distinct yellow and red exterior.

Political heat

In recent weeks, opposition politicians in France and Spain have criticized governing leaders for not having enough operational Canadairs, leading to a lack of preparedness to tackle extreme weather and control wildfires.

Some provincial premiers have lamented the lack of new water bombers for consecutive summers, including Manitoba's Wab Kinew, who said in June 2025, "We could use every water bomber we can get our hands on."

The political heat is being felt by De Havilland.

"We are under pressure. We know that this is a very important aircraft not only for Canada but for the world. We take our responsibility to our customers and the people they serve very seriously," said Neil Sweeney, the company's vice-president of corporate affairs, in an interview inside the Calgary assembly plant.

A Canadair aircraft drops water on a wildfire in the Fox-Amphoux communal forest near Ponteves, France, on July 21. (Manon Cruz/Reuters)

Demand is so high that De Havilland is considering whether to build a second production line, even as it works to produce its first aircraft at existing facilities.

In recent weeks, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she is working with her provincial counterparts and the federal government to support a firm order by Ottawa, which would give the aircraft manufacturer enough certainty to begin constructing a second line.

"We told the Canadian government that if they made an order of 50 aircraft," said Sweeney, then, "we would build a second line tomorrow."

Inside its assembly facility in Calgary, De Havilland's first two water bombers are taking shape, says Neil Sweeney, the company's vice-president of corporate affairs. (Tiphanie Roquette/Radio-Canada)

Currently, De Havilland — which produces a range of aircraft and employs about 4,000 people predominantly in Calgary, Ontario and Victoria — will be able to produce about 10 water bombers annually at full capacity. A second production line would eventually increase output to 20 each year.

De Havilland has existing orders for 38 water bombers. The wait time for delivery of any new orders is between 2032 and 2033.

The Canadair require tens of thousands of parts, of which about 80 per cent are made in Canada. Some of the equipment on the production line dates back to the 1960s.

'Demand is huge'

There is a need for a second and even a third production line for the Canadairs, said John Gradek, an aviation expert at McGill University.

Several countries are panicking because of the wildfire situation and the lack of new water bombers, said Gradek, who estimates hundreds of the aircraft would be snatched up if there were any available.

Demand is coming from around the world, he said, because of a warming planet.

"Right now we're stuck in a situation where the demand is huge," said Gradek. "The world is looking for more water bombers, newer water bombers, and we're not ready.

"Every continent on the Earth, from Australia to Europe to South America to North America — the world is burning up. We need equipment to be able to fight those fires and fight those fires effectively. Canadair water bombers have proven their effectiveness over the last 60 years, no doubt about it."

De Havilland did not provide the price tag for a Canadair, although the figure is believed to be about $80 million per aircraft, based on government announcements.

The under-assembly cockpit of the first Canadair aircraft built by De Havilland, after the company resurrected production of the water bombers. This particular aircraft will be delivered to Greece. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

Threat of potential competition

If De Havilland is unable to respond to the growing demand for water bombers, there is the risk that foreign companies may develop their own rival firefighting aircraft.

Designing a new aircraft would take several years, but it's a realistic threat to Canadian manufacturing jobs, said Gradek.

"Whether it's Russia, whether it's France, whether it's the U.K., whether it's Greece or whoever — they're going to come out and they're going to come out fast and furious," he said.

The warning comes at a time when the federal government is focused on improving the national economy and bolster domestic manufacturing.

"We have the best scooping aircraft in the world, bar none. We've had it for 60 years. But having it for another 60 years is not guaranteed," said Sweeney.

Workers assemble the wing of a Canadair by hand at the Calgary assembly plant. (Tiphanie Roquette/Radio-Canada)

National fleet proposal

One of the recommendations from a Senate report released in June, on the growing issue of wildfires in Canada, encourages the federal government to create a national fleet of modern firefighting aircraft.

This year, the federal government did lease 10 airplanes and helicopters, which are helping provincial wildfire crews this summer.

"The federally funded aircraft are in high demand," said Alexandria Jones, a Winnipeg-based spokesperson for the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre, a national not-for-profit organization responsible for wildland fire management in Canada.

"There definitely have been situations where we've had to triage requests that come through," she said.

While demand is high, different types of aerial firefighting units are just one tool in helping battle wildfires, said Jones.

Aircraft are best suited to slowing the spread of wildfires, helping create perimeters and reducing heat to aid ground crews, she said. But helicopters and planes can also be hindered by widespread smoke and certain terrain.

"Planes don't put out fires, firefighters put out fires," said Jones. "They're not the silver bullet to firefighting. While planes are the sexy part of firefighting, there's a lot of other things that we need to consider with the ongoing threat that we're seeing from wildfires today. And that's mainly prevention and mitigation."

The federal government is committed to protecting Canadians and strengthening the national capacity to respond to "increasingly intense wildfire seasons," said Soraya Lemur, the press secretary for Eleanor Olszewski, the federal minister for emergency management.

"Minister Olszewski remains in close contact with her provincial and territorial counterparts to co-ordinate efforts and identify the best ways to support one another in the face of the growing impacts of wildfires," said Lemur in an emailed statement.

World.title: Lala strengthens into hurricane as it barrels toward Hawaii
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hurricane Lala took aim at Hawaii's Big Island on Saturday on a forecast track for possible landfall, which would be the island's first direct hit from a hurricane in 155 years.

The National Hurricane Center said Lala's maximum sustained winds increased to 120 km/h, making it a Category 1 hurricane. The eyewall was forecast to move over or near the island's southern end by the evening, lashing its worst winds at volcanic slopes thousands of feet above sea level.

Forecasters said higher elevations on the island, dominated by the towering Mauna Kea volcano, could get as much as 63.5 centimetres of rain.

That could cause life-threatening mudslides in a mountainous area where people live off the grid in improvised housing, and authorities urged them to find safe shelter quickly.

Bobby Camara, a 75-year-old lifelong resident of the Big Island, said he planned to "hunker down, cross my fingers, hope the lights don't go out" at a care home just outside Hilo. He said gas stations were busy as people sought fuel for chainsaws and vehicles.

Strong winds lash palm trees on the Big Island of Hawaii on Saturday. (Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/The Associated Press)

"I think stocking up is part of life over here.... You learn to be self-reliant," Camara said.

Hawaii Gov. Josh Green described it as an "enormous storm" and warned of destructive flooding and even the possibility of wildfires kicked up by strong winds across the island chain. Electricity was knocked out for 10 per cent of customers on the Big Island, according to poweroutage.us.

Mike Caputo, who lives in Keaau, near the island's east coast, said the main concern was flash flooding and fallen trees, especially albizia, a common tree.

"They're not very sturdy, but they grow extremely large," said Caputo, 50, a local fire captain. "They can make roads impassable. I made sure my trees were trimmed a few days ago."

People fill sandbags in preparation for the arrival of Lala in Captain Cook, Hawaii, on Friday. (Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/The Associated Press)

The Big Island was under a hurricane warning, and tropical storm warnings were issued for the islands of Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Oahu, Kauai and Niihau.

A Category 3 hurricane hit the northeast corner of the Big Island in 1871, according to research by a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist. The latest forecast has Lala striking "very close to the southern tip of the Big Island," said Vanessa Almanza, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Honolulu.

Shelters were opened, events were cancelled and ranchers were urged to leave their cattle in pastures, rather than structures that might collapse. "It doesn't take landfall to create destruction," Almanza said.

The hurricane centre predicted 20.3 to 30.5 centimetres of total rainfall across Maui and the lower elevations of the Big Island, and 10.2 to 15.2 centimetres across the island chain.

Officials urge taking the storm seriously

State Rep. Jeanné Kapela called for people to remain alert. The southern end of the island is remote and rural, with agriculture including coffee and cattle, but it's growing in population because of its affordability. Kapela was especially worried about people who live off the grid.

"If you feel now that your house doesn't have a great roof or might not be able to withstand hurricane force winds, then first things first you go to a family or friend's house and you kind of hunker down there," she said in a text message to The Associated Press.

Many Hawaiians are still dealing with the aftermath of devastating floods in March. Growers still recovering are worried about more damage, according to Hawaii Farm Bureau director Brian Miyamoto.

Wildfire risks increase during windy weather

As winds ramped up across the islands, Almanza said dry and breezy conditions outside the storm would elevate fire concerns.

In 2023 the Maui town of Lahaina burned during extreme winds as a hurricane passed far to the south.

"Since the fire, everybody is way more aware of weather in general and our environment and things that are happening," said Archie Kalepa of Lahaina, who is well known in the area for his surfing, paddling and other ocean skills.

Kauai, which is several islands northwest up the archipelago from the Big Island, is where Hurricane Iniki made landfall as a Category 4 hurricane in 1992 — an El Niño year like this one, when a warming of the Pacific near the equator increases Pacific hurricane activity and affects weather patterns across the globe.

"It did $3 billion worth of damage. It destroyed thousands of homes, and it did kill six people," said Steven Businger, a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist. "We just can never know if a storm is going to turn."

World.title: Archdiocese of Quebec to pay out $31.5M to sexual abuse victims after judge approves settlement
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Quebec Superior Court judge has approved a historic $31.5-million settlement in a class-action lawsuit against the Archdiocese of Quebec.

The deal ends years of legal action for claimants who said they were sexually assaulted by members of the Archdiocese since 1940.

Quebec Superior Court Justice Danye Daigle approved the settlement earlier this week, led by representative plaintiffs Gaétan Bégin and Pierre Bolduc.

Both men have said they were sexually assaulted by parish priests starting in the 1950s and 1960s when they were aged 14 and 12 respectively.

Daigle heard emotional testimony from victims during a public hearing in July, to determine whether the out-of-court agreement and the requested fees, were in the best interests of the class members.

After the hearing, Bégin described it as a historic day. Now 86, Bégin said the boy whose life was was robbed, is still with him every day.

But he said the worst isn't so much what happened to him, but the suffering he says he unwittingly inflicted on his family.

"The collateral damage is indescribable," Bégin said.

Around 200 people have already joined the class action.

The Dufresne Wee law firm says other victims have 90 days to to submit a claim outlining the alleged abuse and its impact on their lives.

Lawyer Justin Wee has said the $31.5 million settlement is one of the biggest against a diocese in Quebec.

The compensation fund will be financed by the Archdiocese of Quebec, the Séminaire de Québec, Collège François-de-Laval — formerly known as the Petit Séminaire de Québec — and the Mutual Insurance of Quebec Fabriques.

In addition to the $31.5-million compensation fund, the defendants have agreed to cover the costs associated with administering the claims process, including adjudicators’ fees and expenses such as obtaining medical records and expert opinions when necessary.

The amount each person receives will be determined by two retired judges appointed to assess the claims. Victims will also receive a written apology form the Archdiocese of Quebec.

In an online statement, Diocesan officials welcomed the news, saying they hope this next phase of reparation will help victims "continue their journey toward peace and healing. "

World.title: U.K.'s leader calls for reflection after former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism found dead
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

British academic Jason Arday, who resigned from the University of Cambridge last week amid allegations of plagiarism, has died at 41. London police say his death is being treated as unexpected but is not believed to be suspicious.

A British sociologist who resigned last week from the University of Cambridge following weeks of public accusations of plagiarism and media scrutiny was found dead Friday.

Jason Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest Black professor in 2023 at age 37, resigned after coming under intense media pressure over allegations of plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments.

The Times and Telegraph newspapers, along with the BBC and Sky News, reported that Arday, 41, was found "unresponsive" inside a home in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.

In a statement issued by his publisher, Simon & Schuster U.K., Arday's family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son."

"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," the family said, adding that for three years Arday was "subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse … by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him."

The Metropolitan Police said only that a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead in Battersea, without naming the man, in accordance with its policy.

"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," the police statement said.

Cambridge vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice, who earlier announced that the university would investigate the circumstances surrounding Arday's employment, said she was "desperately saddened" by the news.

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she said.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Arday's death was "a tragedy on so many levels."

"It's not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It's a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this," Burnham told reporters.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan said Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced."

Former Conservative home secretary James Cleverly, who is Black, wrote on X that academic institutions "have serious questions to answer."

"They put him into positions he was clearly not qualified for so they could have a Black wunderkind to show off; they pushed him into the spotlight for their own benefit," he said.

'Profound toll'

In resigning as professor of sociology of education, Arday wrote in a statement that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He said his stepping down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me." He has denied plagiarism, but admitted to some mistakes when working on his doctorate.

Supporters, including more than two dozen academics and politicians, had described the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to undermine Arday and other Black people who hold "positions of influence."

Arday's appointment at Cambridge highlighted his personal story of overcoming dyslexia, developmental delays and autism that he said left him non-verbal until the age of 11 and illiterate until his late teens.

Jason Arday, pictured in 2012 carrying the Olympic flame as a torchbearer in London, resigned from the University of Cambridge last week. (Joe Giddens/PA/The Associated Press)

Cambridge opens investigation into accusations

Questions about Arday's qualifications were raised publicly last month by Nathan Cofnas, a former Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the university after his criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion programs sparked widespread protests.

On July 24, the Times published an analysis of Arday's 2015 PhD thesis highlighting what it said were multiple examples of passages that were "identical or near-identical" to an earlier paper written by another researcher.

British media also raised questions about Arday's claims that he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($10.3 million) for charity through feats such as running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days.

Dozens of Cambridge academics had signed a letter calling for an independent inquiry into how Arday was appointed. Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.

The university then changed its stance and said it opened an investigation "following new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."

Prentice said this week that Cambridge would review its hiring processes. She stressed that "our staff of color are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements and the contributions they make to the institution and the wider academic community."

"This particular case is an aberration and should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge," she said Thursday.

World.title: The trouble with backup cameras: Here’s what we know about the many recalls
World.content:
How have backup camera systems performed in Canada?

Like in the U.S., there are myriad media reports about vehicle recalls in Canada over faulty backup cameras. Here are a range of recalls reported in just the last few years.

In late July, more than 17,000 Volkswagen vehicles were recalled, requiring the owners to take them back to a dealership. Transport Canada officials said that “(u)nder certain conditions, a software problem could cause the rearview camera image not to display when the transmission is shifted into reverse.” As a result, it “could reduce a driver’s ability to see behind the vehicle while backing up. This could increase the risk of a crash.”

In early July, Honda Canada recalled 32,289 Odyssey minivans due to an issue with the rearview-camera-image display.

In late May, Honda recalled nearly 1,000 vehicles due to an issue that could affect the rearview cameras.

In April, General Motors recalled more than a quarter of a million Chevrolet Malibus in Canada and the U.S. due to potentially defective rear-view cameras. The number of affected vehicles in Canada numbered 10,098. At the time, the Associated Press reported that a letter from the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration stated that the rearview camera on certain Malibu vehicles could display distorted or blank images when they were reversed, increasing the risk of a crash.

In late January, Transport Canada issued a recall notice for 12,179 Toyota Tundra trucks from the years 2024 and 2025 due to an issue that could affect the vehicle’s backup camera.

In early January, Transport Canada announced an update regarding an earlier recall involving more than 40,000 Volvo cars and SUVs. Again, the issue cited was a software problem that could cause the rearview camera images not to display when the vehicle was reversed. Even vehicles recalled previously required a new fix.

In late December of 2025, Porsche recalled more than 25,000 vehicles in Canada because of the possibility that the rearview camera image might not appear on the display.

In October 2025, Toyota recalled 32,733 vehicles in Canada due to rearview camera safety concerns, according to Transport Canada.

The month before, on Sept. 9, Ford issued a massive recall. It affected more than 120,000 vehicles in Canada due to potentially faulty rearview cameras. The notice from Transport Canada was part of a broader recall affecting around 1.9 million vehicles worldwide.

In November 2024, Hyundai recalled 48,509 SUVs and small cars in Canada because of a potential issue with the rearview camera imaging not showing up on the driver’s screens.

An even larger recall in June 2024 by automaker Stellantis involved more than one million vehicles, including minivans, SUVs, and pickups, in North America due to a software problem that could affect the display from the rearview camera. Transport Canada listed 126,530 affected vehicles.
