World.title: Africa's low-key high-stakes Strait of Hormuz diplomacy
World.content:
African governments have kept a low profile on the international stage during the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz. But that doesn't mean they haven't been engaging with the issue behind the scenes.

One of the principal arteries of world trade has been chronically blocked for almost six months. Maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has been reduced to a bare minimum since the first US-Israeli airstrikes on Iran at the end of February. Cargo ships have at times been fired on by Iranian forces; at others, threats from Tehran or Washington have been enough to bring shipping to a standstill.

So far, various rounds of talks, a joint memorandum and third-party deliberations about the creation of a maritime mission have not succeeded in stabilizing the situation. It remains to be seen whether a deal between Iran and Oman on establishing a shipping route through the strait will do so.

The war has prompted fossil fuel prices to soar all over the world, with inflation rising as a result. Despite its relative proximity to the Gulf region, some parts of Africa have experienced serious shortages because of the bottlenecks, with long lines of cars at gas stations that have run out of fuel. As many fertilizers are also sourced from the Gulf region, this year's harvests also threaten to be bad. African governments therefore have every reason to engage diplomatically in finding a permanent solution.

Cautious diplomacy

"I believe their long-term plan is still based on the assumption that the crisis in the Middle East may continue for some time," says Liesl Louw-Vaudran from the International Crisis Group , an NGO that works to prevent conflicts.

The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but Louw-Vaudran, an expert advisor working with the African Union, comments: "We don't see any evidence that there was some kind of optimism or revising of any economic planning after the MOU. I think everyone literally is just waiting to see how this is going to pan out in the next couple of months."

The Strait of Hormuz, viewed from Oman: There's hope that a recent deal between Oman and Iran can secure passage for shipping Image: REUTERS

It's certainly the case that a low-key approach has dominated African diplomacy with regard to Hormuz in recent months. There have been numerous calls for negotiated solutions, praise for diplomatic initiatives and an emphasis on the rules-based order. Some African governments have also shown solidarity with the Arab Gulf states, which, as US allies, have come under fire from Iran.

The current African members of the UN Security Council — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Somalia and Liberia — also backed a UN resolution adopted in March that strongly condemned Iranian attacks on the Gulf states.

The elephant in the room: Donald Trump

However, it is apparent from their communications that African governments are trying to avoid apportioning blame — especially to the US president, who, together with Israeli president Benjamin Netanyahu, was the one who started the war.

"Every rational human being in the world knows that this crisis has been occasioned by Mr. Donald Trump," says Dismas Mokua, a political risk analyst with the Kenyan advisory firm Tricarta. "But the majority of African leaders, and indeed across the world, fear to call him out because of the consequences. And I've seen European leaders tiptoeing around this issue, I've seen leaders from Asia — leaders all over the world. I've not seen a single leader who has come out to call Mr. Trump, because I guess they fear the consequences of their speech."

African countries have been careful to avoid blaming anyone for the crisis, especially Donald Trump Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

What if the whole of Africa were to speak with one voice — perhaps through the African Union? Louw-Vaudran from the International Crisis Group thinks a recent negative experience is still too fresh.

"The African Union Commission in Addis Ababa burned its fingers in the early days of the Ukraine war, in 2022, when the previous chairperson criticized Russia. And heads of state then immediately silenced him, and said that the commission doesn't have the mandate to speak on foreign affairs issues on behalf of the continent," Louw-Vaudran says.

She points out that the AU, with 55 member states, is "very much divided," and says that, since then, "when it comes to political statements in this big, rapidly changing geopolitical situation, the commission has been hesitant."

Ease the symptoms, don't create new problems

The crisis also requires governments to take action rather than just make statements.

"For most countries, or even companies, to be successful wherever there is a disruption in this global supply, you have to reevaluate your supply chains and find out which fits your interest," Mokua says. "And in my view, Kenya has managed to do that with a lot of success."

He comments that he hasn't seen anyone — and, in particular, commercial farmers — complaining about deliveries.

"And even for the supply of oil and gas products, people anticipated that there were going to be shortages. But there were no shortages. The suppliers have been constant and reliable, despite the increase in cost."

In Ethiopia, gas stations have had to close at times after running out of fuel Image: Marco Simoncelli/AFP

But the experience of neighboring Ethiopia has been very different. Delivery bottlenecks forced the government to temporarily prioritize security agencies, public transport and agriculture when distributing fuel. Private individuals were stuck waiting at empty gas stations.

Before the war, Ethiopia was one of Iran's most important African trading partners. That connection is now also at risk, since Ethiopia also relies on maintaining good relations with the United Arab Emirates and increasingly with Saudi Arabia, too.

Countries like Ethiopia and Kenya may also be about to feel another, delayed effect of the Iran war. If the rich Gulf states' economies falter, East African migrant workers there will transfer less money back home.

Opportunity for African countries to work together

But there are also some African countries for whom the uncertain situation in the Gulf might actually be helpful. Nigeria's huge new Dangote refinery came online at just the right time. Intended to ease fuel shortages in the oil-rich country, it's now a mainstay of the world market. In April, the refinery became the world's largest exporter of aviation fuel.

Responding to the Hormuz crisis, Nigeria has offered itself as a partner for African clients. The Dangote corporation is already planning another refinery in Kenya. And the government is standing with the Gulf states: On the oil market, countries seek to be partners, not competitors.

"Nigeria has been very smart, at least in terms of that economic positioning, having the crude itself," says Liesl Louw-Vaudran. "But obviously Nigeria has got huge governance and security issues that are very difficult to overcome."

Perhaps the least visible issue in the short term but one that is likely to have the most lasting impact: The crisis provides another argument for pressing ahead with the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

"There are a number of countries that do not understand the meaning of dismantling these artificial borders. They fear that they are going to lose political control," says the analyst Dismas Mokua.

But he added that he believes many African countries will eventually embrace the dismantling of arbitrary borders drawn up by European colonizers at the infamous Berlin Conference in 1885. "If you want to immunize yourself from the vagaries associated with the global disruption, then you must learn to trade within Africa," he says.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: How Germany supports recovery of Berlin Pride attack victims
World.content:
After a terrorist attack, public attention tends to focus primarily on the perpetrator. But what about the victims? What support can they expect? And what lies ahead for them?

On the evening of July 25, according to German authorities, Abdul Ballout, drove a white van into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate, where thousands were celebrating Berlin Pride. He then got out of the vehicle and began attacking people at random with a large knife. He killed a 65-year-old woman from Poland and injured her daughter, along with 30 other people, some of them seriously.

Many details have emerged about the perpetrator, his links to extremists, his criminal record and his family. Two days after the incident, he was shot dead by police officers while trying to flee during an arrest attempt.

The identities of the victims, and how they are coping after the attack on the event celebrating LGBTQ+ rights, are not publicly known. Still, many are likely to live with its consequences for months, if not years, to come. The only details disclosed by Berlin's governing mayor concern the age and nationality of the woman who was killed. Otherwise, Germany's strict data protection laws protect victims' privacy.

Victims can approach the media themselves at any time if they choose to make their stories public, Roland Weber, the German federal government's commissioner for victims of terrorism and extremist violence , told DW.

Calls for political consequences after Berlin Pride attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Support for the victims

In Germany, people affected by such attacks are often reluctant to come forward publicly or identify themselves as victims, says Julia Kühne. She should know: Kühne is the spokesperson for the Association for Victims of Terrorism (VoT Germany ), which is part of an international federation of terrorism victims.

"The perpetrator needs to disappear from the media, now that he has been caught and killed. Those affected should naturally be brought much more to the forefront," Kühne told DW.

How are those who were injured in the attack doing today? Weber has visited some of them in hospital.

"What I saw there was distressing. But thanks to modern medicine, and because the doctors are optimistic, there is reason for hope that everyone will recover as fully as possible," he said. "In some cases, however, that remains uncertain. Only time will tell. Some of the injured have already been discharged from hospital and are now receiving outpatient treatment. Others will begin various forms of therapy and rehabilitation."

How are the victims being supported?

The Federal Commissioner for Victims and "Weisser Ring" , a victim support organization, arrange trauma treatment, provide immediate financial assistance, and advise victims on long-term care and victims' pensions.

Weisser Ring is a volunteer-run organization that works closely with the police to provide advice and support to victims of crime in Germany.

"In cases of terrorist attacks, there is also a special provision: victims can apply for hardship payments," says Weber. "These are funds made available by the Bundestag. Hardly anyone knows about them, and making people aware of them is part of our job. We provide guidance and help ensure that applications are submitted as quickly as possible."

Weber is also responsible for supporting the relatives of the Polish woman who was killed and her daughter, who was injured in the attack. Nationality is not a factor in this regard. He assists victims with follow-up costs and compensation whenever an act of terrorism or extremist violence has been committed on German soil.

Number of traumatized victims still unclear

The victims of the attack are not only those who sustained physical injuries. According to VoT Germany's Kühne, even people who witnessed the attack from several hundred meters away may be considered victims.

"There are people who do not develop problems until years later," she said. "They may suddenly begin to suffer from sleep disturbances, experience nightmares, develop panic attacks or struggle with social phobia. In some cases, these symptoms do not emerge until years afterward because those affected were initially either still in shock or had returned to their everyday lives and were therefore able, at least to some extent, to suppress what they had experienced."

Kühne also notes that survivors of previous terrorist attacks may be retraumatized by media coverage of the current attack in Berlin and find themselves in need of support once again. She knows this from personal experience: she herself survived the 2016 attack on Berlin's Christmas market, which ultimately claimed 13 lives and left more than 70 injured.

In the shadow of RAF terror: The children left behind To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Victim support: Problems in practice

Weisser Ring, which supports victims of crime across Germany, believes that adequate compensation schemes and pension entitlements for victims of terrorism are now in place. However, not everything runs smoothly in practice, says Rolf Schmachtenberg, the organization's state chairman in Berlin.

"In cases where people have suffered permanent harm, the assessment procedures are often quite lengthy. We also continue to encounter administrative bottlenecks, with some authorities still relying on paper files and fax communications. They then have to wait for information from other agencies, which can significantly delay the application process. In my view, the main problem is one of implementation."

Over the past decade, Germany has experienced 13 terrorist attacks motivated by Islamist or political extremist ideologies, leaving 39 people dead and 475 injured. The support provided by the federal government's commissioner for victims has no time limit. Roland Weber continues to assist people affected by attacks dating back to the 1980s.

Commemoration continues of the nine people killed in 2020 in a racially motivated terrorist attack in the city of Hanau Image: Kadir Ilboga/Anadolu/picture alliance

Victims seek answers

For many victims, coming to terms with the horror and suffering also means finding answers to the question of why the perpetrator acted and why they, in particular, were targeted, says Weber. In some court proceedings, perpetrators have remained silent. In the case of the Berlin Pride attack, however, the perpetrator was killed, meaning there will never be complete clarity about his motives.

In Germany, investigations are discontinued once a suspect has died. No court will ever determine whether Abdul Ballout selected his victims for one particular reason or another.

"As a result, some questions will remain unanswered,"Weber told DW. "The search for answers is something most victims have in common, but it cannot always lead to certainty."

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Belgium battles record wildfire at German border
World.content:
A rapidly spreading wildfire in the High Fens nature reserve near Belgium's border with Germany has scorched around 2,700 hectares. The German town of Monschau has also warned residents of possible evacuation orders.

Belgium is battling its largest wildfire on record which has burned around 2,700 hectares in the eastern High Fens nature reserve near the German border.

The fire has approached to within some 3 kilometers (almost 2 miles) of the German border, causing authorities in Germany to warn of smoke danger.

On Saturday, the European Union deployed three helicopters and two water bombers as Belgium deployed additional firefighters in a bid to bring the massive blaze under control.

Authorities ordered around 600 residents in parts of Waimes, Sourbrodt and Buetgenbach to evacuate as shifting winds and heavy smoke raised concerns that the fire could reach homes. Tourists were also advised to leave the area.

Reinforcements were pulled from across the country to fight the blaze Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO

"You can't see a thing anymore, there's smoke everywhere," David Rodolfs, a restaurant owner in Waimes, told the AFP news agency.

A gymnasium in a neighboring municipality was opened up to offer shelter.

How have firefighting efforts fared?

The blaze, which broke out on Friday, has spread rapidly across peatlands and pine forests. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin told AFP he was "shocked" at the fire's speed and extent of the destruction.

Residents in parts of the nearby villages were ordered to evacuate on Saturday afternoon as a precautionary measure Image: Dimitri Korczak/AFP

"There is a risk that the fire could reach homes, but we are deploying all available resources to protect them," Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the regional authorities in Wallonia, said.

Difficult terrain has hampered firefighting efforts, with operations relying heavily on aerial resources and forcing firefighters to allow difficult-to-access areas to burn, according to Yernaux.

Meanwhile, Belgium activated the EU's civil protection mechanism, bringing in three helicopters and two water-bombing aircraft from the Czech Republic, Sweden and the Netherlands.

Local farmers have headed to the fire zone to support emergency crews Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO

Firefighters from Germany and Luxembourg have also joined the response, while farmers have helped emergency crews by wetting down the area.

Residents in Germany's Monschau warned of possible evacuation

Authorities in the German town of Monschau in the Eifel region, which is located just 2 kilometers from the border, have warned residents to prepare for possible evacuation.

They also warned of health dangers from smoke and have advised people living in three districts of the town to temporarily seek accommodation elsewhere if possible.

However, the local fire brigade has said it does not expect the fire to enter German territory any time soon.

"We are continuing to monitor the situation," Philipp Krüger, the operations manager of the Monschau fire brigade, told the DPA news agency.

Monschau, a major tourist attraction in the Eifel region, has some 12,000 residents. It is particularly known for its picturesque Old Town with its half-timbered houses.

It is located just some 23 km from the site of another major blaze in Germany's Eifel region that forced some 2,000 people from their homes on Thursday.

Climate change making wildfires spread faster

Belgium has experienced another spell of extreme heat this week, with temperatures reaching 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit) in parts of the country.

Scientists say human-caused climate change is increasing the likelihood of hot and dry conditions that allow wildfires to spread faster and burn longer.

European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib called the blaze the latest sign of the "climate upheaval" affecting the continent.

"Never before has the wildfire season started so early in the year and reached such northern latitudes," she said.

World.title: Iran war: Qatar denies holding missing Iranian fighter pilots
World.content:
Tehran said the three pilots "were captured alive" by Qatari forces after their fighter jets were shot down in the early days of the US-Israel war with Iran. Qatar has denied Iran's claims.

Qatar on Saturday denied that it was detaining Iranian pilots who went missing early in the US-Israeli war with Iran after their aircraft were downed.

"We categorically deny the claims circulating regarding the detention of Iranian pilots and are surprised by these misleading statements," Qatari foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari said on X.

He added that the remains of one of ​the pilots were found and that Qatar contacted Iran to coordinate ​a handover.

However, Tehran had not responded to the invitation, the spokesperson said.

Iran calls on Qatar to release downed pilots

Qatar's response comes after Iranian media published a statement by the head of the Committee for Missing Persons at the General Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces.

"Javad Salehi, Abdolmajid Dashtian, and Omran Behraveshian have been held by Qatari forces for six months,” General Mohammad Bagherzadeh said in a letter.

Bagherzadeh also said that three Iranian pilots had ‌been ​"captured alive" after their fighter jets crashed during a mission targeting a military base in Qatar shortly after the start of the Iran war.

In the letter, the general alleged that Qatar had not allowed the pilots to contact or meet with families or Iranian officials handling their cases.

The official also asked the International Committee of the Red Cross for help to follow up on the fate of the pilots.

Gulf nations caught between Iran, US as war escalates To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Qatar shot down Iranian jets in early March

Tehran responded to the ⁠US-Israeli attacks ​in late February with a series of strikes across the region, including US military facilities in the Gulf.

On March 2 — the third day of the war — Qatar's Defense Ministry said it had downed two Iranian Sukhoi Su-24 bombers. However, it was unclear if those jets were flown by the pilots Iran claims are being held in Qatar.

Qatar had condemned Iran for its "reckless and irresponsible" targeting of its territory .

World.title: Ceuta al límite: urgencias repletas, vecinos desbordados y ruidos de sirena
World.content:
En Ceuta, conocida como la ciudad de las cuatro culturas, hoy caben mil ciudades en una. En el barrio de El Príncipe, a mediodía de este viernes, decenas de niñas y jóvenes migrantes son trasladadas a una nave industrial recién reformada para acogerlas tras acusar la amenaza de violencia sexual. A la misma hora y a pocos kilómetros de allí, en el polígono de El Tarajal, otros tantos menores no acompañados duermen en el suelo entre el hedor a excremento y orín. En una ladera próxima, en la mañana de este sábado, tres legionarios corren con la porra en mano detrás de tres adolescentes. Uno de los agentes les ruega, en árabe, alejarse de las casas. Poco después, en la playa de El Trampolín, el asentamiento principalmente de subsaharianos ha mutado en poblado donde ya se autoorganizan las tareas y matan su tediosa espera en torneos de lucha libre. Las urgencias del único hospital están colapsadas por la afluencia de personas migrantes, con algunos casos puntuales de tuberculosis y sarna registrados, pero sobre todo debido a heridas por reyertas o caídas. Y la psicosis inunda las mentes y los teléfonos de los ceutíes por las informaciones sobre el aumento de la delincuencia, mientras las sirenas de las patrullas no cesan.

“Somos de Ceuta, somos caballas y el que se meta con nosotros, vaya vaya...”. Un lema popular resume la identidad de los 83.000 censados de la ciudad autónoma, apodados como el común pescado que cae en sus redes. Y donde las peculiaridades de su ubicación, un istmo de 20 kilómetros cuadrados rodeado de agua con el único acceso a Marruecos por el paso de El Tarajal, marcan una españolidad que se apercibe en banderas rojigualdas y en los estandartes en honor a la Virgen de África colgados por las calles. La puerta de la feria, que tuvo que ser anulada tras la entrada de unas 80.000 personas, seguía este viernes en pie como si el tiempo se hubiera detenido 15 días después del cruce inédito. Y, con él, la nueva normalidad que se ha instalado entre sus vecinos, que acusan hastío y refieren sentimiento de inseguridad.

A todo el que se le pregunta, saca el móvil y enseña vídeos y fotos que corren en WhatsApp de reyertas o entradas en domicilios. Muchos de los incidentes los confirman los agentes de las fuerzas y cuerpos de seguridad desplegados, aunque también se mezclan los bulos. Buena parte de los ceutíes denuncian “abandono” por parte del Gobierno central y hay quienes incluso aseguran que han dejado a sus hijos con familiares en la península. También están los que apenas pueden dormir. “Esto es una locura. Ceuta no es esto; la gente está saturada, nos estamos deshumanizando”, lamenta Elena Larios, trabajadora social de 45 años, con la voz quebrada en un céntrico bar. Juan Miguel Rocher, arquitecto de 39 años, que se toma una cerveza con un amigo tras dos semanas sin verse al permanecer en casa con las persianas bajadas, resume el estado de ánimo de los ceutíes así: “Somos una gente acogedora y ahora estamos de capa caída”.

Desde este fin de semana, eso sí, la diferencia entre el centro y los barrios que rodean al casco histórico se acentúa cada vez más. Casi todos los consultados reconocen que ya no se ve a tantísimas personas deambulando por las calles del casco histórico, ya sea por el “miedo” a las intenciones del Gobierno central de “devolver” a todos a Marruecos, expresado por el ministro de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares, el martes; o por la mayor presencia de policías, guardias civiles y militares tras la visita del titular de Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, el jueves.

“Está la cosa mejor en el centro, hay menos gente deambulando, pero porque hay una grandísima diferencia entre el centro y la periferia”, apunta Germán Álvarez, de 42 años y administrador de empresas. “Se está recuperando el pulso, la diferencia es notable”, aprecia Nabil, taxista en la ciudad. “La gente está saliendo, pero no te puedes recoger sola. No te puedes fiar”, añade Alba Morcillo, de 26 años y auxiliar de óptica. Las calles del casco histórico están más despejadas, aunque en los barrios el trasiego de personas migrantes no cesa. Y donde soportan unas durísimas condiciones de insalubridad.

Alba Morcillo y María José Vallejo, en el bar de El Mentidero. Foto grupo de voluntarias en el polideportivo Joaquín Sánchez

Según las estimaciones del Ejecutivo central, unas 8.000 personas permanecen en la ciudad autónoma, aunque el Gobierno autonómico del popular Juan Jesús Vivas cree que son más. “La situación es tremenda, los vecinos están muy preocupados, las playas estarían a rebosar y no hay prácticamente nadie”, señala el consejero de Presidencia, Alberto Gaitán. “Las barriadas están más presionadas, pero hay en toda la ciudad, sin duda”, remacha por teléfono. La Moncloa calcula que tendrá que asumir la acogida de 5.000 personas, unos 2.500 menores y otros tantos potenciales solicitantes de asilo, muchos de los cuales son los subsaharianos que han formado un minipueblo en la playa de El Trampolín.

Las devoluciones en masa iniciales cesaron tras el primer fin de semana. Ahora, cada día, en el paso de El Tarajal hay un goteo de personas que siguen regresando por su propio pie. El jueves, la Delegación del Gobierno cifró en alrededor de 600 los migrantes que han abandonado el suelo ceutí voluntariamente. Pero miles permanecen durmiendo en la arena, sobre cartones o sobre el suelo, todavía sin intención de marcharse. Entre ellas, Wafa Atid, 28 años, marroquí de la ciudad de Taza, que lleva dos semanas en las inmediaciones del Centro de Estancia Temporal de Inmigrantes (CETI), situado en una ladera que queda encima de la playa de El Trampolín, tratando de conseguir un hueco dentro. Una meta casi imposible.

Militares españoles en la barriada de Loma Colmenar de la ciudad autónoma, el 15 de agosto. Foto grupo de voluntarias en el polideportivo Joaquín Sánchez

Atid se marchó de casa porque no profesa el islam y rehúsa cubrirse. “Es muy complicado vivir en un país que no va con tu forma de ser”, cuenta en inglés la mujer, de formas menudas, sobre una colchoneta hinchable. A su lado, en una libreta, ha apuntado frases en castellano, que trata de aprender, extraídas de su teléfono móvil. Sueña con vivir en Barcelona y duerme junto a otras mujeres marroquíes que conoció tras entrar a nado. Al lado, dos policías nacionales custodian el lugar día y noche desde hace unas jornadas. Y han separado a las mujeres de los hombres, que están situados obligatoriamente al otro lado de la carretera para evitar problemas. Incluso los maridos de algunas de ellas. “Por la noche no se ve nada y no podemos controlar bien si se acercan a ellas”, explica uno de los agentes.

Ese terror es compartido por las propias mujeres y por Ahmed Enfed-Dal, presidente de la asociación de vecinos del barrio de El Príncipe, situado encima del paso de El Tarajal. “Hay niñas que tienen miedo”, asegura Enfed-Dal. Los voluntarios de su asociación gestionan un polideportivo donde las chicas llevan días durmiendo sobre colchones donados o directamente sobre la pista de juego. “Es como dormir en la calle, pero con un poco de vigilancia”, explica el presidente. Fuentes oficiales de Interior apuntan a al menos seis denuncias por agresión sexual, todas sobre chicas migrantes en Ceuta.

En un halo de esperanza, la situación para algunas niñas y menores ha empezado a cambiar, aunque solo sea de manera ínfima. El Gobierno de la ciudad empezó este viernes a derivarlas desde ese polideportivo a unas naves industriales cercanas. Por la puerta del edificio, donde los albañiles continúan acometiendo reformas, se ven literas de dos camas con las barras azul marino. Las primeras chicas en llegar sonríen desde dentro. Al menos 86 menores habían sido trasladadas ya este sábado por la Policía Nacional.

Nave industrial de un polígono de Ceuta donde se acoge a menores. Joaquín Sánchez

Mientras, otros cientos de niños y adolescentes continúan vagando. Según datos de Interior, 1.898 menores han sido filiados hasta ahora por la Policía Nacional, pero las estimaciones apuntan a muchos más. Lo que sí ha cesado son las largas colas de menores en la entrada de la jefatura de la Policía Nacional, aunque se mantienen las vallas por si acaso. Hay jóvenes, pero también críos que están tirados en las laderas, pidiendo para comer, sobre todo en el Campo Exterior. Cerca del paso fronterizo, en el polígono de El Tarajal, el hedor a excremento se apodera de la pituitaria dentro de un asentamiento donde los menores comen de lo poco que sacan de la beneficencia.

Unos metros más allá, en las laderas próximas, tres legionarios tratan de disuadir a unos jóvenes de entrar en las casas de los vecinos. Hay adultos que continúan recorriendo en grupos o solos las calles. Miran el móvil, están parados y eso intimida a los vecinos. En algunos supermercados, los militares vigilan los accesos como prevención.

Varios menores observan el punto fronterizo, el 14 de agosto. Joaquín Sánchez

Ya en el único hospital de la ciudad, ubicado junto a El Príncipe, varios hombres esperan sentados en la calle a ser atendidos en urgencias. El centro sanitario está a su vez custodiado por dos legionarios. Ayoue Chatal, de 32 años, es uno de los pacientes que aguarda a ser atendido. Tiene la mano vendada. “Tenemos heridas por peleas, por correr para escondernos, por caernos”, asegura el hombre. Sobre la situación sanitaria, el jefe de Medicina Preventiva del Hospital, Julián Domínguez, advierte de que hay “miles de personas sin salubridad, por lo que puede pasar cualquier cosa”. Ha habido un brote de gastroenteritis y algunos casos puntuales de tuberculosis y sarna diagnosticados. “La población está sobrecogida y yo, como epidemiólogo, muy preocupado”, añade Domínguez, quien confirma la saturación en urgencias. “Esto es una crisis humanitaria”, sentencia. En varios puntos hay desplomes de menores, a los que acuden los servicios asistenciales en medio del calor húmedo.

El próximo lunes, la ministra de Inclusión, Seguridad Social y Migraciones, Elma Saiz, se desplazará a Ceuta. La intención del Gobierno es comenzar a poner en funcionamiento de forma escalonada varios dispositivos con el objetivo de que al menos dos de ellos, con capacidad conjunta próxima al millar de personas, puedan estar operativos durante la próxima semana, entre los días 17 y 23 de agosto. Entretanto, y tras desvanecerse la amenaza de entrada de este 15 de agosto, los ceutíes continúan conviviendo con el paso de los coches patrulla, los helicópteros y las incesantes sirenas. “El pueblo ceutí está acostumbrado a la presencia militar, pero para nada a esto”, explica un militar del Ejército de Tierra crecido y destinado en la ciudad autónoma.

World.title: El turismo, la fábrica de oportunidades de España
World.content:
Con cerca de 700.000 empresas y un récord de visitantes en el horizonte, el sector de los viajes, el alojamiento y el ocio premia a los emprendedores que se especializan en un nicho del mercado, buscan soluciones digitales o convierten la sostenibilidad en una ventaja competitiva

Si hay una industria proclive al emprendimiento ahora mismo en España, esa es la del turismo. Este boyante sector, uno de los principales motores económicos nacionales, no para de batir sus propias cifras. Este año se prevé que se acerque a los 100 millones de visitantes —después de alcanzar los 96,8 millones en 2025—, algo nunca visto en el segundo país más visitado del mundo, solo por detrás de Francia. Y ese volumen inédito, explica David Hernández, fundador de la agencia de viajes personalizados Pangea, genera oportunidades de negocio en toda la cadena de valor: desde los alojamientos a la restauración, el ocio y el transporte.

Triunfar en el sector, asegura Asier Baquero, director del máster en Innovación en Turismo de la Universidad Internacional de La Rioja (UNIR), requiere, no obstante, de estrategia. “Hoy no basta con montar un hotel y esperar a que lleguen los huéspedes; el crecimiento también ha multiplicado la competitividad, por lo que resulta esencial diferenciarse para destacar”, explica el experto. Algo que se consigue a través de la adopción de soluciones innovadoras, de la especialización o de la atención a la creciente sensibilidad de los visitantes por la sostenibilidad.

Consejo de empresario Para emprender hay que ser optimista, pero si te pasas de la raya, te puedes llevar sorpresas David Hernández, Fundador de la agencia de viajes personalizados Pangea

Digitalización para abrirse camino en el mercado

Las soluciones digitales se han convertido en una palanca de diferenciación en el sector del turismo. Hoy la mayoría de las empresas de éxito nacen en el ecosistema de start-ups para ofrecer soluciones directamente al consumidor. Es el caso de la barcelonesa ByHours, que comercializa habitaciones por horas en hoteles de todo el mundo, o el de la madrileña Civitatis, que ha revolucionado el mercado de las actividades turísticas en español al programar visitas guiadas y excursiones por ciudades de Europa, Latinoamérica, Estados Unidos y Asia. “Ambas han identificado una necesidad del turista y han aportado una solución digital que, además, se puede exportar a cualquier parte del globo”, puntualiza Baquero, que da una pista de por dónde puede ir el emprendimiento: “El objetivo de España ya no es atraer más a turistas, sino gestionar de manera más eficiente la estancia de los que visitan el país”.

Otras empresas de ese ecosistema digital, explica Baquero, se crean con el objetivo de brindar soluciones a las grandes agencias de viajes o a las cadenas hoteleras. “Así sucede con los asistentes de inteligencia artificial para centralitas que gestionan las llamadas de los hoteles y las conectan con las reservas, algo que les permite ahorrar muchos recursos”, explica Baquero.

Jugar la baza de la especialización y la sostenibilidad

Encontrar una solución para un grupo concreto de consumidores es otra de las maneras de empezar con buen pie en el sector. Baquero afirma que hoy los hoteles o las agencias de viaje necesitan un apellido: “Un hotel burbuja, una agencia de viajes de lujo o para el segmento LGTBIQ+...”, ejemplifica el experto. Esta es una de las razones que explica el éxito de Nomading Camp, una empresa especializada en alojamientos de lujo en entornos naturales, con propuestas como suites y habitaciones burbuja en cinco destinos, desde los Pirineos hasta la sierra malagueña de Ronda. Lo justifica su fundador, Miquel Vila: “En nuestro caso, la experiencia es muy importante. No ofrecemos solo una cama, sino una noche en pleno bosque con todas las comodidades. La propia habitación es la experiencia. Nuestros clientes no nos escogen porque quieren ir a un destino y necesitan un sitio para dormir, sino que primero escogen nuestra experiencia y luego se desplazan hasta donde van a vivirla”, describe el empresario.

Emprender en el turismo tiene una dificultad añadida frente a otros sectores: no se venden productos, sino experiencias. Un fabricante puede controlar casi todas las características de lo que produce, pero una empresa turística depende de multitud de factores que determinan cómo recordará el cliente su viaje: la atención, el clima, las expectativas del viajero, la coordinación entre distintos servicios... Por eso, el éxito no consiste solo en ofrecer un buen servicio, sino en conseguir que el visitante viva una experiencia que merezca la pena recomendar, defiende Hernández, de Pangea. “Vendemos viajes a destinos cercanos, pero también a 10.000 kilómetros de distancia, con 20 proveedores, por lo que hay una alta probabilidad de que algo salga mal”, destaca.

Consejo de empresario Sigue tu propio camino sin fijarte en el camino de otros emprendedores Miquel Vila, fundador de los alojamientos de lujo en plena naturaleza Nomading Camp

La sostenibilidad gana cada vez más peso como ventaja en esta industria, asegura Baquero. Porque no solo responde a una creciente demanda de los viajeros, sino que también contribuye a reducir costes, acceder a financiación y cumplir la normativa. Por eso cada vez más compañías deciden que su propuesta de valor esté claramente ligada a la sostenibilidad, la economía circular o la conservación del entorno. La catalana Turismo Vivencial se ha hecho un hueco en el mercado ofreciendo consultoría sobre ecoturismo, el turismo respetuoso con el medio ambiente, y organiza actividades que contribuyen a conservar el patrimonio natural y cultural, así como generar beneficios a las comunidades locales. Cada vez son más comunes las compañías que ayudan a negocios del sector a medir su impacto ambiental, como la valenciana Bioscore Sustainability y la madrileña GreeMKO, que no es exclusiva del sector turístico, pero desarrolla programas para la gestión ambiental y el cálculo automatizado de la huella de carbono de hoteles.

Lecciones de los emprendedores

David Hernández y Miquel Vila, que protagonizan el último capítulo de El poder de las empresas, el pódcast de los que hacen , de Banco Sabadell, comparten algunas de las lecciones que han aprendido después de emprender y que pueden ser de utilidad para los empresarios de hoy y mañana. Vila, de Nomading Camp, asegura que, con el tiempo y la distancia, le hubiera gustado compararse menos con otros emprendedores y haber hecho caso a su instinto más frecuentemente: “Merece la pena seguir tu propio camino. Por ejemplo, si tus competidores están haciendo rondas de inversión y tú sientes que no necesitas una nueva, no la hagas; tu gran meta ha de ser que tu negocio funcione, no la ronda en sí misma”. Hernández, de Pangea, señala una actitud como clave a la hora de enfrentarse a cualquier decisión: “No hay que ser demasiado optimista. Me explico: creo que para ser emprendedor es imprescindible ser optimista, pero si te pasas de la raya luego te puedes llevar sorpresas”.

World.title: 16 pueblos españoles que piden manga larga cuando cae la tarde
World.content:
Vielha (Lleida). La gran baza de los pueblos seleccionados radica, sobre todo, en la posibilidad de tener que taparse para descansar, algo que se ha convertido en todo un lujo durante la canícula. Es un requisito que cumple Vielha, a la vera de los ríos Garona y Nere, con su casco histórico construido a la manera aranesa, a golpe de piedra, pizarra y madera. Sus mínimas descenderán hasta los 12ºC la noche del domingo; las máximas alcanzarán picos de 33ºC en las horas centrales del jueves y viernes, pero bajarán a los 24ºC (y con probabilidad de lluvias) el lunes, según la Aemet. La capital del Valle de Arán se presenta como un buen campamento base para conocer este territorio del Pirineo catalán, con sus 33 núcleos de población, sus algo más de 10.000 habitantes y sus iglesias románicas. Es recomendable acercarse a la cascada Saut deth Pish, probablemente la más bonita de la zona. Más información: visitvaldaran.com/descubre-la-val-daran/pueblos/vielha/.

Toni M (GETTY IMAGES)

World.title: Hockey World Cup kicks off in Amstelveen with Dutch victory
World.content:
The hockey World Cup has begun, with the Dutch women beating Chile 2-0 in the Wagener Stadium in Amstelveen.

Sixteen men’s and 16 women’s teams are competing for the two world titles over the next fortnight. The Netherlands is co-hosting with Belgium, where matches are at the new Belfius Hockey Arena in Wavre, south-east of Brussels.

Both Dutch teams play all five of their group matches at the Wagener Stadium.

The Dutch women

The women’s team is the clear favourite. It holds the world, Olympic and European titles and tops the world rankings by a wide margin.

The tournament is the last of Xan de Waard’s career. The 30-year-old midfielder, twice named the world’s best player, announced in the spring that she would retire afterwards.

De Waard has won all three World Cups she has played in, in 2014, 2018 and 2022. According to NOS, no hockey player, male or female, has won four.

“I think we are always the favourites, so we are now as well,” she told the broadcaster.

The Dutch men

The men are Olympic champions but have not won a world title since 1998. They are ranked second in the world behind Belgium.

Their first match is against New Zealand on Sunday at 4pm, and they play Argentina two days later. Prime minister Rob Jetten is due to attend the tournament as a spectator. His partner, Nicolás Keenan, plays for Argentina and for Klein Zwitserland in The Hague.

Where to watch

NOS is showing all the Dutch matches live on NPO 1, on its website and in its app. Tickets are still on sale through the tournament website, including day tickets covering every match at one venue.

The women’s final is at the Wagener Stadium on August 29 and the men’s final is in Wavre the next day.

World.title: Jetten condemns Star of David stickers at farmers’ protest
World.content:
Prime minister Rob Jetten has branded it “a disgusting act” that campaign group Farmers Defence Force (FDF) handed out Star of David stickers at Friday’s farmers’ protest in Den Bosch, according to Omroep Brabant.

The stickers show a Star of David in the pattern of a red farmers’ handkerchief, with the letter B for “boer”, or farmer. The star was a reference to the badge Jews were forced to wear under Nazi occupation.

“If you think you can make your point with this, I think you are only damaging your own cause,” Jetten said.

FDF leader Mark van den Oever said the stickers were meant to underline the injustice being done to farmers. Asked whether he thought the comparison with Jews during the WWII was inappropriate, he said revoking permits was also inappropriate.

Van den Oever also told Hart van Nederland permits were revoked in 1938 and that the same was now being done to farmers, that he understood the stickers could hurt people, but that action groups need to cause friction.

CIDI, a Jewish organisation called the comparison baseless and reprehensible. Ronny Naftaniel, a former director of CIDI and former chairman of the Central Jewish Council, said the farmers were undermining their own position by using the symbol.

Farm permits

The protest was called against the provincial executive’s plan to revoke the nature permits of five poultry farms near protected nature areas, which the farmers say would put them out of business.

After a debate lasting most of Friday, the executive said it was provisionally sticking to that plan, and a no-confidence motion against the executive member responsible, Saskia Boelema, was defeated.

Boelema told the council she had sought contact with the five farmers, who had waited eight months for a response to their plans. Broadcaster NOS, which has seen the email she sent to one of them, reported that it was sent two days before the debate.

The only motion to pass tells the executive to meet the farmers as soon as possible and to consider alternatives such as keeping fewer animals or relocating. A formal decision is due on October 1. Two people died on Friday morning in a crash on the A59, at the back of a queue that had built up as tractors drove to the protest.

World.title: Shell and Philips hit by Russian ransomware attack
World.content:
The Russia-linked ransomware group Cl0p claims to have hacked global corporations Shell and Philips. The two are among nearly 50 companies Cl0p has listed on its website, alongside General Electric and payments firm Fiserv.

From the oil giant, the group says it has taken some 89 gigabytes of material, including technical drawings, facility images, scans of test reports and project plans. They claimed to have stolen another 13.5 gigabytes from health technology company Philips, mostly diagrams and blueprints.

Both companies are investigating, with Shell saying it is “aware of a possible incident”.

Philips said it had “identified and contained an attempted cybersecurity compromise of a specific enterprise server related to internal data”. A spokesperson told NOS that the incident is now under control and has no impact on its customers.

Russian hackers

Cl0p, which has been active since 2019, is a Russia-linked ransomware group that has likely already extorted $500 million from other victims.

It operates by stealing files and other sensitive data from companies and then threatens to publish them online unless a ransom is paid.

There’s no word yet on how much money the hackers are asking for in exchange for not selling or releasing the stolen data.

Security researchers have linked the campaign to a flaw in Windchill, engineering software made by American firm PTC, which was patched on June 17. Neither Shell nor Philips has said how it was breached.

Writing about the attacks, TNW editor-in-chief Ana-Maria Stanciuc said the pattern carried an uncomfortable lesson: “When enough of the corporate world standardises on the same enterprise platform, one shared supplier quietly becomes everyone’s single point of failure, and no amount of internal security spending can fully patch a hole in someone else’s code.”

World.title: Jetten tells farmers to get off motorways after two die in crash
World.content:
Prime minister Rob Jetten has said it is “unacceptable” that tractors were driving on the A59 motorway on Friday, after two people were killed and six injured in a crash. The collision happened at the back of a queue that had built up as the tractors drove to a protest in Den Bosch.

“It is unacceptable and incomprehensible to demonstrate on the motorway because it leads to very dangerous situations,” Jetten said during a press conference.

Jetten also said the decision not to stop the tractors earlier was not a good signal and would have to be reviewed. News agency ANP reported that 50 tractors were driving on the A2 towards Utrecht as he spoke. “Don’t do it, get off the motorway,” Jetten said.

Police said four cars were involved and that they were still investigating what caused the collision, but no tractors were involved.

The victims have not been identified. The tractors had been in the right-hand lane and other traffic could pass on the left, but a traffic jam still built up.

Disputed agreements

Tractors are not permitted on Dutch motorways. Earlier this week the public prosecution department (OM) and the police said they would not stop farmers who drove onto them, citing the right to demonstrate.

A spokesperson for the OM in Oost-Brabant told broadcaster NOS that this had not been agreed. The authorities help demonstrations go ahead, the spokesperson said, but once a tractor is on the motorway it is up to the local mayor, police and prosecutors to decide when and how to step in.

“A tractor on the motorway is never allowed, and is a criminal offence” the spokesperson said. The OM did not answer questions from NOS about what had been agreed instead, or why nobody intervened.

Provincial council members held a minute’s silence for the two dead. Mark van den Oever of Farmers Defence Force called on farmers at the provincial offices not to travel home by motorway.

What the protest is about

Noord-Brabant’s provincial executive intends to revoke the nature permits of five poultry farms close to protected nature areas, after environmental groups won a court case in April 2025.

The court found the protected areas were overloaded with nitrogen, and that the farms were a significant cause. But it stopped short of ordering the permits withdrawn, giving the province, the farmers and the environmental groups a year to come up with a plan that would cut nitrogen levels for good.

The farmers sent in their plans in November 2025 but in July were told their permits would be revoked, although that decision is not yet final. The provincial executive has admitted it never gave them a proper response to those plans, Omroep Brabant reported.

Members of the provincial council, which oversees the executive, broke off their summer break on Friday for a debate on the plan demanded by seven opposition parties, led by farmers’ party BBB. Saskia Boelema, the executive member responsible, told them the province should have sat down with the farmers earlier and apologised for the way the process had been handled.

World.title: Mouse invasion plagues Friesland farmers
World.content:
A mouse plague has been destroying fields in Friesland in the northwest of the country, depleting crops as the rodents eat entire patches of land.

According to Omrop Fryslân, recent weeks have seen the mice mostly causing damage in peat meadows, but they have now also infiltrated clay areas.

“They eat the roots and then the grass dies,” farmer Jan Brouwer from Koufurderrige told the broadcaster. He estimates that it reduces his grass yield by up to 20%.

Drought

The outbreak comes on the heels of a countrywide drought, which has also affected the farmers.

But as there’s no irrigation ban in Friesland yet as compared to other areas of the country, Brouwer was able to flood his fields to flush out the mice. The critters drown in their burrows, and those that try to escape are easy prey for birds.

The water has also helped his land come back to life. “We were making silage today and the grass is starting to come back quite nicely in those spots,” said Brouwer.

The nearby Ijsselmeer still has plenty of water, but that could change if the drought persists.

There have been several mouse plagues since 2015 in the region. And with them, comes an owl invasion, including the short-eared owl. “I have seen at least six short-eared owls here in the past few weeks,” says Brouwer.

Researchers expect the number of mice to decrease substantially next year. “With such a plague, at a certain point there are simply too many,” said Niek Bosma of the regional waterboard. “Then a disease sets in, and within a few weeks all those mice are dead.”

But a few ultimately remain, meaning another mouse plague is inevitable.

World.title: Care homes, prisons and asylum centres hit by night-time heat
World.content:
As daytime temperatures continue to soar during the Netherlands’ fifth heatwave this year, night-time heat, where temperatures stay above 20 degrees, has lagged behind in public discourse despite its effects on the population.

“Night-time heat is an under-examined aspect of heatwaves,” Lisette Klok, researcher at the Climate Adaptation Services foundation, told broadcaster NOS and NRC.

Especially for vulnerable people – including the elderly and those living in asylum seeker centres and prisons – “night-time temperature is important because your body needs the chance to recover from the heat at night. Poor sleep [due to the heat] makes that more difficult.”

Hot nights, which are defined from 11pm to 7am, affect how well people are able to cope during daytime heat. People tend to sleep worse, making them less functional during the day. In addition, homes build up heat because they can’t cool down during the night, meaning neither do their inhabitants.

Climate atlas

The foundation puts out the Climate Impact Atlas, which maps climate effects – from threats of flooding, waterlogging, drought and heat – throughout the country. Using the Atlas, NRC and regional broadcasters found that on average, there are some six tropical nights per year in the Netherlands, although there are regional differences.

Going neighborhood by neighborhood, the journalists found that in parts of South Limburg, there is an average of 15 “sticky nights” annually.

Maastricht has the most hot nights in the country, while the Randstad also has a higher number. The north of the Netherlands sees less than the national average. Urban areas also take a heat hit, with city centres becoming “heat islands” on hot days. Heat in these areas is even worse at night.

“As a result, homes can be cooled less effectively by ventilation,” said Marjolein van Esch, urban microclimate researcher at TU Delft. “This depends on the difference in air temperature between indoors and outdoors. The greater that difference, the easier it is to cool. Due to the urban heat island effect, that temperature difference is smaller.”

Elderly

The high night-time temperatures have a particularly strong effect on older people, who are more vulnerable to heat.

That led some nursing homes being evacuated earlier this summer, including the De Taling care home in Den Bosch and a facility in Raalte whose systems temporarily failed in July.

“Many buildings are designed for a different climate,” a spokesperson for the care organization Carinova told NOS. “The climate systems were tested to the limit at some locations this summer.”

Temporary portable air conditioners and moving residents to cooler rooms helped ease the problems.

Asylum seekers and prisoners

Since 2021, new homes must meet certain requirements to prevent overheating, but the rules don’t apply to existing houses and also usually not to care homes, prisons and asylum seeker centres. Requirements also vary depending on the region.

But residents of asylum seeker centres and prisons, who have nowhere else to go, are not allowed to install air conditioners on their own. Refugee settlement agency COA allows only one fan per room.

According to NRC, the Dutch Correctional Institutions Agency said increasing temperatures in prisons in recent years mean it needs more resources to cool things down. “Many buildings are due for major maintenance or renovation.”

Ajax and Twente both reached the play-off round of the Conference League on Thursday, despite drawing both away games.

Ajax drew 2-2 away at Shelbourne in Dublin, going through 5-3 on aggregate after winning the first leg 3-1 in Amsterdam.

The Amsterdam side led twice in the first half, the second time through Anton Gaaei, but the Irish club equalised on both occasions. Substitute Sean Moore scored the second in the closing stages.

Twente had the easier night, leading 6-0 from the first leg, they drew 3-3 away at DAC 1904 in Slovakia to go through 9-3.

NEC chase Champions League

Every result in Europe counts towards the Uefa coefficient, the ranking that decides how many Dutch clubs qualify each season. The Eredivisie lost sixth place on the Uefa coefficient to Portugal in March, costing it a direct Champions League spot from 2027.

NEC, meanwhile, play Bodø/Glimt on August 19 for a place in the Champions League league phase.

The Conference League draw is on August 28.

World.title: Fifth heatwave confirmed as temperatures reach 37°
World.content:
Temperatures will reach 37° on Friday, after forecaster Weeronline confirmed the fifth regional heatwave of the year.

Temperatures will range from 33° in the north to 37° in the south and southeast, the national weather service KNMI said.

Five heatwaves in a single year have happened only once before, in 1947. Then it was Maastricht alone – this year several southern stations have reached the tally.

There will be no national heatwave, which is measured at the KNMI station in De Bilt, near Utrecht. Most of the country, including the Randstad and the north, will fall below the threshold.

KNMI has issued a code yellow warning for heat across the country. The national heat plan, run by public health institute RIVM, puts care homes and health services on alert. It covers the whole country on Friday and only the southeast on Saturday.

Friday night will stay warm, with temperatures holding near 20° in towns and cities.

Saturday will be cooler, with a chance of thunderstorms, although the southeast may still reach about 32°. Sunday will peak at 24°, and next week will be cooler and wetter, with maximums of 21 to 25° and rain likely from Tuesday.

The weekend rain will do little for the drought. Weeronline says short showers run off ground that is baked too hard to absorb water.

World.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary

We cannot do what we do without your support. Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3 📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw — Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026 The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Magyar Péter confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among the thousands to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue, which weighs around 60,000 tons, took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mold into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. World.title: Polish opposition expels 40 lawmakers who formed breakaway caucus led by ex-PM Morawiecki
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction. Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026 On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus). Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said. A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk. Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily. Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.” Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk. The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards. That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest. Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”. Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world. According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build long-term savings and channel billions of zloty into the domestic financial market. Osobiste Konta Inwestycyjne to nowe narzędzie, które ułatwi inwestowanie i oszczędzanie na preferencyjnych warunkach podatkowych. Nowe przepisy wejdą w życie 1 stycznia 2027 r. Szczegóły w komunikacie ⤵️ https://t.co/Z6zEHKkQsY — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 13, 2026 The new legislation, which was signed into law on Thursday by President Karol Nawrocki and will take effect on 1 January 2027, creates Personal Investment Accounts (OKI). All assets held in an OKI will be completely exempt from the usual 19% capital gains tax. Amounts up to 100,000 zloty, including up to 25,000 in savings assets such as bonds and deposits, will be completely tax free. Assets above 100,000 zloty will be subject to a new tax on their value. The government has said the tax will amount to 0.85% in 2027 and will be adjusted annually. Finance minister Andrzej Domański earlier described the introduction of OKI as “the biggest change in years for individual investors and the largest project aimed at building domestic capital to drive the development of the Polish economy”. While Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, regularly clashes with the government and has vetoed a record number of laws, in this case he approved their idea, which he office said “could have a positive impact on both citizens and the state”. “Poles will gain a tool to promote family wealth building thanks to an attractive tax-free allowance and a guarantee of no account maintenance fees,” they added. Sejm przyjął ustawę o Osobistych Kontach Inwestycyjnych. Do 100 tys. zł bez podatku. Kamil Gemra, an assistant professor at the Warsaw School of Economics, said he considered the projection realistic. “Society is getting wealthier; we have record amounts in our bank accounts. It would be enough for just a few per cent of that money to flow into the capital market for the figure cited by the finance ministry be achieved,” Gemra told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The government also forecasts, however, that the tax exemption will reduce state budget revenues by nearly 9 billion zloty over 10 years, at a time when public finances are under increasing strain amid rapidly rising debt. World.title: Polish PM confirms he wants his “right-hand man” to be made constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Prime Minister Donald Tusk has confirmed that he will seek to have Maciej Berek, a government minister who stepped down this week and who Tusk calls his “right-hand man”, appointed as a judge on Poland’s constitutional court. The move has generated considerable controversy given that Tusk’s ruling coalition has repeatedly pledged to “depoliticise” the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after the previous national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government appointed its former politicians to the court. At a press conference on Thursday, however, Tusk defended the idea, describing Berek as an “apolitical and nonpartisan” figure who would help “fix the Constitutional Tribunal” after it was rendered illegitimate by PiS. Premier @donaldtusk potwierdził, że @MaciejBerek – do tej pory minister ds. nadzoru nad wdrażaniem polityki rządu – będzie kandydatem na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. – To jeden z najwybitniejszych polskich prawników – uzasadnił szef rządu.https://t.co/RsKLhLjHhC — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) August 13, 2026 Berek is a longstanding associate of Tusk. During Tusk’s first period as prime minister, from 2007 to 2014, Berek was head of the Government Legislation Centre (RCL) while also serving as secretary of the cabinet. After Tusk returned to power in 2023, heading a coalition of parties ranging from left to centre right, Berek was appointed as a minister without portfolio and then, in 2025, was made minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of government policy. He has, however, been an extremely low-key figure, rarely speaking in public. Berek is also not a member of parliament, and indeed not even a member of any political party. On Tuesday this week, Tusk unexpectedly announced before a cabinet meeting that Berek, whom he called his “right-hand man”, was leaving the government in order to “move on to other tasks”. The prime minister did not say what those tasks would be, but multiple media outlets reported that Berek would be presented as a candidate to become a judge on the Constitutional Tribunal. Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though was never a member of the PiS party). When Tusk’s coalition came to power, it promised to restore the legitimacy of the TK, including by “depoliticising” it. In 2024, it approved legislation that would have banned anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. However, the measures were referred by the then-president, PiS ally Andrzej Duda, to the TK itself, which subsequently declared them unconstitutional, meaning they did not come into force. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. He called Berek “one of the most distinguished Polish legal practitioners, who has made his apolitical and nonpartisan nature a hallmark”. Berek has a doctorate in law and, between his stints in government, worked as an assistant professor in the department of constitutional law at the University of Warsaw. “For him, compliance with the law and the constitution has always been paramount,” declared Tusk. “I don’t know anyone better equipped, better prepared, to help rectify the situation we face with the flawed Constitutional Tribunal.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: Nie mamy żadnych innych interesów w tej sprawie. Those remarks, in which Tusk also called Święczkowski’s leadership of the TK “embarrassing”, were a reference to the fact that the current PiS-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, and Święczkowski have refused to accept four new TK judges chosen by parliament earlier this year. “We have no interests in this matter other than to repair the Constitutional Tribunal so that it is not a tool and is not under the thumb of the president or PiS, but rather that it performs its work as objectively as possible,” said Tusk. Jeżeli to się wydarzy (a raczej nie), to do niedawna czynny polityk nie dostanie głosów klubu @__Lewica, gdyż obiecaliśmy naszym wyborcom, że politycy nie trafią do TK.
