World.title: Swiping a few apples may have ended in a beating in 19th century Estonia
World.content:
Nowadays, those caught pilfering peas or apples from someone else's field or garden may justify it as a folk tradition. In the 19th century, however, getting caught meant a trip to court and a sound thrashing as punishment.

The first apple orchards began appearing on farms 150 years ago and establishing one was a very expensive undertaking at the time. That was also why farmers kept a close eye on their apples. While fences kept animals away from the valuable produce, they were no help against people.

"A very common practice was to plant apple trees near the windows so they could be watched from inside the house. There were also dogs in the yard, of course, and some farmers would stand guard themselves," gardening history researcher Anneli Banner said.

Pilfering apples could land someone in court. In 1874, for example, boys aged 13 to 14 were caught stealing apples in Piilsi village near Avinurme — some took eight, others 10 and one 17.

"This was a time when punishment was either a fine or corporal punishment, meaning a birching. The boys' fathers refused to appear in court because they were afraid they themselves might receive corporal punishment," Avinurme local historian Piret Haav said.

That left the mothers with no choice but to go to court themselves and then carry out the punishment, giving their sons 10 strokes with a birch rod. It was quite unusual for parents, rather than the court, to have to administer the punishment. An adult would not have gotten off so lightly.

"The number of strokes varied, as did the fines. They ranged from 50 kopecks to a couple of dozen rubles, or from 10 to 30 strokes with a birch rod," Haav said.

While pea growers are now the ones who mainly have trouble with people helping themselves to their crops, the Estonian term raksus käima originated in apple orchards and comes from the cracking sound made when branches break.

"The word raks is an onomatopoeic word referring to a sudden cracking sound and the expression is presumably based on that comparison. Going out to pilfer or steal is an emotionally charged activity and emotionally charged activities tend to have many synonyms. These are often based on comparisons and one way of forming them is through onomatopoeia," Estonian Language Institute vocabulary researcher Iris Metsmägi said.

But while such pilfering was considered theft in the past, how is it viewed today?

"I suppose nowadays it is, whereas in the past it wasn't really seen that way. When you were a child and took an apple from a neighbor's garden, you didn't feel like much of a thief, although maybe you did feel a little twinge of guilt inside, but..." Ülle said.

"It's like going into a pea field, secretly eating a few peas there and taking a few with you. Or going into your neighbor's garden to eat a few apples — that sort of thing," Liisa said.

World.title: Anton Aleksejev: Putin does not know the people he lives among
World.content:
By allowing Yabloko to participate in the State Duma elections and failing to anticipate its rise in popularity, Vladimir Putin's administration has confirmed that it does not understand the people it governs, writes Anton Aleksejev.

A legend says that when Yuri Andropov came to power in 1982 after Leonid Brezhnev's death, he told a Politburo meeting: "We do not know the people among whom we live."

More than forty years later, Vladimir Putin — also with a KGB background — has clearly ended up in the same situation. He prefers to believe that people who oppose the war are marginal in number and that the overwhelming majority is actually pleased about it.

In early August, Putin quoted volunteers he had previously met. They asked the president: "When the 'special military operation'"— the official term for the war in Russia — "eventually ends, what will we do then?" Putin did not say what he answered. He likely does not know himself.

Life goes on, however, and since — unlike in Ukraine — martial law has not been declared in Russia, State Duma elections will be held on September 20. "Elections" is a conditional term, because in such cases the Kremlin has long been simply appointing the next composition of parliament.

On July 30, the Central Election Commission registered 11 parties to participate. All share unconditional loyalty to the Kremlin, but as usual only four or five will actually enter parliament. United Russia will get the majority. The Communists, Liberal Democrats, A Just Russia, and the supposedly liberal New People will divide the remaining seats the Kremlin leaves for them.

Among those who have never had access to parliamentary mandates is Yabloko, founded in 1993 and considered democratic and liberal.

"'Elections' is a conditional term, because in such cases the Kremlin has long been simply appointing the next composition of parliament."

They last entered the Duma almost 20 years ago. Since then, their chances have steadily declined — partly because the party refused cooperation with potential allies (including the then‑alive Alexei Navalny), and partly because the Kremlin decided once and for all that the Duma podium would not be given to "odd characters." Even so, Yabloko was regarded as an "old party," one Putin treated with a certain respect, and they never skipped an election.

As befits a marginal party, Yabloko entered the elections with a slogan marginal in today's Russia: "For peace and freedom!"

Sergei Kiriyenko, the first deputy head of the presidential administration responsible for elections, reasoned that Yabloko would again get its two to three percent, fail to enter parliament, and prove to all anti‑war citizens that they are vanishingly few.

But within a week of registration, support for the party rose from three percent to seven — with a month and a half still to go. The outsider and marginal force was becoming a poorly controllable threat right before the presidential administration's eyes.

Of course, according to Stalin's principle — "it doesn't matter how people vote, but how the votes are counted" — no level of public support would have changed anything. No one intended to let Yabloko into the Duma.

Still, the mere fact that during the fifth year of the war, the slogan "For peace and freedom!" would appear on television and in newspapers for six weeks could have unpredictable consequences.

Yabloko did not speak about who Crimea belongs to, did not oppose holding elections in occupied Ukrainian territories, and so on. Two words were enough to signal clearly: if you want the war to end as soon as possible, here are people who share your view. And voting would show how many of you there are.

The FSB's 2nd Service — responsible for protecting constitutional order — understood the problem first. Action had to be swift and decisive. On August 7, it filed a lawsuit with the Supreme Court to remove Yabloko from the elections.

As usual, the FSB chose a suitable executor. Official parties — Communists, Liberal Democrats — rushed to accuse Yabloko of extremism and near‑treason, but none dared go to court demanding a ban.

The role fit perfectly for State Duma deputy Alexei Zhuravlyov of the Rodina party. The party itself is not represented in the Duma, but Zhuravlyov was allowed in during the previous elections, presumably in hopes he might be useful.

So far, his usefulness has consisted mainly of appearances on propaganda TV shows, where he has called for killing at least two million Ukrainians and claimed that Europe has special zoophile zoos where perverts can pay to have sex with animals, even turtles.

"As befits a marginal party, Yabloko entered the elections with a slogan marginal in today's Russia: "For peace and freedom!""

Zhuravlyov did not disappoint his superiors. In his lawsuit, he accused Yabloko of extremism, foreign funding, and even copyright infringement. One Yabloko poster depicted a nuclear explosion as a symbol of war. Zhuravlyov claimed the photo showed the 1945 Hiroshima bombing and that the rights belonged to the U.S. Army.

Even the judge was surprised and asked whether Zhuravlyov could prove his claims. He was unfazed: the photo could not exist without the bombing, and since the bomb belonged to the United States, the image of its explosion must also be U.S. property.

By that logic, anyone wishing to use a photo of a nuclear explosion in the future must build a nuclear bomb, detonate it themselves, and photograph the blast — otherwise they risk being crushed by the Russian legal system.

Despite the absurdity, on August 10 the Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the elections — the first time in Russian history that a party was banned just ten days after being allowed to run.

As the murdered Boris Nemtsov said, in the absence of fair elections and fair polling, the only way to understand a political force's popularity in Russia is through the authorities' reaction.

Everything happened exactly in line with Andropov's words. By allowing Yabloko to run and failing to foresee its rise, the presidential administration confirmed it does not know the people it lives among. The FSB, by removing Yabloko with Zhuravlyov and the Supreme Court, clarified: we do not know them and do not want to know them.

Meanwhile, such unwillingness to know the governed is characteristic of many governments. Volodymyr Zelenskyy likely did not expect that his July decision to dismiss former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov would bring thousands of young people into the streets in protest.

Last Monday, several hundred young Yabloko supporters gathered outside the Supreme Court in Moscow. For a city of millions, that is not many, but in a country where all unsanctioned street gatherings are effectively banned, it is a significant number.

The motivation of young Russians who do not want to go to war and fear mobilization coincides strikingly with the motivation of at least two million Ukrainians trying to avoid mobilization.

And if Yabloko's slogan "For peace!" is interpreted as a call to freeze fighting along the front line immediately and begin negotiations, then nearly 60 percent of Ukrainians today share that view.

How many Russians share it, we will not know — but judging by the authorities' reaction, enough to cast doubt on the continuation of the war. And as Vladimir Putin said: "When the war ends, what will we do then?"

World.title: Mounting public interest seeing teachers brush up on drone knowledge
World.content:
Over the next five months, 20 science and mathematics teachers will visit various companies to gain practical insights and work together to create teaching materials for the future.

The "Lae end" ("Charge Yourself") education program is aimed at middle school physics and mathematics teachers, helping them bring more practical examples and real-life connections into the teaching of science and mathematics. This year, 72 teachers applied to the program, of whom 20 were selected. Participants include both new and more experienced teachers who began the program at Metrosert's drone and defense technology testing laboratory.

"We have a whole range of laboratories here for testing subsystems. What is important about all of these laboratories is that the tests can be replicated," said Rainer Kivimäe, head of Metrosert's drone unit.

Interest in drones and artificial intelligence is also growing in schools, meaning teachers increasingly need to be able to explain these topics to students.

"Starting this academic year, as far as I know, some schools will begin talking more about drones. An educational program is also being developed in Tallinn where young people will be able to play drone soccer themselves. So young people's interest in the field is gradually beginning to grow and teachers naturally need to be knowledgeable enough to discuss it in the first place," said "Lae end" program manager Valentina Moskaljova.

For teachers, this means getting up to speed on subjects they have not encountered before.

"I knew as much about drones as I'd read in the news, basically, and as much as has recently been said about introducing a drone curriculum in schools," said Getriin Kokk, a mathematics teacher at Lodijärve School.

The program will also produce teaching materials for students in grades seven through nine.

"Young people need to understand which formulas they can use in both mathematics and physics. Right now, we're giving teachers the opportunity to work together in groups to create materials specifically designed to support that learning," Moskaljova said.

World.title: Iraq’s oil exports jump to two million barrels per day
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s oil exports have increased dramatically since the beginning of August 2026, hitting an average of approximately two million barrels per day, as Baghdad continues to maximize export quantities and open up additional oil and gas export outlets.

Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair revealed on Friday that the country’s oil exports have averaged two million barrels per day since the beginning of August.

Iraq’s seaborne oil shipments fell dramatically in 2026, averaging roughly 1.31 million barrels per day during the first seven months of the year, compared to 3.33 million barrels per day during the same time in 2025.

The Iraqi Ministry of Oil is trying to boost production and export capacity while improving infrastructure and crude oil export terminals, given the government’s focus on diversifying oil and gas export routes.

Khudair indicated that the Ministry of Oil is working tirelessly to increase exports, which account for more than 85 percent of the country’s budget.

The Iraqi oil minister noted that crude oil shipments in July were roughly 49 million barrels.

Iraq’s average seaborne oil shipments during the first seven months of 2026 were at 1.31 million barrels per day, representing an almost 60 percent decline compared to the same time in 2025.

Sea shipments increased significantly in July, hitting nearly 39 million barrels compared to 15 million barrels in June, reflecting a monthly rise of more than 153 percent.

Iraq’s oil exports fell to its lowest level in May 2026, at roughly 98,000 barrels per day, a 97 percent decline compared to the previous year.

World.title: Iraq Ministry of Oil inks deal with Japan’s JGC to resume FCC project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Friday, August 14, 2026, an agreement with Japan’s JGC Corporation to officially resume construction and operational work on the massive Fluid Catalytic Cracking (FCC) complex at the South Refineries Company (SRC) in Basra.

The deal follows negotiations led by a ministerial committee under directives from Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair Al-Abadi, chaired by Ministry Advisor Hamid Younis alongside SRC Director General Hussam Hussein Wali. Under the finalized agreement, JGC remobilized its technical personnel to the Basra site starting August 10 to prepare processing units for full design-capacity operations, advancing Iraq’s target of refined petroleum self-sufficiency.

Key Operational Deliverables & Production Capacity

High-Octane Gasoline: Adding 5 million liters per day to domestic fuel supplies.

Gas Oil (Diesel): Producing approximately 7 million liters per day.

Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG): Delivering 400 metric tons per day for commercial and domestic consumption.

Project Milestone: Mobilization of JGC engineering teams began on August 10, 2026, to finalize site preparations and run commissioning sequences.

Strategic Objective: Eliminating fuel import expenditures and converting heavy refining residues into high-value white petroleum products.

The FCC complex at the Shuaiba refinery in Basra is among Iraq’s most critical downstream modernization projects, designed to upgrade heavy vacuum gas oil into premium fuels.

By adding 12 million combined liters of daily gasoline and diesel alongside substantial LPG yields, the facility will significantly curtail state spending on imported refined fuels and support domestic market stability.

World.title: Iraq customs revenues hit 2.5 trillion IQD in Seven Months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s General Customs Authority collected 2.5 trillion Iraqi Dinars (approximately $1.9 billion) in revenues during the first seven months of 2026, matching total receipts recorded for the entirety of 2025, Director-General Thamer Qasim Al-Taie announced on Saturday, August 15, 2026.

Speaking to state-run Al Iraqiya News, Al-Taie stated that July alone generated 560 billion IQD, representing a 150% year-on-year surge compared to July 2025. With revenue collection accelerating across all federal border crossings, full-year receipts are projected to surpass 3.5 trillion IQD ($2.67 billion)—the highest annual total in modern Iraqi state history.

Key Revenue Indicators & Technical Upgrades

Seven-Month Total:2.5 trillion IQD (~$1.9B) collected through July 2026, equaling full-year 2025 custom receipts.

July Revenue Surge: Recorded 560 billion IQD, a 150% increase compared to July 2025.

Annual Projection: Forecasted to exceed 3.5 trillion IQD (~$2.67B) by year-end 2026, setting a national historical record.

Automation & Anti-Corruption: Revenue jumps were driven by the nationwide rollout of SCADA systems, automated customs processing, and integrated digital networks connecting border crossings with government agencies, drastically curbing tariff evasion and illicit clearances.

The sharp rise in customs collections reflects Baghdad’s wider push to modernize border controls, plug financial leakages, and reduce structural dependence on crude oil sales amid regional market volatility.

By implementing mandatory automated documentation and digital data-sharing across federal transit checkpoints, the Customs Authority has systematically reduced tariff evasion, accelerated cargo clearances, and fortified federal non-oil revenue streams.

World.title: Popular Lebanese restaurant Al Beiruti to open in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Al Beiruti, a popular Lebanese restaurant, is set to build its first Iraqi branch in Iraq Mall in Baghdad, adding another significant regional dining name to the capital’s growing restaurant scene.

The Baghdad inauguration will be the next chapter of Al Beiruti’s regional development, after previous launches in Jordan and Qatar, as well as its established presence in the UAE.

The restaurant announced that its Iraq Mall restaurant is about to open, with a local franchise arrangement handling the expansion.

Al Beiruti has become a renowned location for Lebanese food in the Middle East, providing both classic dishes and a more modern restaurant experience.

The menu includes Lebanese favorites, including manakish, fattoush, hummus, baba ghanouj, and grilled halloumi, as well as shawarma, wraps, and mixed grills. Larger meals include steak, chicken escalope, and grilled salmon.

Al Beiruti joins a growing number of international and regional food and beverage companies in Baghdad, as new malls and commercial expansions change the city’s retail and entertainment markets.

Iraq Mall has emerged as a focal point of that expansion, drawing new restaurants, boutiques, and entertainment ideas as consumer spending and private-sector investment continue to rise in the capital.

World.title: Baghdad and Erbil agree on unified digital customs system across Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Baghdad and Erbil have agreed to fully adopt the digital ASYCUDA customs system across border crossings, with non-oil border earnings shared equally by the federal and Kurdistan regional governments.

The deal is a significant step toward standardizing customs processes across Iraq and addressing long-standing disagreements over border revenues and claimed import quantities.

ASYCUDA, designed by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), digitizes customs declarations, payments, and clearing processes, allowing authorities to better monitor products entering the nation and the income they earn.

Linking customs operations to Iraq’s banking and electronic payment systems may help limit the potential for underreporting, revenue leakage, and corruption at border crossings.

The deal comes as Iraq’s Finance Ministry and Central Bank work to digitize customs, payments, and government financial data in collaboration with UNCTAD.

A combined computerized customs system for Baghdad and Erbil might give more accurate revenue data while resolving one of the two governments’ ongoing financial issues.

The change is also significant for Iraq’s overall economy.

More open and uniform customs processes might facilitate cross-border commerce, boost governmental revenues, and enhance the business climate as Iraq pursues more foreign investment and closer integration with international markets.

World.title: Iraq’s Chief Justice Faiq Zidan meets Syrian President Al-Sharaa in Damascus
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zidan met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus on Thursday, marking another high-level Iraqi outreach to a neighboring Arab state as Baghdad seeks to bolster regional relations under rising security problems.

Al-Sharaa welcomed Zidan and an Iraqi delegation to the People’s Palace, which also included Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais.

According to the Syrian president, the talks focused on extending judicial and legal cooperation between Iraq and Syria, as well as resolving mutual concerns.

The visit also resulted in more practical conversations among the two nations’ judicial officials. Iraqi and Syrian authorities agreed to set up joint judicial committees to continue working on cases involving Syrian prisoners and other cross-border legal issues.

Zidan’s visit is crucial as he is one of the most prominent persons in Iraq’s state institutions, and it coincides with Baghdad’s increased diplomatic, security, and judicial interaction with its neighbors.

The Damascus meetings come after a separate Iraqi security group visited Riyadh, where senior military official Abdul Amir al-Shammari met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman.

Zidan had also just visited Ankara as part of a larger Iraqi effort to build ties with Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Turkey.

That approach has become more urgent in light of the regional escalation involving Iran-backed Iraqi forces.

In late July, the United States and Saudi Arabia conducted synchronized attacks against locations used by Iran-aligned organizations in Iraq, after Riyadh accused militias operating from Iraqi territory of firing drones against Saudi energy infrastructure.

The incident put Baghdad under strong pressure to prevent armed organizations from exploiting Iraqi territory to launch assaults on neighboring nations and also highlighted the potential that militia activity may harm Iraq’s improved ties with Arab governments.

Against this setting, Zidan’s encounter with Al-Sharaa is significant beyond regular court cooperation.

Iraq and Syria share a long border and confront shared concerns such as terrorism, organized crime, prisoners, and cross-border security. Baghdad also has a strategic interest in preserving stable ties with Damascus, as Iraq strives to boost regional connections and prevent unrest from spilling over its borders.

Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s administration sees recent diplomatic efforts as part of a larger effort to strengthen Iraq’s ties with its neighbors while keeping the nation out of the developing conflict between Iran and its regional adversaries.

Baghdad has increasingly emphasized that choices on security, armament, and relations with neighboring governments must be made by Iraqi official authorities rather than armed groupings.

The travels to Damascus and Riyadh therefore convey an essential message: although Iran-aligned militias have exacerbated tensions between Iraq and certain of its neighbors, Iraqi official institutions are working directly with those nations to restore cooperation and avoid further escalation.

Strengthening judicial, diplomatic, and security ties with Syria, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey might serve as an essential regional buffer for Iraq as it seeks to safeguard its sovereignty, control armed groups, and avoid being drawn further into the region’s crises.

World.title: Iraq’s Al-Shammari visits Riyadh to meet Saudi Defense Minister
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — A top Iraqi security team has traveled to Riyadh for meetings with Saudi Arabia’s leadership, as Baghdad and the Kingdom work to improve security and military cooperation after weeks of heightened tensions in Iraq involving Iran-backed militias.

First Lieutenant General Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman on Thursday to discuss military cooperation, regional developments, and increased coordination between the two nations.

According to reports from the visit, the conversations included cross-border drone concerns, air defense, and intelligence collaboration.

The conference is especially significant in light of the combined US-Saudi attacks on Iran-linked militia locations in Iraq on July 29.

Washington and Riyadh said the operation targeted Iran-backed terrorists’ weapons and logistical facilities in response to a series of drone assaults on Saudi oil installations that they said originated in Iraqi territory.

The strikes drastically escalated tensions between Baghdad and Riyadh, highlighting the Iraqi government’s problems in preventing armed groups from exploiting its territory to target neighboring nations.

Thursday’s visit indicates that both parties are now attempting to move beyond that conflict via direct military and intelligence collaboration.

Prince Khalid underlined Saudi Arabia’s commitment to Iraq’s security, stability, and economic growth, identifying it as an essential neighbor with whom the Kingdom has strong political and social relations.

The meetings in Riyadh follow Saudi intelligence head Khalid bin Ali al-Humaidan’s visit to Baghdad last week, during which he met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and reiterated an offer for the Iraqi leader to visit Saudi Arabia.

Baghdad’s security cooperation with Riyadh has grown more vital as the government seeks to prevent Iran-backed militias from drawing Iraq into a larger regional conflict.

Al-Zaidi has frequently said that Iraqi soil should not be used to attack other nations and has stepped up efforts for weaponry to be put solely under state control.

The most recent Iraqi trip to Riyadh symbolizes more than just normal defense diplomacy. It is part of a joint effort by Baghdad and Saudi Arabia to restore security trust after the July escalation and prevent militia activities from dragging the two neighboring nations into conflict.

World.title: Rare blind fish found in underground river in Iraq’s Anbar desert
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security and environmental teams have discovered a fascinating underground water system deep under the dry Anbar desert, where rare eyeless fish thrive in total darkness.

The location is in the Al-Khasfa region near Haditha, and crews traveled through a remote desert cave and sinkhole system to access running groundwater hundreds of meters under the surface.

The expedition’s footage shows little, pale fish moving in the subterranean water in the lack of sunshine.

The fish have evolved to live in darkness by losing their eyes and pigmentation, giving them a characteristic white-to-pink look.

The crew traveled more than 500 meters into the cave system despite challenging terrain and low oxygen levels.

The difference between above- and underground has piqued interest: underneath what seems to be an isolated and very arid stretch of western Iraqi desert, there is flowing freshwater and a specialized ecology.

Initial investigations have also suggested a link between the subterranean water system and the Euphrates basin, with the watercourse possibly running for a long distance under the desert.

However, environmental experts have highlighted that the blind fish themselves are not a novel finding.

Qais Najeh, the chairman of the Anbar Environment Directorate, stated that experts first confirmed the occurrence of eyeless fish in Al-Khasfa in 2010.

Similar fish have also been discovered in subterranean water near the Sheik Hadid mausoleum in Haditha district.

According to experts, the fish may grow to be roughly 49 millimeters long and survive in rather steady groundwater temperatures ranging from 20 to 22 degrees Celsius.

Their lack of vision and pigmentation are adaptations to generations of living in perpetually dark subterranean habitats.

The recent mission is nonetheless noteworthy because it has refocused attention on one of Iraq’s least-known natural ecosystems, perhaps allowing scientists to better research the subterranean water network, its geology, and the creatures that rely on it.

The fish’s severely limited environment renders it vulnerable.

Changes in groundwater levels, pollution, or human intervention might endanger a population that has acclimated to highly particular subsurface circumstances.

The Al-Khasfa location offers a unique dimension to Anbar, a region best known for its wide western desert and the Euphrates.

Hidden under that terrain lies an environment few Iraqis have ever seen: flowing subterranean water that feeds fish who have evolved to survive their entire lives without sunshine.

World.title: Parliament at a standstill, protests on streets: The Monsoon session story
World.content:
For 25 days, Parliamentâs Monsoon Session played out on two different stages.

Inside the Houses, proceedings were repeatedly disrupted, adjournments were frequent and Question Hour had barely any time remaining.

Outside, political activity rarely stopped.

Students marched, Opposition leaders protested, ministers traded charges, and the Parliament complex itself became a stage for demonstrations and symbolic political performances.

Held from July 20 to August 13, the session produced an unusual contrast: legislation moved forward, but much of the political confrontation surrounding it played out beyond the floor of the two Houses.

Parliament sees low productivity

The numbers underline that contrast. Lok Sabha functioned for approximately 19% of its scheduled time, while Rajya Sabha functioned for around 39%. Question Hour was particularly badly hit, with less than 1% of its scheduled time utilised. The session had 19 sittings spread over 25 days.

Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju acknowledged the distinction between legislative output and debate.

âIt was a good sessionâ¦we have passed 13 bills; but it was not a good session in terms of discussion,â he said, while accusing the Opposition of avoiding debate despite the government's willingness to discuss issues.





'Not a good session in terms of discussion'

Yet government business did move, much of it through voice votes amid Opposition sloganeering.

Bills passed in Parliament

Eleven Bills were introduced in Lok Sabha and two in Rajya Sabha. Twelve Bills were passed by Lok Sabha and 12 by Rajya Sabha, with 12 Bills cleared by both Houses during the session.

Two Bills replacing and incorporating the provisions of ordinances issued before the session, the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 and the Income-Tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, were also passed by both Houses.

The Demands for Excess Grants for 2022-23 were taken up, with the related Appropriation Bill passed by Lok Sabha on August 4 and returned by Rajya Sabha on August 6. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was referred to a Joint Committee for examination.

Among the more politically significant measures was the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, introduced amid concerns over public examinations and paper leaks.

Bills passed by both the Houses

The Bill came after Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced stringent measures to prevent such incidents in the future, including multiple selfie videos directly addressing students.

It provides for speedy investigations and time-bound trials, with investigations to be completed within two months and trials within three months. It also provides for Special Fast Track Courts and Special Public Prosecutors, allows the Centre to constitute Special Task Forces where necessary, enhances penalties and creates a time-bound appellate mechanism before a Division Bench of the High Court.

The Bill was passed by both Houses and received presidential assent.

Its debate also offered a glimpse of how political parties were trying to speak directly to younger voters. BJPâs younger leaders took the lead in explaining the legislation and the Centreâs position, while the Opposition made its own pitch. Both sides adopted Gen Z vocabulary, trading barbs with phrases such as âclock itâ, âFOMOâ and âdeluluâ.

Other major Bills passed during the session included the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, which seeks to bring Vande Mataram within the ambit of the 1971 Act; the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, which proposes stricter procedures for delayed registration; and the MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, which provides for a national digital platform for voluntary registration and seeks to improve access to finance and resolve delayed-payment disputes faster.

The Bankers' Books Evidence Bill expands the definition of bankers' books to cover physical, electronic, digital, virtual and cloud-based records. The Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill proposes changing the stateâs name from Kerala to Keralam. Other legislation dealt with cooperative development, tribunals and the mining sector.

But these measures were not what defined the political atmosphere of the session.

That distinction belonged to the protests outside.

The session began with a protest

The Monsoon Session opened against the backdrop of a large student mobilisation at Jantar Mantar over NEET examination irregularities.

The protest had been building for weeks. Scientist and activist Sonam Wangchuk had been on a hunger strike for more than 20 days when the Centre intervened and removed him from the protest site.

His removal intensified the agitation, with students going ahead with their scheduled âSansad gheraoâ.

Security personnel, including the Rapid Action Force and Delhi Police, were deployed as the protesters marched towards Parliament.

The distance was less than 1.5 km, but the march quickly turned into a major confrontation.

Pellet guns, lathi-charge and tear gas were used, with more than 60 people injured and admitted to nearby Lady Hardinge Medical College and Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital.

The police action immediately became a political issue, with Opposition leaders turning their focus towards Union home minister Amit Shah because the security forces involved came under the home ministryâs jurisdiction.

The student protests subsequently spread beyond Delhi. The pressure group Cockroach Janta Partyâs delegation met PM Modi-led cabinet ministers Jagat Prakash Nadda and Jitendra Singh, after which the situation moved towards normalcy.

One of the protestersâ major demands was the removal of Dharmendra Pradhan as education minister.

On July 25, Pradhan resigned from the post, making his departure one of the defining political developments of the session.

From Pradhan to Shah

Pradhanâs resignation did not end the political confrontation.

Lok Sabha leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi had not joined the initial Jantar Mantar protest but emerged as a prominent voice in the political battle that followed. His focus shifted from Pradhan to Shah, whom he repeatedly attacked over the police crackdown on students on July 20.

âAs home minister, did you approve the use of lethal force including pellet guns against students? If not, who did? Are the people in plainclothes seen beating students with lathis police personnel or volunteers? Youth and students, future of our country, are demanding answers and accountability,â Rahul said.

Rahul Gandhi trains guns at Amit Shah

He argued that Shah either directly ordered the use of pellet guns, shock batons, lathicharge and tear gas, making him âculpableâ for the treatment of the protesters, or did not know what the police were doing, making him âincompetentâ.

âIn either case, he has to go,â Rahul said, calling on Prime Minister Narendra Modi to sack the home minister.

Rahul also alleged that students were facing threats, including through face recognition and Bajrang Dal.

âThese are our children and the govt has no business threatening them or beating them. They have not committed any crime. They should not be punished,â he said.

He later made the demand for Shahâs removal explicit, saying: âShah is responsible and we are not going to let him get away with it.â

At the AICC headquarters, with Shahâs photograph displayed on a large screen, Rahul accused the home minister of being responsible for the treatment of students and criticised his absence from Lok Sabha, saying it showed that he was âguiltyâ.

Inside Parliament, Opposition leaders across parties continued to seek answers from Shah and Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The issue contributed to repeated disruptions.

The government, meanwhile, maintained that Shah was ready to discuss the student protests.

The debate that moved between the House and outside

In the final week of the session, Shah offered to address the Oppositionâs concerns directly.

He offered to sit in Parliament from â3pm till 3pm the next dayâ to hear the Opposition and respond to its points.

Rahul rejected the offer, saying they âseek answers, not lecturesâ.

Shahâs offer came amid demands that he make a statement in Parliament on the police action during the July 20 march over the NEET paper leak.

He later wrote to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla seeking time for a discussion on the student protest and NEET paper leak.

âAs you are aware, Honâble parliamentary affairs minister Shri Kiren Rijiju has agreed, on behalf of the government, to a discussion in Parliament on the student movement concerning the NEET examination, during the meeting of the Business Advisory Committee,â Shah said.

He also pointed out that the Lok Sabha had already discussed the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill during the session, but Opposition MPs had not raised the NEET examination issue during that debate.

The exchange captured the central political tension of the session.

The government pointed to its legislative response and willingness to debate. The Opposition demanded direct answers over the handling of the protests and accountability for the police action.

The argument was therefore no longer simply about an examination paper leak. It had become a contest over responsibility, policing and ministerial accountability, much of it fought outside the chamber.

Jharkhand adds another layer

Examination irregularities also became a political issue in Jharkhand, where the Centreâs political opponents were in power.

Students in the state protested over alleged irregularities in competitive examinations, including JPSC and JSSC, under the Hemant Soren government.

In Ranchi, protesters marched towards the state assembly in an âassembly gheraoâ. The Soren government said it was open to talks and held rounds of discussions with student delegations.

For the BJP at the Centre, the Jharkhand protests provided an opportunity to counter Rahul Gandhiâs attacks over the student movement in Delhi.

Pradhan, days after resigning as education minister, turned his fire on Rahul.

âThe leader of opposition, who habitually lies, neither wants to come to Parliament nor listen to answers.

They just want to spread their lies and shed crocodile tears,â Pradhan said.

Pradhan calls Rahul Gandhi a 'habitual liar'

He also accused Rahul of making âbaseless, factless false accusationsâ against Shah.

The political irony was clear: the examination issue that had put the Union government under pressure in Delhi was now being used by the BJP to target the Congress, which is part of the ruling alliance with the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha government led by Hemant Soren.

Then came the Ram Mandir protest

The student protests showed how street mobilisation could shape parliamentary politics. Another demonstration showed how the Parliament complex itself could become a stage for political messaging.

The alleged theft of donations at the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya became another Opposition issue during the session.

On Friday, Independent MP Pappu Yadav, along with other Opposition MPs, staged a symbolic protest at Makar Dwar over the alleged embezzlement of Ram Temple donations.

Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Samajwadi Party MPs Awadhesh Prasad and Dharmendra Yadav, and Jharkhand Mukti Morcha MP Mahua Maji participated.

The MPs held placards and a large banner reading âAmit Shah Sadan Se Gayab Kyun?â They also raised slogans demanding Shahâs resignation and his presence in the House.

Pappu Yadav, whose real name is Rajesh Ranjan, dressed as a temple priest carrying a photograph of Lord Ram and sat beside donation boxes.

Opposition MPs acted as devotees and placed money in the box. Yadav then symbolically slipped the money into his pocket, representing the Oppositionâs allegation of theft.

Videos circulating online also showed Rahul Gandhi putting money into the donation box. Another MP, playing a devotee, confronted the âpriestâ over the alleged act.

The priest denied wrongdoing before theatrically leaving the scene. The INDIA bloc said the demonstration was intended to highlight the alleged embezzlement of Ram Temple donations and demand accountability from the Centre.

It was a symbolic protest, but it reflected the broader character of the session: political messaging increasingly spilled into the physical spaces around Parliament.

A Parliament that worked, but talked less

The Monsoon Session cannot simply be described as one in which Parliament failed to function. Bills were introduced and passed, financial business was completed, ordinances were replaced and the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill became law.

But the productivity figures tell another story. Lok Sabha functioned for approximately 19% of its scheduled time, while Rajya Sabha functioned for around 39%.

Inside the Houses, protests and sloganeering repeatedly led to adjournments. Key government Bills were passed, often through voice votes. Outside, meanwhile, Parliamentâs premises became venues for demonstrations and political performances.

That contrast defined the session.

The Jantar Mantar protest became a parliamentary issue. The police action turned into a political battle over Amit Shah. Pradhanâs resignation followed sustained pressure over the examination controversy. The same issue travelled to Jharkhand, where it became another weapon in the Centreâs political contest with the Opposition. The Ram Mandir controversy then produced a symbolic demonstration inside the Parliament complex.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

In each case, the politics extended beyond the floor of the House.

The Monsoon Session thus offered an unusual picture of parliamentary politics: legislation continued inside, while confrontation, mobilisation and political messaging increasingly took place outside. The Houses passed 12 Bills, but some of the sessionâs most visible battles were fought through protests, slogans, press statements, letters and demonstrations.

Parliament was still working. But it was talking less, while the political argument increasingly moved beyond its walls.

On August 13, both Houses adjourned sine die and will meet again in the Winter Session.

World.title: Cauvery water row: Supreme Court to hear Tamil Nadu plea against Karnataka on August 17
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court is set to hear on Monday the Tamil Nadu government's plea seeking directions to Karnataka to release its due share of Cauvery water immediately.

The case is listed before a bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta, according to the court's cause list for August 17.

The matter was scheduled for hearing after the Supreme Court said on August 12 that petitions filed by Tamil Nadu and others, including the DMK, would be taken up on August 17.

Tamil Nadu approached the top court on August 3, arguing that it was not receiving its allocated share of Cauvery water despite the state facing a rain-deficient year.

The state government has alleged that both the quantity recommended for release by the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee and the actual water supplied by Karnataka were far below its requirement.

ALSO READ |

Tamil Nadu flags shortfall in water release

At a meeting on July 28, the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee directed Karnataka to release 3,500 cusecs of water to Tamil Nadu for 15 days from July 29.

Tamil Nadu, however, said the actual flow recorded at Biligundlu on the Karnataka-Tamil Nadu border was only between 158 and 550 cusecs from July 29 to August 2.

The state government also pointed to water storage levels in Karnataka's four reservoirs. As of August 3, the combined storage in the Krishna Raja Sagara, Kabini, Harangi and Hemavathy reservoirs was 77.537 TMC, according to a Tamil Nadu government statement.





Tamil Nadu argued that Karnataka would be able to release its due share without facing difficulty.

State claims 26.954 TMC is due

Tamil Nadu said recent rainfall in the catchment areas of the KRS and Kabini reservoirs had increased the amount of water that should flow to the state.

According to the state government, the proportionate quantity due at Biligundlu should be 26.954 TMC.

"Accordingly, the Cauvery Water Management Authority order allocating 4.536 TMC is very less," the release added.

Tamil Nadu has alleged that Karnataka has "failed" to release its due share and maintained that the state should receive 26.954 TMC.

The Supreme Court will now hear the Tamil Nadu government's plea seeking immediate directions to Karnataka over the release of the Cauvery water.

World.title: ‘Feeding my friends’: PM Modi’s quiet Independence Day morning with cows, peacocks
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday shared a glimpse of his morning routine, posting a video of himself feeding cows and peacocks before leaving for the Red Fort for India's 80th Independence Day celebrations.

In a post on Instagram, Modi said feeding the animals was part of his daily routine and that they appeared to realise he was leaving earlier than usual for the Independence Day programme.

âFeeding my friends every morning is a daily routine. Yesterday morning, they somehow realised I'm leaving early, so they came to meet me as I was leaving for the Red Fort,â Modi wrote.

The video showed the Prime Minister spending time with the animals at his 7, Lok Kalyan Marg residence before departing for the historic monument.

He was dressed in his traditional attire for the Independence Day celebrations.

âSpecial, as always!â Modi said at the end of his post.

The PM has also been increasingly active on Instagram in recent days, sharing selfie-style videos, personal reflections, GR and glimpses of his daily routine.

The social media post offered a personal glimpse of the Prime Minister's morning ahead of the formal Independence Day programme, which included the flag-hoisting ceremony and his address to the nation.





Modi later reached the Red Fort, where he hoisted the national flag from the ramparts as part of the 80th Independence Day celebrations. The ceremony was accompanied by a 21-gun salute using indigenous 105 mm Light Field Guns.

In his address, Modi outlined his government's priorities for India's development, with a focus on youth, manufacturing, technology, innovation and self-reliance. He also highlighted India's energy transition and plans to expand nuclear power capacity.

The Prime Minister spoke about strengthening domestic manufacturing and reducing dependence on external sources, while highlighting sectors including defence, food processing, connectivity, green and blue economy and technology.

He also stressed the goal of building a Viksit Bharat by 2047, when India will mark 100 years of independence.

World.title: ‘Congress should feel ashamed’: Amit Shah targets Sonia Gandhi over Vande Mataram row
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Union home minister

on Sunday launched a sharp attack on Congress over a controversy surrounding the rendition of Vande Mataram at the party's Independence Day event, accusing it of insulting the national song and alleging that the incident was driven by âvote-bankâ politics.

Addressing a rally in Chittorgarh, Rajasthan, Shah alleged that Congress leader

had asked party workers to stop the rendition while it was being sung at the Congress headquarters on Saturday.

âLook at their (Congress's) shamelessness. The anthem Vande Mataram was being sung at the

headquarters. During the anthem, Congress leader Sonia Gandhi told the Congress President to stop singing. We all just kept watching on TV,â Shah said.

He directly addressed Sonia Gandhi, saying, âSonia ji, 140 crore people are watching you. This sin you have committed will never be forgiven by the people of this country.â

âHow can anyone even dream of leaving the anthem Vande Mataram incomplete? The people of Congress should feel ashamed,â he added.

Shah also accused the Congress of having âforgotten Vande Mataram out of greed for vote banksâ and said the party should apologise to the people for allegedly insulting the national song.





Congress denies BJP's allegation

The controversy erupted on Saturday after the BJP shared video footage from the Congress's Independence Day programme at Indira Bhawan and alleged that Sonia Gandhi had objected while Vande Mataram was being played.

The Congress rejected the allegation and maintained that the full version of Vande Mataram was sung at the event.

Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the party's position on the song was rooted in its history and cited a 1937 meeting of the Congress Working Committee in Calcutta, attended by leaders including Mahatma Gandhi, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and Jawaharlal Nehru.

Ramesh said the CWC had decided, following advice from Rabindranath Tagore, that the opening stanzas of Vande Mataram would be sung at Congress sessions.

He also rejected the claim that Sonia Gandhi had sought to stop the song. According to Ramesh, she was asking party workers to arrange a chair for Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, who had been standing for some time.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

âThe full version was sung at Saturday's event, there is no question of a controversy over it,â Ramesh said.

BJP has continued to target the Congress over the incident, with party leaders accusing it of showing disrespect towards Vande Mataram.

The row comes shortly after Parliament passed legislation dealing with disrespect towards the national song.

The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was cleared by the Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha in July and accords Vande Mataram a status on par with the

national anthem

, Jana Gana Mana.

Shah's remarks came after he attended an event in Chittorgarh with Rajasthan chief minister Bhajanlal Sharma, where they unveiled a statue of former prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee on his death anniversary.

World.title: 'Apologise': Bankim Chandra descendant writes to Sonia Gandhi over Vande Mataram 'insult'
World.content:
NEW DELHI: West Bengal

MLA Sumitro Chatterjee on Sunday demanded an unconditional apology from senior Congress leader

for allegedly disrespecting

.

Chatterjee is a direct descendant of renowned poet Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, who wrote the national song.

In his letter, Chatterjee described the alleged incident on August 15, as the country celebrated its 80th Independence Day, as "not merely unfortunate but a shameless repetition of a historical mistake."

He stated that he was writing as an "ordinary citizen, a patriot and a direct descendant of Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay," and expressed "deep pain, emptiness, and anger" over the episode.

He termed Sonia Gandhi's alleged reluctance to fully recite "Vande Mataram" an "insult" to the sacrifices of martyrs such as Khudiram Bose.

Chatterjee also cited the song's role in the freedom movement, including its recitation by Sarala Devi Chaudhurani at the 1905 Benares Congress session, its singing by Bal Gangadhar Tilak's supporters during his 1909 sedition trial, and its use as a rallying cry by nationalist students at Hyderabad's Osmania University in 1938 despite the Nizam's restrictions.

He also referred to Rabindranath Tagore's rendition of the song at the 1896 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress.





Chatterjee further claimed that the Congress' so-called "dual policy" was not new, recalling that in 1937, the party had "bowed" to Mohammad Ali Jinnah's objections and truncated the song that October. He argued that the shadow of that "compromise" was visible again in the party's conduct.

Asserting that Vande Mataram was not the property of any one political party but the country's collective memory, Bankim Chandra's eternal legacy and a sacred national symbol earned through the blood and sacrifice of martyrs, Chatterjee maintained that respecting the song was tantamount to respecting the history of India's freedom struggle.

He warned that "history forgives no one" and that any leadership which fails to respect its own mantra of freedom would be pushed by history into "the darkness of oblivion."

Chatterjee added that the incident had "deeply" hurt the sentiments of the people of West Bengal and appealed to Gandhi to introspect and tender an unconditional apology to all countrymen, particularly the people of West Bengal, without any conditions.

The incident he referred to took place during Independence Day celebrations at the

Congress party

headquarters in Delhi. A video from the event went viral, with several BJP leaders and social media users alleging that there was "discomfort" and repeated attempts to stop the full version of Vande Mataram from being sung.

The 80th Independence Day marked the first time since independence that the national song was played at the official August 15 celebrations at Delhi's Red Fort. Vande Mataram was played both before and after Prime Minister Narendra Modi's address to the nation from the ramparts of the iconic monument.

World.title: Jharkhand protests continue: Students to gherao CM residence on August 20 if demands not met
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The protest by students and job aspirants over alleged irregularities in Jharkhand recruitment examinations entered its 23rd day on Sunday, with the agitators announcing plans to burn effigies of chief minister

and congress leader Rahul Gandhi across all 24 districts.

The protesters, under the banner of JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch, accused the ruling JMM-Congress alliance of failing to take âconcrete actionâ on their demands. They also announced plans to gherao Soren's residence in Ranchi on August 20 and demanded his resignation.

JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch leader Ravindra Paswan said the protesters would intensify their agitation unless their demands were addressed.

âWe will gherao the chief minister's residence on August 20.

We seek his resignation as both the JMM and the Congress are playing politics with us. We also demand that Rahul Gandhi withdraw support from the JMM-led coalition if the CM is not listening to him,â Paswan said.

The protesters are seeking cancellation of the JSSC-CGL examination and certain Jharkhand Public Service Commission examinations over alleged irregularities. They have also demanded a CBI probe or an inquiry by a panel of retired judges from outside Jharkhand.





Students and job aspirants held a 'Tiranga Yatra' in Ranchi on Saturday to mark India's 80th Independence Day and press for recruitment reforms. Thousands participated in the march from Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium to Albert Ekka Chowk, including two wheelchair-borne protesters who were on hunger strike.

Meanwhile, JLKM leader and student activist Devendra Mahto, who has been fasting for 15 days, alleged that police prevented him from joining the march after he tried to leave Sadar Hospital.

Videos purportedly showing Mahto in a confrontation with security personnel were circulated on social media. The protesters alleged police high-handedness during the Independence Day programme.

This comes as Jharkhand leader of opposition Babulal Marandi urged the state government to engage with the protesting aspirants.

âThe government should not remain adamant on its stance. It should pay attention to the students' demands...

The government should hold talks with the students without any delay,â Marandi told ANI.

However, the state government has said it is taking steps to strengthen the recruitment process. In his Independence Day address, Soren said questions over examination irregularities had shaken the trust of a generation of job aspirants.

He said investigations would be impartial and that those found guilty would face strict legal action, while cautioning against declaring anyone guilty without evidence.

The state government has proposed an annual examination calendar, technology-secured examinations, timely publication of answer keys and OMR sheets, and multi-level accountability.
