I believe these sea routes, nautical technology, and geographical knowledge helped lay the intellectual and technical foundations for the arrival of European explorers more than half a century later. However, this topic needs further research.

Sixth Tone: Since you mention the European explorers who came later, I have to raise a common critique: that unlike the explorers who launched Europe’s Age of Discovery, Zheng He’s expeditions — for all their grandeur — were a mere flash in the pan that left no lasting imprint. How do you see it?

Zou: This view is indeed very common. I would point out that Zheng He’s seven voyages were not merely official acts of diplomacy by the Ming court; they also facilitated exchanges of goods, species, and technologies between Asia and Africa on an unprecedented scale.

The exotic animals the fleet brought back from foreign lands — giraffes, lions, ostriches, zebras — and the rare plants and fruits such as pepper, sappanwood, and durian greatly enriched China’s native stock of species. Wherever it went, the fleet shared nautical and astronomical knowledge with local peoples, deepening mutual learning among the civilizations of Asia and Africa.

The most representative example of all this is blue-and-white porcelain. Zheng He’s fleet carried large quantities of porcelain into the Islamic world, while the cobalt pigment needed to produce blue-and-white ware, known as “Sumali blue,” originally came from Persia. This pattern of “bringing finished products out and importing raw materials in” was itself a cross-cultural dialogue of technology and aesthetics.

As the Ming dynasty’s most sought-after export in overseas markets, blue-and-white porcelain was among the important gifts carried on every mission. Pieces dating from the period of Zheng He’s voyages have been unearthed at Fustat in Egypt, at Aydhab in Sudan, at Aden on the Arabian Peninsula, and elsewhere.

The huge overseas demand, in turn, stimulated a massive increase in early Ming porcelain production: according to historical records, in 1433 alone the court ordered the firing of 443,500 pieces in a single decree.

What does this tell us? It shows that nearly a century before Columbus set sail, Zheng He’s fleet had already opened up the east-west sea routes of the Indian Ocean and built a regional network of trade and cultural exchange. I call this the “Zheng He exchange.”

Sixth Tone: That concept readily brings to mind the “Columbian exchange” — the massive exchange of people, plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia that opened up after Columbus’ voyages.

Zou: I did indeed borrow the theoretical framework of the “Columbian exchange,” but my concept points to an earlier wave of civilizational interaction — one that unfolded between Asia and Africa. In many respects, Zheng He was a key catalyst on the eve of globalization.

Of course, while the “Zheng He exchange” and the “Columbian exchange” share many similarities, their purposes were fundamentally different. Zheng He’s voyages never established colonies overseas, and they were extremely restrained in their use of force.

As you mentioned, many Chinese people feel rather regretful about this, believing it caused China to miss a golden opportunity to dominate the globe. Liu Cixin’s short science-fiction story “Xiyang” (“The Western Ocean”) expresses exactly this sentiment through an alternate-history framework: in the story, Zheng He’s fleet sails farther west from the East African coast, rounds the Cape of Good Hope, and eventually reaches Europe, defeats the combined Anglo-French forces, and conquers the European continent, turning China into an empire on which the sun never sets.

But in my view, Zheng He radiates the light of pacifism and cultural pluralism — and that is precisely where his example can offer inspiration for our own time.

(Header image: A statue of Zheng He in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, 2024. 500px Essential)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.title: An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.content:
“My contact lenses are comfortable even after wearing them all day. Do you want to try them?”

So says a young woman in glasses with transparent lenses, in response to a friend who says her contacts are painful. She then takes a contact box out of a black handbag, offers it, and says, “You can blink without worry.”

The endorsement seems genuine enough — except neither woman is real.

This , featuring the popular AI actress Fang Taozi endorsing colored contacts, has recently sparked controversy in China over whether an AI character can vouch for a product’s quality.

Released in late July on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by domestic contact lens brand Nutnutlook, the ad was taken down without comment last week.

In response, Chinese netizens criticized the  for using an AI avatar instead of a human actress. “What makes me uncomfortable is that someone without eyes now has the right to speak about eyes,” one user commented.

“AI doesn’t even know what it feels like to actually wear the product,” another wrote.

Neither the company behind the AI actress, Guangzhou-based World Media Film and TV Culture, nor the contacts brand has responded to the controversy.

The fictional 20-year-old Fang Taozi was unveiled in the AI short drama “The Laid-off Girl” in June this year. The series, which tells the story of a small-town girl moving to a fictional city to pursue a modeling career, has been viewed more than 320 million times on Douyin.

In the months following the series’ release, directed by popular content creator Fei Feifei, Fang’s personal Douyin account — created by companies to boost AI actors’popularity — gained more than 470,000 followers. Her account posts content ranging from so-called “behind-the-scenes” footage during the show’s production to snippets of her supposed daily life, such as making breakfast.

Fang has been lauded by fans for having, unlike many AI characters, moles and blemishes, giving her an imperfect and realistic appearance. In “The Laid-off Girl,” she struggles with relatable Chinese workplace challenges, such as pressure to attend business dinners and getting bullied by her colleagues.

Domestic media reported that on Juliang Xingtu, Douyin’s influencer marketing platform, Fang Taozi’s advertising rates are 168,000 yuan ($24,900) per video for clips under 20 seconds, 208,000 yuan for videos between 21 and 60 seconds, and 258,000 yuan for videos over 60 seconds — significantly higher than ad rates charged by most human influencers.

Ma Lihong, a senior partner at Beijing DHH Law Firm, told domestic media that, despite AI avatars not being considered people under Chinese law and therefore not legally considered  endorsers, the video could still constitute false advertising.

Ma added that advertisers are responsible for the truthfulness of their content and that by making a first-person claim about experiencing a product, the AI character could be seen as fabricating user experience. As such, the brand and the ’s producer could potentially be in violation of the law.

Compounding the severity of the issue, colored contact lenses are classified as Class III medical devices under China’s regulatory system, reserved for items that pose the highest risk to consumers. Actors are prohibited from recommending such products in s, a rule aimed at preventing brands from misleading consumers.

This is not the first time Chinese brands have experimented with AI-generated figures in advertising. Major bottled water company Nongfu Spring made headlines last year for using AI-generated images in promotional posters, while companies ranging from yogurt brands to office chair suppliers have collaborated with various AI-generated actors to endorse products and use slogans. Tutorials on using AI-generated videos for livestream commerce have also become common.

Entertainment law expert Qiu Zhimiao said AI-powered endorsements will become increasingly common, and regulating them is a new frontier. As s endorsed by virtual influencers exist in a legal gray area, he said, there is a need for clearer regulations.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot of the AI actress Fang Taozi in the  promoting colored contact lenses. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018881/1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.title: 1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018881/1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.content:
On a rain-washed weekend morning, mist clings to the peaks surrounding Ze’e Village in the southwestern Sichuan province. Over the sound of a rushing mountain stream, 24-year-old Jifu Lama leads a procession of children in matching kits. They navigate through rice paddies, along irrigation canals and over earthen mounds until they reach their destination: a soccer pitch carved out of a former cornfield.

Perched halfway up a mountain at an altitude of 1,300 meters, Lama’s pitch looks like a vibrant green terraced field folded into the sweeping landscape of Sichuan’s Daliangshan region. Standing in the center circle, the young coach directs his players — mostly children aged 6 to 13 from six neighboring Yi ethnic villages — to lace up their boots, arrange the cones and begin their warm-ups.

Ze’e Village is remote, accessible only by winding mountain roads, but the children’s imaginations stretch far beyond the peaks. During the buildup to the 2026 World Cup, the young athletes devoured match highlights on smartphones. Winning and losing are secondary to the star players: the children argue passionately over the goals scored by superstars like Cristiano Ronaldo, Kylian Mbappé, Lionel Messi and Harry Kane.

Seven-year-old Aluo, a first-grader with lightning-fast footwork, idolizes France’s Mbappé. His cousin, Yang Xiaojun, a skinny third-grader, became a die-hard Gareth Bale fan after watching a clip of the Welshman’s legendary bicycle kick.

When they score on this mountain pitch, the kids leap into the air, spinning to land in Cristiano Ronaldo’s iconic, arms-down “Siu” celebration.

For these children, soccer is bright spot in childhood marked by economic hardship. Local data shows rural per capita income in Daliangshan is around just 12,700 yuan ($1,770) a year. To make a living, parents migrate to factories in the southern Guangdong province, Wuhan in the central Hubei province, and the northern Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, returning only once a year for the traditional Yi New Year.

Raised by aging grandparents in households with multiple siblings, these “left-behind” children have few outlets for their energy. A piece of candy or a lucky draw at the school gate used to be the highlight of their week. Now, soccer offers them friendship, structure and a window to the outside world.

To keep them invested, Lama implemented a reward system. Players earn four points for every practice they attend, which they can exchange for free gear. That is how Hu Feifei, one of the girls who recently joined the squad, earned her jersey, socks and boots.

Hu remembers when the pitch was nothing but sand dumped over uneven soil. When it rained, they played in puddles and went home with scraped knees, but they were happy. Today, thanks to a corporate sponsor moved by the team’s story, they play on an artificial turf pitch that Lama proudly claims is “better than the ones in the county town.”

The sponsor discovered them because of Lama, who is no stranger to the spotlight. But his viral fame is a chapter of his life tinged with both pride and heartbreak.

Lama’s obsession began in middle school when a friend gifted him a Neymar Barcelona jersey. The self-described rebellious teen found his anchor in soccer. To play, he transferred to a vocational school with a pitch.

To master the game, he did the unthinkable and dropped out, hiked to an altitude of 2,000 meters, and built a wooden hut on a flat peak. There, with no electricity and relying on a wood fire to cook, he trained alone for days at a time. His goal was to become a professional soccer player within five years.

He documented his solitary, high-altitude drills on short-video platforms. The stark contrast between the primitive, breathtaking environment and the boy’s fluid footwork captivated the internet. He amassed hundreds of thousands of followers, drawing the attention of FIFA on the eve of the 2022 Qatar World Cup. At his peak, he was earning up to 6,000 yuan a month from his videos.

But soon this felt wrong, money was not why he played soccer. “It felt like I was using soccer to make a profit,” Lama says. “It betrayed my original love for the game.”

However, his online presence earned him a spot in professional tryouts. It was here that Lama’s dream collided with reality. “My technique was too poor, I couldn’t understand the tactics, and my receiving and passing were all wrong,” he said.

In May 2023, he finally earned a spot with Jingchuan Wenhui, a fourth-tier club in the Chinese Champions League. Stepping onto the pitch, the cheers of the fans made the experience feel unreal.

It lasted exactly 45 minutes. Half a match that Lama doesn’t dare to rewatch. “My muscles were constantly tense, and I felt I performed too poorly,” he said.

The experience made clarified the insurmountable chasm between himself and real professional players, he said he could “never keep up with the rhythm and physical confrontation.”

The failure was a brutal watershed moment. But instead of continuing to chase trials across the country, Lama packed his bags and looked back to the dirt fields of Ze’e Village.

Today, he serves as an unpaid, unofficial soccer coach for two local primary schools. He runs training sessions five days a week and spends his weekends driving his minivan across the mountains to ferry kids to and from practice.

The transition from viral star to grassroots coach hasn’t been easy. The internet money has dried up, and his public welfare coaching model is financially unsustainable. He is considering charging a modest annual fee of 1,200 yuan for new recruits this fall, but he agonizes over whether the cost will price out the very kids who need the game most. He regularly visits skeptical parents, trying to convince them that soccer isn’t a distraction, but a vital tool for development.

“I want these children to start changing from this generation,” Lama said. “I want them to learn manners and be driven.”

In a region where educational resources are sparse and academic struggles are common, Lama sees soccer as a safety net. His vision is already bearing fruit: four of his sixth-graders recently passed a specialized sports exam, securing them spots in a superior middle school in the county town.

Eventually, Lama plans to build a fully registered professional club. He has already chosen the name: Leke, the Yi word for plowshare.

It is a fitting moniker for a young man breaking tough ground. “I don’t even have a first team yet,” Lama said, looking out over the mist-covered pitch. “I’ve only just lifted my foot to take the first step, and it hasn’t even landed yet.”

This piece was originally published by Caixin Global. It is republished here with permission.

Reporter: Zheng Haipeng.

(Header image: Players from Jijia Primary School pose for a group photo, imitating the signature moves of their favorite soccer stars, Ze’e Village, Sichuan province, June 2026. Zheng Haipeng/Caixin)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.title: Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.content:
A Shanghai court has ordered a father to pay 4,000 yuan ($590) in damages and legal fees after urging other parents in a group chat to ostracize his son’s classmate, domestic media reported last week.

According to a ruling by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Court, the father was found to have infringed on the classmate’s right to reputation under China’s Civil Code. He was ordered to pay 2,000 yuan in emotional damages and 2,000 yuan in legal fees, as well as issue an apology to the boy.

A Beijing court handled a similar case in 2022, ordering two parents to apologize to a student after defaming them in a parent group on messaging app WeChat, widely used in China as a key channel for teachers and parents to exchange information and discuss student issues. However, they were not ordered to provide financial compensation.

The Shanghai dispute began after the father’s son, surnamed Zhang, was hit on the head with a tree branch by his middle school classmate, surnamed Zhao. After reviewing surveillance footage, teachers concluded that Zhao had not acted intentionally, domestic media reported.

Zhang’s father then attacked Zhao in a WeChat group of more than 80 parents. “This child has psychological problems,” he wrote in the group. “My son suffered a concussion after this student hit him with a stick.” He also claimed that the school was “well aware of this child’s mental health problems” and called on other parents to collectively demand that the school expel Zhao.

Zhao was subsequently isolated at school by his classmates and was unable to continue attending classes as normal. The boy later sued Zhang for infringing on his right to reputation.

Han Yini, the judge presiding over the case, told domestic media that the chat records from the parent group showed that Zhang’s remarks were “clearly derogatory and insulting” and “lacked sufficient factual basis.” The comments caused “panic” among other parents, some of whom demanded that Zhao’s parents provide a psychiatric assessment report of their son before he returned to school.

“This seriously damaged Zhao’s social reputation and placed significant stress on his studies, daily life, and friendships,” Han said.

“Student bullying includes not only physical conflict but also malicious exclusion and isolation through verbal or online means, which can harm minors both physically and psychologically,” said Zhang Jiawei, a judge specializing in juvenile and family cases at the court. He also called on schools to strengthen oversight and mediation.

School bullying has received growing attention in China in recent years. The revised Law on the Protection of Minors, which took effect in 2021, requires schools to establish mechanisms to prevent and address student bullying. In 2024, Chinese authorities launched a nationwide campaign targeting bullying and violence in schools.

Zhang added that when children have conflicts with others at school, parents should work with teachers to resolve them and, when necessary, seek help from educational authorities or judicial bodies.

“Every parent should understand that there are boundaries to what they can say and that infringement carries consequences. Respecting others is a prerequisite for protecting your own child,” Zhang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Kate3155/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Exposing the Revilla flood control contracts — the easy part
World.content:
For more than 20 years, it had been the talk not just in Cavite but in national political circles that the company of Princess Revilla (Rebecca Bautista-Ocampo) was getting contracts either from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) or from contractors who were bagging projects from the agency.

Her company, Graia Construction Corporation, was formed in 2003. That year, her father, Ramon Revilla Sr., was nearing the end of his final term as senator. He had been the longtime chairperson of the Senate committee on public works — a body that had a hand in shaping the budget of the DPWH. The following year, her brother Ramon “Bong” Revilla Jr. would be elected senator and “inherit” — yes, like a family property — the chairmanship.

As I said, however, these things were only talked about in frustrated or disgusted whispers. (I’ll spare you the Tagalog expressions we had heard, but you can use your imagination.)

Until the flood control scandal broke.

Until the public realized how this newest form of corruption, difficult to detect before now, was perfected during the Duterte administration.

Until Rappler called on citizens to help us verify the leads we had gotten or to give us new ones from their localities.

Until Rappler started a series on “policontractors” and their relatives cornering projects in their fiefdoms, and Caviteños started asking: “Kelan ‘nyo iimbestigahan ang mga Revilla? (Followed by unpublishable words…)”

Until a curious and courageous campus journalist from the University of the Philippines Manila named Axel Cainglet took on the challenge, and once and for all looked for solid proof of what, for the longest time, was only “common knowledge” of conflict of interest (which is a crime), if not alleged full-blown corruption.

Axel, news editor of The Manila Collegian, is under my mentorship in the current cycle of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship. Quick to absorb instructions and understand contexts and relationships, he extracted from the DPWH portal almost a decade’s worth of contracts that Graia Construction got from the agency. He cross-tabulated them per city and town.

Together, we plotted the contracts against a timeline of political events involving members of the Revilla clan who were in the legislature. And the result was this story, which was our most-read one, with impressive numbers, for a full day — from morning until late night: Bong Revilla’s sister bags almost P5-billion DPWH contract in family’s Cavite bailiwick.

Instantly, Rappler got thank you messages from Caviteños, and most readers were commenting with variations of “What have we been talking about?” and “This has been going on for so long.”

Thankfully, sources privy to the projects are offering us more information. Like they knew we will see this issue through.

Providentially, when an ABS-CBN reporter asked the Ombudsman about Rappler’s findings (start at 6:09 mark), he revealed that a team of prosecutors too had already been gathering evidence for months.

If you’d ask me, though, all this was the easy part. We expose, anti-corruption advocates are encouraged, citizens appreciate the work, government prosecutors start the arduous process of building a case…

And then the election comes. And voters still reelect the contractors or their relatives. And the national budget stays as “unsexy” news that most people choose not to follow. And contractors like Graia, even if projects are proven to be substandard or unfinished, continue getting DPWH projects unless they are banned.



I am not being pessimistic. I’m just trying to say, we — journalists, watchdogs, and every citizen who cares enough for clean and honest governance — need to continue the work, and work harder at what we do.

If you believe in Rappler’s work and the part that independent journalism plays in building a better nation, I hope you can support us by becoming a Rappler+ member or by contributing to our investigative journalism fund. – Rappler.com

Inside the Newsroom is a newsletter delivered straight to your inbox every week. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to manage your newsletter subscriptions.

World.title: How Janine Berdin learned to trust in her own artistry
World.content:
The breakout Bisaya artist shows why her voice, lyrics, and overall craft are here to stay

Cebuana singer-songwriter Janine Berdin has always been known for her iconic voice. From being the champion of Tawag ng Tanghalan in 2017 and a regular on ASAP Natin ‘To, her distinctive tone and vocal power has made her one of the most unique singers in OPM right now.

But with her first self-written album, LAB SONGS NG MGA TANGA, and her viral worldwide hit, “What if I miss you for the rest of my life?” she is growing into an artist with a masterful command of not only her vocals, but also her own sound and lyricism.

Her debut album is a sleeper hit full of grunge, pop punk, emo, and shoegaze influences, with the grit and intensity of the instrumentals perfectly matching Janine’s iconic vocals. However, it is the narratives contained in her album that make her an artist worth watching.

Vulnerable, relatable, raw, witty, and weirdly specific, Janine’s biggest strength as a songwriter is her generosity and ability to share her rich inner world with her audience.

Turning heartache into material

“I think everything we experience is the same with other people, just dressed differently or in a different font,” she said. “I just like to write about the stuff that I don’t hear being talked about yet. I needed something that could relate to my feelings. So I make it my responsibility to write a song that makes me feel like this.”

This is how she described the writing process for fan-favorite track “Friendship Over” on her deluxe album, MORE LAB SONGS NG MGA TANGA. It’s a riff-heavy pop confessional that captures so specifically the universal pain of growing apart and mourning a lost connection.

Janine’s songwriting is sincere and honest, as she usually gets material from her own personal experiences. But even if her lyrics come from very specific parts of her life (the line, “Di ka man lang nag-hi sa akin” was a real experience she had with an ex), her listeners can still deeply relate and connect with her songs.

When asked, though, if she finds it difficult or embarrassing to go back to her painful experiences to make art, she readily answered that she doesn’t.

“It’s okay, I got through it, that’s why I get to talk about it, and it might help someone out there who is going through the same things,” she said. “I am really okay with tapping into stuff I have moved on from, I’ve grown from, and it’s good writing material.”

One beautiful song of hers borne from a painful experience is “PROMISE..!!!” a track that has solidified itself in Janine’s discography as one of her most emotionally vulnerable, fragile, and, in her own words, “pathetic.” It carries in both its lyrics and instrumentation the desperation and denial of trying to hold on to someone who no longer wants to stay.

She shared that her painful past experiences have led her towards the life and identity she is grateful for today. “I learned how to respect myself. I love myself, I also met someone who takes good care of me. So thank you to the people who treated me like shit, I am now a grown woman.”

Make what we like, everything else will follow

This unapologetic sincerity and authenticity is what Janine and her team anchor themselves on as artists.

“I wanted to be the number one fan of my own songs,” Janine shared. “When it came to making this record, me and my bandmates were like, we have to make this honest and make stuff we like and not think of anything else. If we like it, then someone else will have to like it as well.”

A track that encapsulates this attitude perfectly is “Mirisi,” a standout trilingual track with lyrics in English, Filipino, and Bisaya. The word mirisi is a Bisaya term that captures the expression, “serves you right.”

“I built the song around the chorus, and for some reason I heard Bisaya in my head,” she said.

Born and raised in Cebu, the word mirisi sparked Janine’s imagination, as she has never encountered a direct translation in any other language she speaks. “’Mirisi’ is something I’m super proud of. It’s the only track I have produced.”

She shared that “Mirisi” is one of the songs that represents her growth as an artist who is now more confident in her choices, takes risks, and trusts her own vision. “I feel like I am most honest with my music, because I did grow up as a people pleaser.”

From other people’s expectations to voices that planted doubts in her heart, Janine has had to overcome loneliness and uncertainty in order to commit to her vision and believe in her own art, especially when success felt slow or out of reach.

“I was saying to people, ‘Okay lang naman talaga kung walang streams (it’s okay if there are no streams), cause what’s important is there are people who listen to me.’ But it came to a point where I thought, ‘What is my art for if no one else hears it?’ So I became very lonely for a time.”

There is no song that represents this triumph better than her breakout hit, “What if I miss you for the rest of my life?” Many people’s first encounter with this song was by stumbling upon it on social media, when Janine posted a performance snippet with the simple caption, “I wrote this song while shitting on the toilet.”

No one could scroll away, however, when they were attacked by Janine’s powerful vocals, her band going all out on the instrumentals, and, most of all, the heartwrenching lyrics of someone refusing to move on from a past relationship.

The song went viral all over the country and beyond, with international superstars like Demi Lovato, Lauren Jauregui, Doechii, and SZA praising Janine’s work.

As the song that pushed her voice further than it has gone before, Janine has always had faith in this track. “I really worked hard for this song and when no one believed in it, I believed in it the most, so I am grateful that it got to where it is now.”

All worth the wait

From shooting her own videos to promote the song with her friends and bandmates, Janine always knew this song was special. Watching the flood of streams and reactions to her song in real time kept driving her to tears.

“When I saw the streams, when I saw real people making edits to the song, it was a super emotional experience. And I knew people would connect to this song! I never stopped believing in it.”

Throughout the ups and downs of life, and the uncertainties that come with being a rising young artist in the Philippines, Janine’s greatest strength is her faith in her team and her vision.

“I told my band all the time, ‘Someday, someone will get it.’ So again, I knew it was going to come, because I was a fan of my music. But when it came, I wasn’t prepared for how big it was going to get.”

Her very first headline concert, “Concert ni Janine Berdin,” live at the New Frontier Theater on October 7, is a testament to just how much her music has finally reached the people who she knew would love it as much as she does.

By being brave enough to be honest, strong enough to have faith in her artistry, and possessing the power of both her words and her voice, Janine Berdin is on her way to becoming one of OPM’s most exciting rising stars. The day she had been waiting for, the day that people would finally “get” her music, looks like it’s finally arrived. – Rappler.com

Elise Suarez is a Rappler intern from Puerto Princesa City and a Humanities student of the University of Asia & the Pacific.

World.title: [Finterest] Concentrix rolls out matched PERA for employees. Is it time to start yours?
World.content:
In case you haven't heard of the hottest retirement savings program, PERA offers you a way to start investing for your retirement while getting tax advantages

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ biggest private employer is putting an increasingly used retirement product in front of tens of thousands of its workers.

Concentrix Philippines is rolling out an employer-matched Personal Equity and Retirement Account (PERA) for its employees nationwide through investment platform DragonFi, potentially giving the government’s tax-advantaged retirement program one of its biggest corporate pushes yet.

DragonFi and Concentrix described the initiative as the largest employer-matched PERA program offered to Filipino IT-BPM workers. Concentrix describes itself as the largest private employer in the Philippines across all industries, with over 100,000 employees in the country.

Bringing PERA into a workforce this large could be a big boost for a retirement program that has yet to gain mass adoption but is quickly growing. By June 30, 2026, the number of PERA contributors had surged to 30,055, nearly five times the 6,193 recorded a year earlier, with combined investments reaching P755.6 million, according to Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas data shared with Rappler.

So what exactly is PERA?

In a sense, PERA is the Philippine’s counterpart to tax-advantaged individual retirement accounts in other countries, like the 401(k) system in the US.

Created under the PERA Act of 2008, it is a voluntary retirement savings program meant to supplement SSS, GSIS, company retirement plans, and a worker’s other investments. Money placed in a PERA can be invested in qualified products, including money market, bond, and equity funds. Note, however, you can’t pick individual stocks and bonds to be included in your PERA.

One of its main attraction is the tax treatment.

An employee or self-employed Filipino may contribute up to P200,000 a year, while overseas Filipinos may contribute as much as P400,000. Qualified contributions earn a 5% tax credit, meaning someone contributing the full P200,000 may receive up to P10,000 in tax credits. Investment income earned by qualified PERA investments is also tax-exempt, as are qualified retirement withdrawals.

For those interested to open a PERA, just remember that it’s designed for retirement, not as a savings account that you can freely dip into.

To make a qualified tax-free withdrawal, a contributor generally has to be at least 55 years old and have contributed for at least five years. Early withdrawals can trigger penalties and the repayment of tax incentives, with limited exceptions such as prolonged hospitalization or permanent total disability. – Rappler.com

Finterest is Rappler’s series that demystifies the world of money and gives practical advice on managing your personal finances.

World.title: Ateneo plays through grief, prevails in first game since Baterbonia, Adili deaths
World.content:
TEAM. Kieffer Alas (1) and the Ateneo Blue Eagles before their game against Our Lady of Fatima University in the 2026 Pinoyliga Cup.

Ateneo beats Our Lady of Fatima University in the Pinoyliga Cup, marking the Blue Eagles' first competitive game since the team building incident that claimed the lives of Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili

MANILA, Philippines – Things have not felt normal for the Ateneo Blue Eagles since the deaths of Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili. But for at least 40 minutes, they did.

Ateneo returned to action and soared to a convincing 71-60 victory over the Our Lady of Fatima University in the Pinoyliga Cup at the Blue Eagle Gym on Sunday, August 16.

The win marked the first time the Blue Eagles, now coached by Louie Alas, played in a competitive game since the June 8 drowning incident that claimed the lives of Baterbonia, 18, and Adili, 21, during a team bulding activity in Dipaculao, Aurora.

“We did not talk after the game. We just praised God for allowing us to play,” said L. Alas in a mix of Filipino and English. “We’re very thankful.”

Play Video

Travis Roberts led the way with team-highs of 17 points and 7 rebounds, while Kieffer Alas supplied 12 points, 5 rebounds, and 2 assists as Ateneo shook off the jitters and pulled away in the fourth quarter.

OLFU remained on the Blue Eagles’ heels until the end of the third period, 47-50, before Ateneo unloaded a 19-7 run capped by back-to-back K. Alas buckets to mount a commanding 69-54 lead with under three minutes remaining.

“I expected us to struggle early on. But seeing the way we practiced over the last two weeks, I told them that we will eventually cope up with this,” said L. Alas.

Waki Espina added 9 points and 3 steals, Jared Bahay chimed in 7 points and 5 rebounds, while Ian Espina contributed 6 points, 3 rebounds, 3 steals, and 2 assists in the win that opened with a moment of silence for Baterbonia and Adili.

A sizable crowd, including school president Fr. Bobby Yap, turned up to give the Blue Eagles a morale boost, with the Ateneo Blue Babble Batallion leading the cheers.

Play Video

The school implemented strict protocols for the game and restricted media access, except for a brief interview reporters were able to conduct with L. Alas.

Looking back

The deaths of Baterbonia and Adili sparked public outcry and prompted probes by the National Bureau of Investigation and the Philippine National Police – Criminal Investigation and Detection Group, which looked into possible negligence involving Ateneo and former Blue Eagles head coach Tab Baldwin.

Ateneo also launched an internal fact-finding inquiry, requiring an extension before submitting its report to the UAAP.

The UAAP used those investigations as the basis for its decision to impose a lifetime ban on Baldwin and indefinitely suspend members of his coaching staff who were present during the team building, including assistant coaches Dean Castaño, Sandro Soriano, and Jon Jacinto.

While Baldwin has already resigned from his post and has not been seen around the Blue Eagles, Castaño, Soriano, and Jacinto showed up on Sunday and assisted L. Alas in calling the shots.

Ateneo is using the Pinoyliga Cup as a warm-up tournament as the Blue Eagles received the green light from the UAAP to compete in the upcoming Season 89, which is set to tip off in September.

The UAAP recognized that the remaining Ateneo players were merely “victims” as well, paving the way for the Blue Eagles’ continued participation. – Rappler.com

World.title: Lawyer, technologist Karlo Dizon wants to make PH law easier to understand with AI
World.content:
KARLO DIZON. Dizon is a Stanford Law graduate and currently serves on the NY Bar Association's emerging tech committee

Serving on the NY State Bar Association’s Committee on AI and Emerging Technologies, Karlo Dizon believes AI can widen access to the law, reshape legal education, and eventually help the government with legislation

MANILA, Philippines – For Karlo Dizon, the idea behind Kartilya.PH — a free research archive of selected Philippine legal materials powered with an AI search engine — began with a basic problem that the Philippines is still in the process of solving: widespread access to justice.

Dizon, a Filipino lawyer and technologist who was born in Bataan, and now moves between New York, the Philippines, and Guam, said he had seen relatives struggle to access legal services. For many people, hiring a lawyer is something they consider only in the most serious circumstances, he said.

But Dizon believes the law should not feel like an exclusive resource.

“The law is a public resource,” he said. “It’s publicly available.”

The problem, he argued, is that having the law publicly available is not the same as making it accessible.

People may know the question but it’s often intimidating to even attempt to begin looking for these legal answers.

That, Dizon said, is where AI can change the equation.

Dizon is a political science graduate from Yale, holds a masters in comparative politics from the London School of Economics, and a juris doctor from Stanford. He currently serves on the New York State Bar Association’s Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies.

Meanwhile, Rein Serrano is Kartilya’s tech lead, a graduate of the Ateneo de Manila University in Management Information Systems and a full-stack software engineer at Manulife.

Turning legal research into natural-language questions

Remember how AI made computing coding more accessible to people by letting people program using natural, everyday language?

Kartilya works like that. It turns legal language, which could be esoteric to lay people, into something far more understandable.

Instead of requiring a user to know the relevant doctrine or case citation, the platform allows them to ask a question in ordinary language and search a corpus of Philippine legal materials.

AI, Dizon said, allows people to approach legal information by asking a specific question in plain language.

Isn’t this something that a general use LLM like ChatGPT can already do?

What makes Kartilya unique is that it features a “structured corpus” that contains over 8,000 provisions, the 1987 Constitution, major Codes, statutes and rules, text from the LawPhil project including court decisions and a jurisprudence catalog of 4,164 records from 2019 through April 29, 2026. It’s a body of data that continues to be expanded as well.

Dizon explains: “Instead of having an unbounded LLM that searches its entire corpus of information, you have a more bounded LLM that searches only legal information — Philippine law in this case.”

Aside from a closed, protected database, Dizon also highlights other instruction layers for Kartilya that ultimately aims to strengthen its information retrieval, and information synthesis process to address the problem of hallucinations.

KARTILYA. A sample query on the Kartilya website.

“We added a verification layer where every single proposition that is presented to you is linked to an actual source [that you can look at],” Dizon said. The AI also checks that actual source before it’s ever presented to you. A more technical explanation can be found on the site.

Dizon acknowledged that the system can still encounter problems behind the scenes. Legal language can be extremely precise, and even seemingly minor differences in wording can matter. An AI system may treat words as interchangeable when lawyers would not.

That is why, he said, users are encouraged to inspect the underlying primary sources themselves.

Kartilya works under the philosophy that AI explanation is not meant to replace the law, but it is meant to make the law easier to reach.

“Primary sources are always going to be there,” Dizon said.

For privacy, search queries are immediately hashed into keys, making them non-readable to humans, and are deleted after approximately seven days. Public queries are never stored or viewed by the team.

Making lawyers more accessible, not obsolete

That distinction is also important to Dizon’s vision for the legal profession.

One of the common fears surrounding AI in law is that it will eliminate the need for lawyers. Dizon sees the possibility of the opposite happening.

A person might use the platform to understand a contract involving family property, or to get a basic sense of their rights in a dispute with a landlord. But when the matter involves criminal liability, significant amounts of money, numerous parties, or complex litigation, Dizon said, the need for a lawyer becomes greater.

“Just because people understand the legal process doesn’t mean that they have the time or the ability to go through the whole rigmarole of litigation,” he said.

There are filings to make, evidence to collect, witnesses to depose, and cases to pursue.

His hope is therefore that AI can lower the barriers to entering the legal system while creating more opportunities for lawyers.

Better access to information could potentially make legal services more competitive and affordable, while bringing more people into the system who previously might have been too intimidated or unable to afford representation.

Even the threat of legal action can be intimidating, Dizon noted. Simply being told that someone is taking you to court can be enough to discourage a person from pursuing something they may actually have a legal right to do.

More information, he believes, can make that process less frightening.

The next step: explain the law itself

Kartilya is still a work in progress.

Dizon said the platform has a few hundred regular users, with feedback generally positive. One recurring problem, however, is that a search can lead users to a judicial opinion or a provision in a code, only for them to encounter another wall of difficult legal language.

The next step, therefore, is to put AI tools directly on opinion and code pages.

The goal is to allow users to ask questions about particular provisions and have the system explain portions of a judicial opinion or statute.

Language accessibility is another part of the roadmap. Dizon said the team wants to make the platform available in Philippine languages, including Tagalog.

For now, the startup platform is being built by a small team of roughly four full-time people, along with interns, volunteers, and other contributors. The team has been developing Kartilya for about a year.

AI belongs in the law school, too

That experience informs Dizon’s view of another emerging debate: whether law schools should restrict students’ use of AI.

He pointed to the different approaches being taken by American universities. Some institutions have restricted AI use such as University of the Philippines, while others have been more open to students experimenting with the technology.

Dizon understands why schools are concerned but he also believes the legal profession has reached a point where avoiding AI altogether may leave students unprepared for the world they are about to enter.

“I think the reality is all the lawyers and all the judges are going to be using AI,” he said.

The question, in his view, is no longer simply whether students should use AI. It is how they can learn to reason and write effectively while using it.

Legal education has always adapted to technological changes, Dizon noted. Legal research once meant working through physical books. Technology eventually transformed that process, and AI is the latest major change.

He believes law schools should retain traditional approaches to teaching, but also create spaces — such as AI labs or dedicated programs — where students can develop the skills they will need in practice.

He also says they are exploring a version of Kartilya that could be enhanced for legislative use.

At the most immediate level, that could mean giving congressional offices better tools for legal research and bill drafting, as well as establishing integrity and traceability of legal documents.

The Filipino’s role in the AI race

Dizon’s ambitions for Kartilya are also tied to a broader question about the Philippines’ place in the AI economy.

He believes the country needs a national and sovereign AI strategy.

He pointed to countries such as Saudi Arabia that are investing heavily across the AI stack, from energy and chips to large language models.

The Philippines may not be able to compete with those countries in every part of that infrastructure.

But Dizon believes there are areas where the country has advantages — particularly language and the country’s broader educational and human-capital base.

That could mean developing AI systems and infrastructure around distinctly Philippine needs rather than simply importing technology built elsewhere.

Legal AI is just one possible example, and learnings from Kartilya, for instance, may be adapted and deployed in other settings.

Kartilya, for Dizon, is an attempt to rethink how Filipinos encounter the law: from something that can feel distant, technical and intimidating into something that can be searched, questioned and understood.

Dizon is also watching the possibility of a national legal AI database in the Philippines.

He wants to see a verified legal corpus become part of the country’s broader legal and governmental infrastructure, and hopes that if a national system is eventually created, some version of the ideas behind Kartilya will be part of it. – Rappler.com

World.title: North Korea’s Kim, Russia’s Putin reaffirm ties on Korean Liberation Day
World.content:
TIES. File photo shows North Korean leader Kim Jong Un with Russian President Vladimir Putin during their visit to Beijing to attend China's commemoration of the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II, in Beijing, China, September 3, 2025.

Pyongyang and Moscow have grown closer since the reclusive state began deploying troops and weapons to support Russia's war against Ukraine

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un reaffirmed the deepening of ties with Russia in a message to President Vladimir Putin as Pyongyang marked the anniversary of independence from Japan’s colonial rule, KCNA state news agency said on Sunday, August 16.

Kim was replying to a message of congratulations from Putin marking the 81st anniversary of Tokyo’s surrender in World War II. The Russian leader said the bond was forged as Soviet soldiers fought against Japan and that cooperation would continue “in all the sectors.”

The North Korean leader expressed hope for the future of ties that had “carried forward the history of common struggle for justice and precious traditions of friendship.”

Pyongyang and Moscow have grown closer since the reclusive state began deploying troops and weapons to support Russia’s war against Ukraine in what has been Pyongyang’s most significant involvement in a war since the 1950s.

The Russian ship Pallada arrived at Wonsan port for a goodwill visit on Saturday tied to the liberation anniversary, and was greeted by North Korean provincial officials and Russian embassy staff, KCNA said.

Also on Saturday, August 15, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for talks with the rival North aimed at peaceful coexistence, telling Seoul’s Liberation Day ceremony that the two Koreas need safeguards to prevent conflict and should work to replace their armistice with a “peace regime.”

Lee urged dialogue to formally end the 1950-1953 Korean War, which ended in a ceasefire but no peace treaty, and said the talks could explore ways to curb Pyongyang’s nuclear programme.

Pyongyang has rejected Lee’s overtures and criticized US-South Korean military exercises as provocations.

On Thursday, August 13, Putin drew Tokyo’s condemnation with a visit to an island off Hokkaido, claimed by Japan, that Moscow seized in the days after Japan’s 1945 surrender. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Two Pronged] Her emotional missteps from imagining a future he doesn’t want
World.content:
'He told me that he wasn't looking for an exclusive relationship... But hearing it felt like the air had been knocked out of me because it didn't seem to match the closeness I thought we had been building.'

Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.

Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.

Dear Dr. Holmes and Mr. Baer,

I’m writing because I’m trying to understand a reaction I recently had that feels completely out of character for me.

A few weeks ago, I met someone at a time when I was already under a great deal of stress from work. Being with him gave me a sense of calm that I hadn’t felt in a while. I wasn’t expecting much, but I found myself looking forward to spending time with him because, for a little while, everything else seemed quieter.

What confused me was how inconsistent things felt. There were times when he was incredibly warm and affectionate. He would initiate conversations, make plans for things we could do together, and make me feel like he genuinely wanted me in his life. Then, almost without warning, he would become distant. I found myself constantly trying to make sense of the change.

Eventually, he told me that he wasn’t looking for an exclusive relationship. He was honest about it, and I respected that. But hearing it felt like the air had been knocked out of me because it didn’t seem to match the closeness I thought we had been building. I realized that, somewhere along the way, I had begun imagining a future that apparently existed only in my own mind.

What has surprised me most is the intensity of my reaction. I’ve experienced rejection and heartbreak before, but I’ve usually been able to process them and move on without falling apart. This time has been different. I’ve been struggling to regain my emotional footing, and I can’t fully explain why.

I’m wondering whether this reaction has less to do with him and more to do with the state I was already in before we met. Is it possible that the comfort he provided became tied to my need for relief from everything else I was carrying? How should I understand the emotional impact of the inconsistency I experienced? And most importantly, how do I begin moving forward without getting stuck trying to make sense of what happened?

Thank you for taking the time to read this. I would greatly appreciate your perspective.

Sincerely,

Miss F

Dear Miss F,

First, you need to give yourself credit for the soul-searching you have already undertaken. You have suggested that there is a connection between your state of mind before you met this man (let’s call him Ed) and the outcome of the relationship you then established with him. You have also realized that the reason your reaction to the loss of the relationship, or rather your hopes for it, is greater than previous instances is due to more than just finding that Ed is not the viable long-term partner that you had thought he might be.

You have in addition concentrated on yourself rather than tried to blame Ed. He has ultimately behaved reasonably honestly even if it took him some time to tell you that he wasn’t looking for an exclusive relationship. There is no doubt that it would have made your life easier if he had done this earlier, but at least he came clean eventually and that alone redeems him somewhat.

Your reaction to the demise of your relationship with Ed does seem closely linked to your frame of mind before Ed. You were under stress, he provided comfort and distraction from the other things going on in your life and you benefited from this until he dashed your hopes (realistic or otherwise) for a future together. You were and are left facing your previous demons and, in addition, mourning the loss of a potential mate.

The way forward is perhaps to differentiate very clearly between the two problems. Try to block out your feelings and thoughts about Ed. The relationship is over. No looking back, no ‘what if’ musings. Instead, concentrate on resolving the issues you faced before Ed and now so that you can face the future with greater equanimity and contemplate new relationships on a more even keel.

In other words, put yourself first so that you can face the world from a better place.

Best of luck,

– JAF Baer

Dear Miss F,

Thank you very much for your letter. I agree with everything Mr Baer has written above — especially regarding your capacity to look at yourself unflinchingly.

What I would like to do is “explain his explanation” (Mr. Baer’s) by using Sternberg’s Triangular Theory of Love and how it weaves into your very own words.

We have used Sternberg’s theory many times in this column because to us it is the only theory of love (among thousands!) that has been accurately validated in 45 countries and counting. It suggests that interpersonal relationships are built on three core components: intimacy (emotional closeness), passion (physical attraction/romance), and commitment (the decision to maintain the relationship).

Here are the questions you asked in your letter:

Is it possible that the comfort he provided became tied to my need for relief from everything else I was carrying?

Mr. Baer has already answered this question. What I would like to answer is closely connected to this: “(EVEN if) I’ve experienced rejection and heartbreak before, but I’ve… been able to process them” WHY is this time different?

This time is different because this is the first time your actual self-concept has been affected. Your past relationships merely confirmed that “It is what it is; Love is complicated for women like me.”

But this relationship questions whether you are actually the woman you merely thought you were: a woman who welcomed boyfriends, but got over them quickly enough when they ceased being so.

This time you realized that you were much more than that: Yes, you welcomed boyfriends, but you needed much more than that. You need not just romance and passion that boyfriends provide, you also need the intimacy that true friendship brings.

How should I understand the emotional impact of the inconsistency I experienced?

By accepting the fact that, like many people, you are lonely. You need people to thrive. We all do because, as neuroscience has shown, our brains are wired to connect to others.

So, when a friend you thought you had no longer feels like a true friend, of course you feel it much more than merely losing a boyfriend. To you, Ed was not just possible (boyfriend) material.

To you, Ed was someone you felt emotionally close to (intimacy); someone you felt you could open up to about your fears and stress.

You wrote, “(Ed) gave me a sense of calm… because… everything else seemed quieter.” You can only feel this way if you feel safe. You felt safe with Ed; you felt seen by him, you could tell him things you couldn’t tell others.

What else is intimacy but this? Where everything is calm because you do not have to be hyper vigilant, because you both have each other’s back.

And most importantly, how do I begin moving forward without getting stuck trying to make sense of what happened?

By accepting all the above and realizing it, you did not need a guy who could whisper sweet nothings to you and make you kilig.

What you needed was a true friend. Period.

All the best,

– MG Holmes

– Rappler.com

Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

World.title: At first truth hearing, mother recounts PWD son’s death in Duterte’s drug war
World.content:
STILL GRIEVING. Luzviminda Siapo retells the story of her son Raymart, who was killed during former president Rodrigo Duterte's drug war in March 2017.

MANILA, Philippines – After nearly 10 years, Luzviminda Siapo had a chance to retell the story of how her son was killed under former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs.

Siapno shared the tragic fate of her son Raymart during the first public truth-telling session of the Philippine Truth and Reconciliation Commission on Friday, August 14. These sessions are part of the truth commission’s effort to document the lives of extrajudicial killing victims, as well as the lived realities of the loved ones they left behind. (READ: Here’s how a truth commission will investigate Duterte’s war on drugs)

Raymart, 18, was gunned down in Navotas City in March 2017 after being falsely accused of selling marijuana. He was among the thousands killed during Duterte’s war on drugs, during which the government officially recorded 6,252 deaths in police anti-drug operations as of May 31, 2022. Human rights groups estimate the true death toll, including vigilante-style killings, reached nearly 30,000.

“Sinong presidente mo? (Who’s your president?)” Luzviminda asked Raymart a decade ago. It was 2016, and he had just gotten his voter’s identification in time for the national elections.

“Si Duterte,” Raymart answered.

Raymart liked Duterte’s stance on drugs and his simplicity, so it was no surprise then that the former Davao mayor was the first – and last – president Raymand had voted for.

Siapo’s son suffered from a deformity. He had a clubfoot which is a condition “where a baby’s foot is fixed in a downward and inward position.” Despite this, Raymart still made the effort to help out with physically tasks, and was also preparing to go to work.

While Raymart was in the Philippines, Siapo was working in Kuwait as a domestic helper.

In March 2017, Siapo received a text from one of Raymart’s friends containing nothing but a crying emoji. Later on, another person told her that Raymart was killed.

Siapo recalled that gunmen in plainclothes surveyed their home. Later on, the assailants put on masks and went up to their house, slapped Raymart with a gun, then took him on a motorcycle.

Raymart was later found by his family in a funeral home – with a hole in his head.

“Sana kung may kasalanan anak ko, may due process din. (If my son had committed a crime, I wish he had been given due process),” said Siapo.

“Ang bilis. Ang bilis ng oras ng pagpatay nila. Ganoon silang kabilis pumatay ng tao. Wala silang awa eh. Hindi ko pa alam na may quota, may pera. Sabi nila sampung libo daw isang ulo. Naisip ko sana pinatubos niyo na lang po ‘yong anak ko, ‘di ba po? Kasi mayayakap ko pa kung kinulong man lang,” she added.

(It was quick. That’s how quickly they kill someone. They don’t show any mercy. I didn’t know yet that there was a quota, that there was money involved. They said it was P10,000 for a head. I thought ‘Why couldn’t they have made my son pay instead? I still could have hugged him if he was just brought to jail.)

Siapo found out that her son was included in the drug watchlist based on false accusations of peddling marijuana. The reports she obtained from the barangay, however, indicated that Raymart had a sachet of shabu (crystal meth) and a gun with him.

Raymart had previously been reported to the barangay for allegedly stealing his neighbor’s chicken, but he had never been involved with drugs, according to his family.

Siapo also alleged that police officers asked her to lie.

“Papalabasin natin na si PJ Fortaleza, ‘yong nagpa-report sa kanya sa barangay, siya ang nagpatay, at papalabasin natin na nandodoon siya nang time na namatay si Raymart,” Siapo recounted her conversation with cops.

(We’ll make it look like that a certain PJ Fortaleza, the one who reported Raymart to the barangay, was the killer.)

But Siapo said this was not the justice that she wanted. For her, the only way to bring justice to her son is if the real culprits are held accountable.

“One of the goals of these sessions is to awaken the conscience of those responsible for the killings, as well as to ensure that a culture of violence and human rights violations does not become normalized,” truth commission executive director Christopher Magno said in Filipino.

The sessions come as the Philippines prepares for the November 30 opening of Duterte’s trial before the International Criminal Court.

Play Video

Sloppy police probe

To help piece together the story of Raymart’s killing, forensic pathologist and truth commissioner Dr. Raquel Fortun presented her team’s findings after examining the teen’s remains.

The skull incision from the initial autopsy was improperly made, Fortun said. Additionally, the medico-legal report described Raymart as “fully nourished” which Fortun questioned because Raymart was thin.

During the public session, Fortun also said that there was no reconstruction of the shooting, nor initial attempts to confirm if there were drugs in Raymart’s system. This, amid the report that the victim was found with a sachet of shabu.

There were also no attempts to determine whether the drugs allegedly recovered from Raymart were actually his.

“Bottom line is, he still should not have been killed to begin with, but still, something as basic as [forensic toxicology], ginawa ba ‘yan? Hindi (Was that done? No),” she emphasized.

Despite the limited evidence and incomplete postmortem documents, Fortun confirmed that Raymart’s death was a homicide – caused by gunshot wounds in his head.

Several civil society members launched the truth commission in May in an effort to provide credible documentation of the killings linked to Duterte’s drug war. Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David, Bishop of Kalookan, serves as its convenor and adviser, while former International Criminal Court judge Raul Pangalangan serves at its chair.

The commission will continue its truth-telling sessions to humanize drug war victims, analyze evidence, and demand accountability and reforms. – Rappler.com

Isabel Victorino is a fourth year AB Communication student at Ateneo de Manila University and a writer for its school publication The GUIDON. She is currently a Rappler intern.

This story has been edited by a Rappler reporter and editor.

World.title: Scholars Call for Broader View of Golden Horde’s Legacy
World.content:
ASTANA – Three historians from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and the Republic of Tatarstan in Russia explored how the Golden Horde continues to shape the historical narratives and identities of their countries during a podcast organized by Kazakh historian and Golden Horde researcher Zhaksylyk Sabitov.

The discussion highlighted both the shared historical legacy of the medieval empire and the distinct national perspectives that have emerged across Central Asia and the Volga Region.

According to Damir Iskhakov, an ethnologist and researcher of Tatar ethnogenesis at the Marjani Institute of History in Kazan, perceptions of the Golden Horde have changed significantly in recent decades.

“There was a time when many Kazakhs believed their origins lay primarily with the Kipchaks or other earlier peoples rather than the Golden Horde. Today, historical evidence and the composition of Kazakh clans clearly demonstrate a direct connection with the Golden Horde,” he said.

He added that growing scholarly interest has strengthened understanding of the Golden Horde’s contribution to the formation of the Kazakh nation.

Gaibulla Babayarov, a specialist in ancient Turkic epigraphy and numismatics at the Institute of Oriental Studies in Tashkent, noted that bringing together experts from different countries enriches understanding of the Golden Horde.

“Each country has its own unique perspective, which makes discussions like this especially valuable,” Babayarov said.

Babayarov highlighted that the Golden Horde is often mistakenly viewed as unrelated to Uzbekistan’s history.

“In reality, the Golden Horde period played an important role in the ethnogenesis of the Uzbek people,” he said.

While most of present-day Uzbekistan belonged to the Chagatai Ulus, the country’s northwestern territories, particularly Northern Khorezm, were part of the Golden Horde. Many Uzbek clans originated in the Dasht-i Kipchak, with Babayarov estimating that nearly half of traditional Uzbek tribal groups trace their roots to that region.

“For this reason, the histories of the Golden Horde and the Chagatai Ulus should be studied together rather than separately. They share common roots and represent a shared historical heritage,” he said.

Clan system united Turkic peoples

The discussion also focused on the Golden Horde’s clan structure.

Iskhakov described the subject as one of the least studied areas of medieval history because of the limited number of surviving historical sources.

“One of our main tasks today is to trace how a relatively small number of original clans, perhaps 12 or 14, eventually evolved into the much larger clan system described in the Edige epic, which refers to the ‘Ninety-Clan Horde.’ What is remarkable is that many of these clans can still be traced among various Turkic peoples,” Iskhakov said.

He also noted that the Golden Horde was organized through a strict hierarchy of clans. The ruling dynasty was closely connected through marriage alliances with the leading emir families that helped govern the state.

Babayarov added that Soviet-era scholarship often overlooked clan history in Uzbekistan because Uzbeks were portrayed primarily as a settled people rather than a society with strong tribal traditions.

He noted that ethnonyms and clan names remain preserved in village names across much of Uzbekistan, particularly in the Samarkand, Kashkadarya and Surkhandarya regions.

Balancing genetics and history

Sabitov urged caution when interpreting genetic research in historical studies.

“Genetics is an important research tool, but it should not be used to determine who is or is not a ‘real’ representative of an ethnic group,” he said.

He noted that genetic studies often produce various conclusions depending on the questions researchers ask.

“If you search for similarities among Turkic peoples, you will find similarities. If you search for differences, you will find differences. Ethnicity cannot be reduced to DNA,” he said.

Iskhakov agreed, saying genetics is useful for tracing family relationships over several centuries but becomes much less reliable when applied to medieval populations.

“Ethnic identity is shaped primarily by shared historical memory, language and culture. Genetics represents only one small part of that much larger picture,” Iskhakov said.

Revisiting Tatar history

Iskhakov also recalled how Soviet historiography largely excluded the Golden Horde from the history of the Tatars.

He said that during the Stalin era, official scholarship promoted the theory that modern Tatars descended exclusively from the Volga Bulgars. While the Golden Horde was portrayed as unrelated to Tatar history.

Only after the collapse of the Soviet Union did historians begin integrating the Golden Horde into mainstream interpretations of Tatar ethnogenesis.

“Today, the Golden Horde occupies its rightful place in the multi-volume history of the Tatar people. We now recognize the contributions of the ancient Turks, the Bulgar period, the Kipchaks and the Golden Horde as equally important stages in our shared history,” Iskhakov said.

World.title: Archaeological Discoveries Across Kazakhstan Shed New Light on Medieval Life
World.content:
ASTANA – A series of recent archaeological discoveries across Kazakhstan is offering new insights into the history, culture and everyday life of communities that lived on the Great Steppe centuries ago.

Findings from archaeological sites in the Zhambyl, Turkistan and Pavlodar regions include medieval buildings, a mosque and paved streets, valuable artefacts and a remarkably preserved mobile dwelling associated with the Kimak-Kipchak period (9th-10th centuries). Together, the discoveries highlight the diversity of life in the medieval steppe and the region’s links with neighbouring civilisations.

Archaeologists working at the Akzhar settlement in Zhambyl Region have uncovered remains of structures dating to the 11th–12th centuries. The medieval settlement is located west of the Kurenbel village in the Zhualy district, between tributaries of the Akzhar River.

The excavations revealed structures made of mud brick, along with fragments of ceramics, iron and glass objects, stone tools and bones of domestic animals, reported the region’s Culture and Language Development Department. Researchers say the findings can help reconstruct the daily life of the people who inhabited the settlement during different periods.

The animal remains are of particular interest to researchers, as their study could provide information about the diet, economy and lifestyle of the settlement’s residents.

The excavations are being carried out as part of a scientific program studying the Syr Darya and Karatau regions in antiquity and the Middle Ages. Researchers expect the findings to help clarify Akzhar’s role in the development of medieval urban culture in the Karatau region.

Further south, archaeological work at the Otyrar settlement in the Turkistan Region has revealed several layers of historical development dating 13th-18th centuries.

Researchers identified five construction horizons containing residential and household areas, brick-paved streets and kilns used for firing bricks. One of the most notable discoveries was a collective burial site, known as a dakhma, identified for the first time at Otyrar.

At the lowest, fifth construction horizon, archaeologists uncovered the remains of a mosque dating to the Golden Horde period. A street paved with large stones led to the building and connected to a staircase made of fired bricks. According to the researchers, a paved street of this scale had not previously been documented at Otyrar.

The excavations also revealed painted window grilles, parts of inkpots, door or gate fittings, Chinese-style ceramic fragments, Chinese coins and coins minted in the names of rulers of the Golden Horde, a powerful state that dominated much of the Eurasian steppe from the 13th to 15th centuries.

One particularly notable discovery was a ring bearing an inscription, which researchers believe may have served as a seal in the medieval period.

The archaeological evidence points to Otyrar’s extensive connections with other parts of the region. Similar materials have been found at sites associated with Sogdiana, Tashkent, Fergana and Zhetysu, while imported objects and coins indicate the city’s participation in wider trade and cultural networks.

Researchers also believe the newly uncovered street could help reconstruct the layout of medieval Otyrar and identify commercial and public spaces that once stood along it. The excavations at the Otyrar settlement were conducted by a team led by Mukhtar Kozha, a professor and chief researcher at the Institute of Archaeology of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi International Kazakh-Turkish University.

In the Pavlodar Region, archaeologists have uncovered what researchers describe as an exceptionally rare example of a mobile dwelling from the Kimak-Kipchak period, reported the region’s press office.

The discovery was made at the Baidala burial ground in the Kenzhekol rural district of Pavlodar. The site is considered one of the significant archaeological monuments associated with the era of the Kimak Khaganate. According to researchers, the area may correspond to Imakia, described as a political center of the Kimak Khaganate, a medieval state or tribal confederation that existed roughly from the 9th to the early 11th century in what is now northeastern and central Kazakhstan and parts of western Siberia.

The most significant discovery is a fully preserved mobile dwelling consisting of a wooden wheeled structure with a tent-like covering. Archaeologists said its construction is similar to that of the traditional Kazakh yurt and that the discovery appears to be unprecedented in the archaeological record of the Eurasian steppe.

The dwelling was accompanied by a wooden saddle, stirrups, a bit, weapons, jewellery, silk textiles and other artefacts. These objects provide additional evidence about the material culture and everyday life of medieval nomadic communities. Before the discovery, knowledge about similar mobile dwellings largely came from written sources and schematic depictions.

Archaeological research at Baidala has been conducted for more than two decades led by archaeologist Timur Smagulov. Further excavations, conservation and restoration of the finds are planned, along with proposals to turn the complex into a museum site and develop it as an important historical and cultural heritage attraction.

The remains of buildings and streets reveal the organization of settled communities and their urban infrastructure, while the mobile dwelling offers a rare physical representation of nomadic life. Artefacts from Otyrar, meanwhile, point to the movement of goods, technologies and cultural influences across Central Asia and beyond.

For archaeologists, such discoveries are more than isolated objects or structures. They provide pieces of evidence that can be combined to reconstruct how people lived, travelled, traded and interacted across the Great Steppe.

While excavations and conservation work continue, researchers expect further discoveries to contribute to a more detailed understanding of Kazakhstan’s medieval heritage and its place in the broader history of Eurasia.

World.title: Preparing for Economy That Doesn’t Yet Exist: Why Kazakhstan’s Experiment Is Worth Watching
World.content:
One of the things that has surprised me most over the past year is how rarely my conversations with futurists actually stay focused on artificial intelligence. We usually begin there. We talk about generative models, autonomous agents, the next version of ChatGPT, the speed at which these systems are evolving. Yet after twenty or thirty minutes, AI almost disappears from the conversation. We find ourselves talking instead about labor markets, education, political institutions, governance and, eventually, something much larger than technology itself: the possibility that we are approaching the end of an economic model that has shaped modern societies for generations.

AI isn’t the story

That shift in perspective has been difficult to ignore. We often compare AI to the internet or smartphones because it makes the transformation easier to understand. Those technologies undoubtedly changed our lives. But they never challenged one of the central assumptions underpinning modern economies: that human labor is the primary engine through which value is created and wealth is distributed. Artificial intelligence might.

During one of our interviews, futurist Brett King made an observation that has stayed with me ever since. The more automation we introduce into the economy, he said, the less the traditional mechanics of capitalism function in the way they were originally designed. As he put it, it will be the end of capitalism as we know it. Whether or not one agrees with his conclusion is almost secondary.

The more interesting question is what governments should do if he is even partially right. Because history suggests that institutions rarely have the luxury of waiting until structural change is complete before deciding how to respond. By then, the transition is usually far more painful than it needed to be.

Perhaps this is why I have gradually become less interested in AI itself and more interested in leadership. Not political leadership in the conventional sense, but the ability of governments to think beyond immediate political cycles and prepare societies for an economy that does not yet fully exist.

Brett challenged another assumption that many of us have taken for granted over the last four decades: that markets, left largely to themselves, will eventually solve most problems.

“The free market hasn’t solved climate change. The free market hasn’t solved poverty. It hasn’t solved homelessness. This is not something that the free market is going to solve. This is a function of coordinated governance,” he told me.

It is a provocative argument, particularly at a time when governments around the world are still trying to determine how much they should regulate artificial intelligence and how much they should simply allow innovation to unfold. Yet there is something compelling about the distinction he makes.

Artificial intelligence is not disrupting a single industry. It is beginning to influence healthcare, transportation, logistics, finance, manufacturing, education and public administration simultaneously. Unlike previous technological revolutions, it does not fit neatly within the responsibility of one ministry or one regulator. It cuts across virtually every institution that modern states have spent decades building.

If that is true, then leadership acquires a different meaning. It becomes less about managing today’s economy efficiently and more about preparing citizens for tomorrow’s economy before it fully arrives. This is perhaps why Kazakhstan has become an unexpectedly interesting case study.

Preparing before the future arrives

For years, discussions about Kazakhstan’s future largely revolved around energy, critical minerals, connectivity and its geopolitical position between major powers.
