World.title: Death in Tasmanian prison after reports man 'unresponsive' in cell
World.content:
A 23-year-old man has died while being held in custody at the Hobart Reception Centre, Tasmania Police said.

Police said prison staff alerted them to the man's death after they found him unresponsive in his cell just before 11am on Sunday.

Tasmania Police Assistant Commissioner Doug Oosterloo said the deceased man was from New Norfolk, north of Hobart.

He had been arrested on Saturday in relation to a wounding incident in Claremont the day before, and was transferred to the Hobart Reception Centre about 5:30pm, police said.

The New Norfolk man had been in custody for one night before being found unresponsive. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"Ambulance Tasmania crews were called, Hobart uniform police attended and Hobart reception prison staff all attempted to revive the man," Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo said.

" But tragically those attempts were unsuccessful. "

Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo said forensic specialists, detectives from Tasmania Police's professional standards unit and the coroner had attended the scene.

"The professional standards investigation includes examining CCTV footage at Hobart Reception, records and interviewing all witnesses, and that is information that will come out in the investigation," he said.

Tasmania Prison Service acting director Tristan Bell said the service would not comment further, with the matter being referred to the coroner.

"On behalf of the Tasmania Prison Service, I extend my sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased man at this difficult time," Mr Bell said.

Claremont incident 'targeted', police say

On Friday about 5am, police responded to reports of an assault at a home on Curlew Parade, Claremont, which they believe to be a targeted incident.

Police said they were told two people had entered the residence and assaulted two occupants.

A man his 20s was shot in the hip and is now in hospital in a serious condition.

The other occupant, a woman in her 20s, was reportedly struck multiple times with the side of an axe.

She received medical treatment but was not hospitalised, police said.

Police did not confirm what role the deceased man was alleged to have played, if any, in the incident.

World.title: Shock defeat to Bangladesh reveals bigger picture hiding in plain sight
World.content:
You could pick a handful of moments during the first Test at Marrara Oval in Darwin where it was clear not everything was as it seemed on surface level.

On day two, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted off with his usual exuberance from the infield to chase down a shot that trickled towards the boundary.

The immaculately manicured outfield, offering a playing surface that was nigh on pristine, had already been praised for its lawn-like quality.

Mark Waugh on Fox Sports noted you could probably play bowls or tennis on it.

Yet as soon as Labuschagne slid for the ball, the ugly truth was revealed, as a huge clump of turf was ripped up in a heaped mass of mud and grass and injury potential.

This was a pattern repeated throughout the match: The outfield's undoubted beauty was only surface deep.

Australia's standing at the top of the Test match rankings may only be surface deep, as deep fissures have been revealed in Darwin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

An analogy to what transpired over the next four days, as the number nine-ranked Test team that were missing two of their best bowlers, thumped the world number one side at full strength on their own turf, could not have been clearer.

Bangladesh's stunning victory in Darwin has delivered Australian cricket the shock that it undoubtedly needed.

A team that arrived without fanfare or pedigree has slapped down the world's number one Test playing nation by playing simple, sensible Test cricket.

The bowling was slow but accurate. The batting, unspectacular but patient and disciplined.

The Tigers' attitude was exceptional.

As the growth of the big three has accelerated inequalities between the haves and have-nots of Test cricket, Bangladesh are one of those teams that have been left firmly on the outer, yet proved in Darwin that the paucity of opportunities that have come their way has in no way blunted their potency or hunger for success within the format.

They were here to play Test cricket and play it well.

Najmul Hossain Shanto led his team with skill and composure throughout. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Given it had been 23 years since they last played a Test on Australian soil, their commitment to playing such an impressive style against a country that has snubbed them for so long was more than admirable.

Credit for that has to go to coach Phil Simmons and unflappable skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto.

Shanto made correct decision after correct decision on the pitch, Bangladesh never succumbing to the pressure or enormity of what was transpiring around them right up until Mominul Haque crushed Beau Webster through the covers to seal victory, a simple hug between the two not out batters sufficing as the bench finally exploded in joy on the boundary.

Bangladesh's historic win deserves all the praise that will undoubtedly be heaped upon it, the context of which will forever be extraordinary.

Bangladesh held their nerve throughout a tense contest. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Legendary English cricket writer Neville Cardus once wrote that to properly consider Test cricket, you need to see the big picture.

"I wish to present the Test matches in their setting," he wrote in the introduction to his book chronicling the 1936/37 Ashes series.

"To me cricket must be put against a background."

So what is the background here for Australia?

Australia is about to embark on as busy a Test match year as they have ever had, playing as many as 20 Tests in the next 12 months.

From the Top End, the men's Test team will head to South Africa, play New Zealand and England at home, then face overseas tours to India and England for the Ashes in 2027.

It is a demanding schedule both as physically gruelling and mentally taxing as they come.

Steve Smith and Australia have a lot of thinking to do ahead of the next Test. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Starting off with a two-Test series against Bangladesh, a country Australia has only deigned to host once before for a Test series and only played against in red ball cricket six times in total before this week was considered by most to be a friendly warm up, a competitive practice during a winter sojourn in the Top End sun.

It is, of course, incredibly admirable Cricket Australia is taking Test matches to regions that cannot ever hope to host an Ashes contest.

For financial reasons as much as from a societal responsibility, playing these sorts of Tests in this continent's more remote, northern reaches is undoubtedly the right thing to do.

But maybe there is a sense that this is considered a form of benevolence to the lesser-populated areas of the nation.

Perhaps, for some, even playing Bangladesh is a form of charity to a nation that simply does not have the financial pull of the major nations, little more than an obligation to the World Test Championship.

Maybe, despite protestations to the contrary, that attitude sneaks into the minds of the players, so subliminally that they themselves do not even notice it.

Pat Cummins defended the team's preparation, but perhaps they didn't even realise they were underdone. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

For how can playing in front of about 5,000 spectators in a venue where only half the oval is bordered by a grandstand compare with the cathedral-like cavernous majesty of the MCG, or the lack of pressure contrast with the parochial furnace of a packed Gabba?

Marrara Oval offers neither the stately splendour of the Adelaide Oval or SCG, nor the admittedly under-populated grandiosity of the new Perth Stadium.

Darwin is definitively off-Broadway.

And although Australia's defeat didn't seem to be for lack of effort, the application and necessary quality was lacking throughout the match.

Horror drops from Steve Smith and Nathan Lyon were surely aberrations, but the lazy stroke play and jittery, muddled thinking of the batters was very not.

Steve Smith was not his usual best in the field. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

This shock to a team that has been creaking under the weight of their own success for a number of years now is one that has probably arrived eight months too late.

It was due last summer against England before those Bazballers tripped up over their own hubris.

A papering of the cracks was the result of that emphatic 4-1 Ashes victory, the foundations of sand upon which the top order was built were never tested, the supposedly seismic impact of a fired up England bowling attack never coming to bare, self-sabotaging itself amidst a storm of recriminations in the boozy sand of Noosa.

So on we continued. Australia's brittle batters went off to earn their coin in meaningly limited overs matches and failed to address the issues that have plagued them in red ball cricket, perhaps even accentuating the problems by promoting angled bats and rash shots.

Now the show moves to Mackay and presents Australia with an ever-bigger list of questions and problems to face.

Jake Weatherald's status as opener has to be looked at. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia were rusty and not up to speed in Darwin.

Even if Mackay's Harrup Park, the newest venue to host a men's Test in Australia, provides a suitably refreshed outlook and attitude from Australia next Saturday, will victory there do anything else other than to plaster even more paper over gaps that are swiftly turning into chasms?

It's been eight years since a rambunctious tour almost boiled over, a sorry spectacle that was quickly overshadowed by a sandpaper-scraping that was barely as coarse as the friction generated by two teams flirting on the edge of respectability throughout.

Any weakness in Australia's psyche will be ripe for exploitation in southern Africa, and the venom is unlikely to be as hidden as it was in the far north of Australia.

World.title: 'Eleventh hour' expert submission delays former Sydney nurses' trial
World.content:
The criminal trial of two former Sydney nurses accused of making menacing comments towards Israeli patients is expected to be delayed until next year, after a dispute over expert testimony on the Israel-Palestine conflict.

Bankstown Hospital nurses Sarah Abu Lebdeh and Ahmad Rashad Nadir were due to stand trial on August 31, but the date will now likely be pushed back after an "eleventh hour" submission of expert evidence.

A report from Dr Rodger Shanahan has been submitted at the last minute. (ABC News)

Mr Nadir's lawyer, Zemarai Khatiz, said the trial was vacated on Thursday after the Crown served an expert report compiled by Middle East analyst Rodger Shanahan at the last minute.

"The additional brief material was dated May 31 and provided to us on August 5," Mr Khatiz said.

He said the defence had not had enough time to properly assess the report before it would be used as evidence and would need time to secure its own expert.

"We have to obtain our expert in order to address the matters in the report," he said.

" It will probably take between two and three months for us to obtain our own expert. "

Dr Shanahan is also expected to be called as a witness at the trial.

Mr Khatiz (right) says they received the additional material on August 5. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

New trial date to be set

Ms Abu Lebdeh and Mr Nadir were charged after Israeli content creator Max Ilinsky, who goes by Max Veifer online, filmed the pair allegedly making threats against Israeli patients at Bankstown Hospital.

The video was filmed on the cam-chat app Chatroulette and drew international attention when it emerged in February 2025.

Both nurses have pleaded not guilty and were sacked following the incident.

The video was ruled admissible last month after previously being excluded on the grounds it was improperly obtained and breached privacy laws.

The matter will next be heard in Parramatta District Court on August 21, when a new trial date is expected to be set.

"It is anticipated that new trial will take place sometime in 2027," Mr Khatiz said.

World.title: Quick hits: Das's redemption and Mehid's Messi attempt
World.content:
Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them, as Mitch Starc's desperate review spoke volumes and Cameron Green's redemptive arc proved to be in vain.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test, as Bangladesh claimed a stunning victory, their first ever in a Test on Australian soil.

1. Das's day four redemption

Das made amends after missing a chance early on day four. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia began the day still 67 runs in arrears, knowing that any early slip-ups could prove fatal to their hopes of pulling off an unlikely escape.

So, Alex Carey's heart was surely in his mouth as the excellent Hasan Mahmud had him edging during the fourth over of the day.

It was a tough chance, but one experienced Bangladeshi wicketkeeper Litton Das would have been hopeful of gobbling up.

Das was too slow to react, and the ball flew past his outstretched left glove and to the boundary.

But Carey was unable to profit from that early slice of fortune, finding himself walking back to the pavilion just three overs later.

This time, Das made no mistake with what, probably, was a more difficult chance, with Carey feathering one through off the bowling of spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz.

It was a superb delivery from Mehidy, pitching and gripping and turning away from the Australian wicketkeeper.

Das had his redemption and Bangladesh was on its way.

2. Webster falls to a beauty

Mehidy produced a peach to dismiss Webster. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Spin bowling is an art form built on deception, with guile and sleight of hand as important as pin-point accuracy.

On a pitch offering few surprises and only the minimum of turn, it is the impetus of a genuine spinner to trick their way into the minds of their rivals.

Beau Webster had played sensibly through the first 20 balls of his innings, alert to the threat of Mehidy Hasan Miraz's off spinners.

Mehidy was probing at the off stump of Webster, but the ball that deceived him was simply wonderful.

Angling the ball so that the seam would not bite, Mehidy just pushed the ball through a couple of kilometres per hour faster than the balls before.

With no seam to grip, the ball skidded on, perhaps a little lower, and took the top of his off stump.

A master magician couldn't have disguised his intents better and Australia's tail was exposed.

3. Starc's desperate review

Australia began the second session with a 15-run lead and just three wickets in hand, requiring something very special from both Cam Green and Mitch Starc.

So, when Starc nicked off in the third over after lunch, the final nail was well and truly closing in on the Australian coffin.

There was a clear noise and a dramatic deviation, but Starc, well aware of the value of his wicket, decided to send the call upstairs.

Unlike Steve Smith on day three, who had so defiantly called for a review even before Kumar Dharmasena had raised his finger, Starc questioned this decision with embarrassment.

He began his walk from the middle with the review still underway.

There were no ghosts in the machine, no undetected front foot no ball, and Australia was in touching distance of a chastening defeat.

4. Mehidy's footwork lets him down

Given the magic that had been cascading from Mehidy's right hand all day, you wouldn't have put it past the off spinner from doing something special with his foot.

But Mehidy was more messy than Messi when presented with opportunity.

Nathan Lyon, new to crease, was slow to take off for a single, and there was a real chance of a run out, with a Bangladeshi fielder circling in the infield.

But the throw was off target, and Mehidy was forced to improvise, attempting to sidefoot the wayward effort towards the pegs.

Instead, the ball thudded into his ankle and fell limply to earth, Mehidy wincing as he returned to his mark.

It looked like a really painful one, but, thankfully, he was right to continue.

5. Green's drought-breaking ton

Cameron Green scored his first Test century since February 2024. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having not passed 50 in his previous 13 Test innings, Cameron Green's position in the side was very much a topic of conversation heading into this Test.

A jittery run-a-ball 13 in the first innings would have done little but amplify those calls for him to be replaced.

But on days three and four at Marrara, Green delivered everything that he has promised, a third Test century and first on home soil.

There was some luck, Green didn't look good last night and was delivered some divine intervention when an inside edge onto his leg stump didn't produce a wicket, the bail held in place by some benevolent force far in excess of that provided by mere gravity.

But since that fortuitous slice of relief, Green made hay, playing the ball teasingly late from under his eyes, and with the balance and poise of a man who deserves to be batting in Test cricket.

It was his first Test century since he scored 174 not out against New Zealand in Wellington back in February 2024.

World.title: She designed jumpers worn by Princess Diana and Olivia Newton-John, then lost everything
World.content:
Eighties knitwear designer Liz Newman walks into a gallery space hung with the quirky, colourful jumpers made from patterns she created decades ago.

She thought these designs were lost forever.

"I'm absolutely amazed, a bit overwhelmed, and just awe-struck," Ms Newman said, looking around at dozens of newly knitted jumpers sporting the Australiana themes she developed in her early 20s, and some well-kept originals.

Liz Newman at her surprise Knitwear: Back to the Future exhibition at the 2026 South Australian Living Artists Festival. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

At just 20, Liz Newman started a knitwear label that became globally renowned.

She said it really took off in the mid-80s when Hey Hey It's Saturday star Jacki MacDonald started wearing her jumpers.

"Every time Jacki wore one of the designs on Hey Hey, the Channel Nine switchboard would jam with people wanting to know where they could get the knitwear," Ms Newman said.

Liz Newman was a national and global success. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

From a boutique in Twin Street in the Adelaide CBD, she was selling jumpers to stars like ice-skating duo Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean, Olivia Newton-John, and even Princess Diana.

Stars align in the US

She ventured into the US at the time the Australian international hit Crocodile Dundee arrived in cinemas, with designs like "Australian pizza with the lot", a jumper covered with Aussie tourism icons.

"Australiana was very, very popular and Americans couldn't seem to get enough of anything Aussie," Ms Newman said.

"All the stars seemed to align, and it just took off."

Liz Newman's exhibition is being held in the Adelaide Hills until the end of August. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

At the height of her success, she was supplying 150 stores in the US, two Liz Newman boutiques in Sydney, one in Melbourne, another in Surfers Paradise and the original Adelaide store.

She was employing more than 500 hand knitters, many based in country locations around Australia, to make the jumpers using intarsia, a style of knitting complex patterns using multiple colours.

"It was a huge part of my life and an amazing time of my life, and then it all ended very quickly," Ms Newman said.

Hard times ahead

A culmination of unfortunate events, including the collapse of the SA Bank, led to the label's demise in the mid-1990s.

"The state bank was going under, and they took me with them," Ms Newman said.

Jayne Torvill, Christopher Dean, Olivia Newton-John, and Princess Diana are some celebrities who have worn Liz Newman's designs. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

"It was probably one of the worst periods of my life because I had worked so hard."

But there were more hard times to come.

In 2011 she was diagnosed with a brain tumour that she said was the size of an orange by the time it was eventually identified in an MRI scan.

She said the doctors likened it to dismantling a time bomb.

"They said, 'Liz you don't have that much time, there's been so much wear and tear on it, that it's likely to burst'.

"If I'd continued, I'd have three months left to live."

Rock bottom

After she recovered from the operation, she had to spend 14 months in brain injury rehab, learning how to do everything again.

"Even making a cup of coffee was a challenge," she said.

"I knew you needed a kettle, I knew you needed coffee and sugar and milk, but I couldn't remember what to do first."

Ms Newman said confronting her mortality led her to make some big life decisions.

"I made a promise to myself that I'd make big changes and leave a very unhappy relationship," she said.

It was not an easy journey.

At rock bottom, she was living in housing trust accommodation and surviving on the disability pension.

"It's been really hard. I don't have any superannuation, I don't have anything to fall back on, and surviving on a pension is really hard," she said.

Meanwhile, her now vintage jumpers were selling for huge sums of money, but Ms Newman had kept only six of them, and lamented the loss of the patterns, which had been sold off with the business while she was unwell.

"My cousin rang me, he works in South Korea, and he said there was a shop with one of my jumpers in the window and it was $1,000," she said.

Another turn of fate

A social media post and a chance encounter with vintage clothing collector and media personality Amanda Blair led to another turn of fate in Ms Newman’s life journey.

Ms Blair, an avid collector of 80s jumpers, had recently gifted a mohair Liz Newman featuring bears doing Aerobics Oz Style to friend and popular podcaster Monique Bowley, who posted it to Instagram.

Amanda Blair at the Liz Newman Knitwear: Back to the Future exhibition.

When Ms Newman introduced herself as the designer of the jumper, the story of the missing patterns intrigued Ms Blair, who already had a sizeable Liz Newman collection.

"I used to get on eBay and search for ugly Australian jumpers," Ms Blair said.

"That's not to say that Liz Newman jumpers are ugly, but I wanted to preserve some South Australian fashion history.

"I think I've watched CSI far too many times, and watched too many crime shows, and I'm like, 'I am going to find those patterns for her'.

"And I did. I found the patterns."

Amanda Blair gifted a Liz Newman jumper featuring bears doing aerobics to popular podcaster Monique Bowley, who posted it to Instagram. (Supplied: Instagram)

Facebook Marketplace led Ms Blair to a seller, who was helping an elderly couple who had bought the Liz Newman business after the state bank fiasco.

It turned out they still had the 300 patterns stored in the cellar of their home in Birdsville in the northern Adelaide Hills.

"Liz was huge nationally, and internationally, from Twin Street in Adelaide," Ms Blair said.

"These jumpers were worn in New York; they were worn on the catwalks of Paris.

"She really spearheaded the whole kind of fashion movement of Australiana jumpers.

" To be able to preserve that, and then say to this woman, 'Hey, guess what, I found your patterns, and they're coming back to you', it's just awesome. "

Twelve years after promising Ms Newman she would find her patterns, Amanda Blair not only returned the treasure trove of designs, but with the help of volunteers from the Hand Knitters Guild of South Australia, recreated 34 of her designs for a surprise exhibition.

Liz Newman's designs have been spotted in international vintage stores, still selling for large amounts of money. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

Ms Newman only learned about the project two months ago.

She says she didn't dream it would be so big.

"To meet Amanda and for all this to happen, and for her to know that she had found the patterns, and that secretly she was organising this incredible surprise, the amount of work that she did was just amazing.

"This has given me something to look forward to, the possibility of doing something else.

"I think the jumpers were fun, and now I'm starting to get that sense of fun back in my life."

World.title: Swans secure two home finals, Gulden picks up 47 touches in Dons demolition
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Sydney are guaranteed two home finals with their likely qualifying opponent being Brisbane Lions.

Melbourne’s premiership aspirations have been dealt a major blow after star forward Jacob van Rooyen was suspended for three matches for an ugly hit. Sydney already looked secure in second spot ahead of their clash with Essendon but they made sure even Harry Houdini could not break their lock on their ladder position with a 36-point win at the MCG. They sit two games clear of third place with one game remaining and are guaranteed two home finals with their likely qualifying opponent being the reigning back-to-back premiers, the Brisbane Lions. A blistering open quarter was the difference between the two teams as Sydney piled on nine goals to Essendon’s three to lead by 37 points at the first break. Cop that: An Essendon player feels the brunt of Sydney’s Chat Warner. Getty Images



At that point it looked like a massacre was in play as Charlie Curnow had added three goals to his Coleman Medal-winning tally and Chad Warner had chimed in for three majors himself. The ball was criss-crossing the MCG as Sydney moved the ball with ruthless efficiency in front of a low crowd (not unexpected) of 24,767 spectators and Errol Gulden looked in the mood to break his career best disposal tally of 42. Whether it was a case of Sydney dropping their foot off the accelerator or Essendon finding the brakes the game changed in the second quarter. Essendon began creating forward half turnovers as Zach Merrett and Will Setterfield made their Sydney opponents rush. Their efforts were admirable given the quality of the opposition and in the end the Bombers won the quarter by 13 points to get a sniff. When Will Setterfield kicked Essendon’s second goal in the second half, they had dragged the margin back to 11 points. It was built on the back of hard work with defender Zach Reid restricting Curnow and Vigo Visentini laying two of the biggest tackles an Essendon ruckman has laid in the one game for some time.



The 20-year-old, who also kicked his first AFL goal, humbled Sydney stars Tom Papley and Warner in the second and third quarters as the Bombers forced the harbour town team to wake up. Logan McDonald was the man who steadied the team with two score involvements that stretched the lead to 23 points. He handballed to Jai Serong who kicked a walk-in goal and then kicked a long goal from the boundary. With the threat extinguished the main interest became whether Gulden would break the metres gained record he holds and also lift his career best disposal tally above 42. He finished with 47 touches and the Swans are at the SCG for the next month at least, hoping to return to the MCG on the last Saturday in September. Star midfielder Isaac Heeney said he was excited at the prospect of having another crack at a grand final if they made it. “I think our game style suits [the MCG],” Isaac Heeney said on Fox Footy. “We have done a lot of work to make sure if we get back here on that last day, we will make sure we are mentally ready and physically really prepared.”



MRO verdict is in, and it’s not good news for the Dees Jon Pierik Melbourne’s premiership aspirations have been dealt a major blow after star forward Jacob van Rooyen was suspended for three matches for an ugly hit that ended Aliir Aliir’s 200th game celebrations prematurely. The Demons’ clinical 76-point demolition of Port Adelaide was overshadowed by the van Rooyen incident in which he leapt in the air, took his eye off the ball and carelessly made heavy contact with his hand to Aliir’s head in the second quarter. In trouble: Melbourne forward Jacob van Rooyen clashed with Port Adelaide’s Aliir Aliir. Fox Footy



Aliir lay on the ground for some time before being slowly helped to his feet and to the Power dugout shortly before half-time. Match review officer Michael Christian on Sunday graded the incident as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact, handing van Rooyen a major ban. With one game remaining in the home-and-away season, he appears likely to miss Melbourne’s first final since 2023. Related Article AFL 2026 Why the Hawks and Pies both won out of their historic draw The Demons have until Monday lunchtime to decide if the club will challenge the ban at the tribunal this week. The club was contacted for comment. “Jacob’s one of the nicest blokes you’ll meet in footy,” said van Rooyen’s teammate Bayley Fritsch, who booted four goals in the rout.



“I saw him go up to Aliir after the game to say sorry. Obviously, he didn’t mean it at all.” Van Rooyen, who was roundly booed for the remainder of the contest, apologised to Aliir twice – immediately for his spoil gone wrong, then again one-on-one after the game. Demons coach Steven King didn’t witness the collision real time, but it appears likely he’ll have to prepare for next Saturday’s clash with the Western Bulldogs and at least the start of the finals without the man who leads the Dees’ goalkicking leaderboard this season (42). “I haven’t really seen it, to be honest,” King said on Saturday night. “Obviously, Aliir went down, and it was really unfortunate for him, being such a brave intercept player.”



Big hit: Jacob Wehr and Balyn O’Brien rush to the aid of Aliir Aliir after the latter was hit. AFL Photos via Getty Images Power counterpart Josh Carr noticed Aliir wasn’t his usual ebullient self in the home rooms after the game. “He’s OK. He’s, obviously, a little bit flat and a bit quiet, but Aliir’s Aliir,” Carr said. “He’ll find a way to get himself up. This is the honest truth, but I haven’t looked at it (incident) closely, but at first thought I can see how it happens. “It didn’t look great, but I didn’t think it was overly (with) malice either.”



Meanwhile, Collingwood’s Beau McCreery has been fined $5000 for careless umpire contact for the third time this season. It is the Magpies’ fifth offence, putting them at risk of a big fine from the AFL. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: The knock on the door: 57 years on, a Vietnam War widow tells her story
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life The knock on the door: 57 years on, a Vietnam War widow tells her story Carolyn Webb August 16, 2026 — 7:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To this day, Lynne Moore can’t stand to watch images from July 20, 1969, of the first humans walking on the moon. Her husband, Private Ray Moore, was killed in action in the Vietnam War that week. Never forgotten: Lynne Moore, with her son Craig Moore, lays roses in memory of her husband, Ray Moore, at Croydon war memorial on Sunday. Chris Hopkins And so rather than evoking a sense of wonder, the moon landing reminds her of army officials arriving to break the bad news at her mother’s house in Kilsyth, in Melbourne’s east, which she was visiting. “It brings back the knock on the door,” Lynne says. “I have to walk away.”



War widows, she says, were expected to get on with their lives, but now at age 80, she is telling her story. The Ray Moore she loved was fun-loving, a hard worker and could talk to anyone. Ray Moore visited his children Rhonda, Craig and Gary at Holsworthy army base in Sydney two months before he died in 1969. She said it felt very emotional laying a bunch of roses – “Ray’s favourite flower” – with their son Craig and grandson Brendan at the Croydon war memorial on Sunday, at a ceremony for Vietnam Veterans’ Day. The family features in a new book, Vietnam – Long Hard Years Not Forgotten, about Lilydale region residents’ Vietnam War experiences.



“It’s nice to know Ray is going to be remembered now, for generations to come,” said Lynne, now a great-grandmother of eight, on Sunday. “He died for his country, and they should be proud of that.” On active duty: Moore posing in Vietnam with a Florida flag belonging to US soldiers. The book’s author, Lilydale RSL secretary Anthony McAleer told the service how in the early 1960s, Ray Moore and Michael Hannaford were teenage apprentices together in the same Croydon butcher shop. Years later Moore joined the army while Hannaford was conscripted. Hannaford, 21, was killed on December 14, 1968, when the tank he was driving hit a mine. He left a young wife, Margaret. Moore, 23, was shot dead by a Viet Cong sentry on July 24, 1969.



Ray and Lynne Moore had three children – Rhonda, aged three at the time, Craig, 2 and Gary, six months. Historian Anthony McAleer addresses the crowd at the Croydon service. Chris Hopkins Both widows suffered indignities, McAleer said, which was “a sad indictment” of institutions at the time. Before Moore’s burial, the army evicted Lynne from their house at Holsworthy army base in Sydney. She was ignored by older war widows, and even parents at her children’s school were hostile. How did she get through it?



“I think you put one foot in front of the other,” she said. “I had three children to look after. It was just something you did.” Margaret Hannaford, who attended Sunday’s service, tells in the book how someone from the army said Michael should be buried in a war cemetery in Vietnam, and so not ruin people’s Christmas in Australia. Vietnam War veterans marching from Croydon Oval to the service at the war memorial on Sunday. Chris Hopkins Margaret refused, and Michael’s funeral was held on Christmas Eve 1968 in a Croydon church. McAleer said it was important to remember the widows who were among the victims of the Vietnam War.



RSL Victoria senior vice-president Des Callaghan pointed out Tuesday is the 60th anniversary of the Battle of Long Tan, in which Australian soldiers bravely fought an overwhelming enemy force. It was a time to remember the 523 Australians who died on active duty in Vietnam, the 2400 who were wounded and service people who returned to an Australia that was divided about the war, Callaghan said. Australia had matured in its treatment of veterans. “We have learnt the vital truth that one can disagree with the politics of war without diminishing respect for the men and women who put on the uniform,” he said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: No Joshing: Draw confirms Carlton’s stunning run to AFL finals after parting ways with Voss
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 No Joshing: Draw confirms Carlton’s stunning run to AFL finals after parting ways with Voss Marc McGowan Updated August 16, 2026 — 7:56pm ,first published 6:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

A heart-stopping draw after a second-half arm wrestle with the Western Bulldogs has secured Carlton a wildcard berth and continued their unlikely revival under interim coach Josh Fraser. The Blues had one win from nine matches when Fraser took over in May after the club parted ways with Michael Voss. The 12.10 (82) deadlock at Marvel Stadium on Sunday means Carlton have 10 wins and a draw from 13 matches with the former Collingwood and Gold Coast ruckman in the coaches’ box. All square: The Bulldogs and Blues played out a draw. Getty Images “I’m really proud of the work that the [players] put in, and it’s been a collective,” Fraser said. “It’s the 23 who represent the club today, but it’s the entire playing list and their willingness and want to grow and improve certain parts of our game and drive standards [is impressive] – it’s been an incredible 13 weeks at this point.



Related Article AFL 2026 Swans secure two home finals, Gulden picks up 47 touches in Dons demolition “There’s a lot more work in front of us, but I think the players deserve an enormous amount of credit for the resilience they’ve shown, and the appetite to want to keep getting better.” The result not only locks Carlton into September action, but ends St Kilda’s and Greater Western Sydney’s finals hopes with one round left in the season. A Francis Evans snap at goal levelled the scores with about three minutes left – albeit with some confusion after teammate Wade Derksen claimed a mark, and dribbled the ball through – and set the scene for a thrilling climax. Neither team scored again, with Bulldogs star Ed Richards pinged for running too far in what proved effectively their final chance as he threatened to drive his side inside 50 with barely 90 seconds to go.



The Blues knew a draw would be enough to lock in their well-earned wildcard spot, and made their players aware of that in the dying stages as they went into preservation mode. View post on X “It was a bit weird. You don’t really celebrate draws too much, but we’re in [wildcard round], so we’re rapt as a group, and as a club,” Derksen told this masthead. Fraser was puzzled in the moment when Derksen marked the ball on the goal line, and even the man himself described his action as “random”. “Sometimes I do some random things. The boys pull me up on it a bit, but it was just a bit of a random action that came out,” Derksen said. “Once I saw [the ball] go over, I marked it just to have a bit of fun.”



Will Hayward soared onto Bulldog Ryley Sanders’ shoulders. AFL Photos Ex-Swan Will Hayward lodged a mark-of-the-year contender with a skyscraping vertical effort where his knees ended up on Bulldog Ryley Sanders’ shoulders in the third term – followed by a goal that tied the scores – but injured his right ankle in doing so, and took no further part. Fraser said it would be clearer on Monday what Hayward was dealing with, but that he was “sore” enough not to be able to return despite attempting some run-throughs along the boundary line. Fraser only days earlier finally threw his hat in the ring to be Carlton’s next senior coach, including presenting to the selection panel, and every positive result heightens his chances of being Voss’ permanent replacement. The 44-year-old has been at pains to avoid the club’s second-half surge being about him, but the Blues’ stunning transformation is intrinsically linked to him, particularly the ball-retention approach designed to tighten their defence. They racked up 146 marks and 310 uncontested possessions on Sunday.



“I think when you’re not getting results, you need to scratch the surface around why,” Fraser said. “But the culture internally, I’ve felt, has been quite strong. Sometimes, when you’re not getting results, it’s hard to know a different way. “They had an identity that was attached to contests and stoppage, which held us in good stead, and we just wanted to build that out … but we’ve still got to find the best version of ourselves that’s a consistent product on field, and we’re working towards that.” Derksen said Fraser had “done the group wonders”, including encouraging the players to embrace “blue-collar actions” and a mindset to get better each day.



Patrick Cripps, Sam Walsh, Blake Acres and George Hewett all won at least 30 disposals for Carlton, while Hayward slotted three goals from 14 disposals before exiting the contest. Richards was the Dogs’ standout with 31 touches and two goals, the second of them a brilliant effort on the run in the last term – after receiving a handball from Aaron Naughton – that briefly put Luke Beveridge’s men eight points up. The Bulldogs played without Marcus Bontempelli, who sat out as he manages a “grumbly” Achilles issue, knowing they were already assured of a wildcard spot. “If it’s still hanging around, and we feel like another week will help him prepare for the wildcard game, then we’ll probably rest him again,” Beveridge said.

Leigh Sales’ The Assembly has taken home the trophy for best factual or documentary program. This is quite the win for them given they were nominated last year, but weren’t quite able to clinch the win.

Accepting the award on behalf of the show, Leigh Sales thanked the celebrities who took part, as well as the fans.

“Thank you … to the celebrities who trust us and come in and do a two-hour interview where anything can be [asked of] them, and also to the public who have just gotten so behind this show. People stop me all the time to talk about it and say how much they appreciate the representation of the autistic community. So thank you very much,” the veteran journalist said.

For those who haven’t seen The Assembly, it follows Sales as she mentors a group of autistic journalism students who carry out unfiltered interviews with prominent public figures and celebrities. It beat out other titles such as But Also John Clarke and Revealed: Death Cap Murders, and is definitely worth a watch.

World.title: Plenty of fringe and a bit of leg: The Logies red carpet winners
World.content:
CultureTV & radioLogies Plenty of fringe and a bit of leg: The Logies red carpet winners Courtney Thompson Updated August 16, 2026 — 7:33pm ,first published 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Follow our live coverage of the 66th Annual TV Week Logie Awards here. Say what you will about the Logies red carpet, it’s never dull. Trading international luxury designers for local labels and couturiers, it serves as a reminder that not all Australian fashion is subtle. Before the ceremony at The Star in Sydney, here are the celebrities who emerged as outliers of style on Sunday. Philippa Northeast in Maticevski Photo: Getty Images



A standout moment from Australian Fashion Week was Toni Maticevski staging his first show in 10 years, bringing the audience to their feet. So it’s little surprise his custom dress for Philippa Northeast was a highlight at the Logies. The tiered baby pink gown had the architectural edge of Maticevski’s best work, but the feathered detailing added an element of whimsy that really took it to the next level. When Northeast moved, the texture and movement made it come alive. The My Brilliant Career actor kept her make-up and accessories minimal to great effect, keeping all eyes on that dress. Allison Langdon in Velani Photo: Getty Images



You pull no punches when nominated for the biggest award of the night, so naturally, Gold Logie nominee and A Current Affair host Allison Langdon looked like a knockout in custom Velani couture by designer Nicky Apostolopoulos. “It’s just a beautiful simple silhouette in a beautiful fabric,” Apostolopoulos says of the striking bronze column dress that features hand-beaded embellishments. “Ally really rocks a good gown.” Emma Harvie in Effie Kats Photo: Getty Images If you weren’t familiar with the work of Emma Harvie, her masterclass in understated elegance rectified that.



The actor, nominated for the best drama program award along with her RFDS castmates, emerged as a hero of refined style in a gorgeous, off-the-shoulder chocolate gown by Melbourne designer Effie Kats. Working with stylist Kerem Hulusi, Harvie paired her asymmetrical dress perfectly with jewel-toned Cleopatra’s Bling jewellery. Chloé Hayden in Romance Was Born and Ayesha Madon in Versace Chloé Hayden (left), Ayesha Madon and James Majoos. Getty Images for TV Week Following the final season of Heartbreak High, actors Ayesha Madon and Chloé Hayden proved playing to your strengths always pays off.



Madon paid tribute to past Logies looks in a glamorous Versace dress and Paspaley jewels. “We chose this dress because it’s fabulous,” Madon’s stylist, Tori Knowles, says simply. For her debut Logies appearance in 2023, Madon wore a modish polka-dot outfit from Dua Lipa’s Versace collection. Her choice this year felt more elevated, appropriately so given the graduation from her Heartbreak High roots. Meanwhile, Hayden, a longtime Romance Was Born fan, opted for its Still Life Rose dress. The one-of-a-kind bias cut apricot gown is made from a vintage Italian jacquard bedspread with sequined embroidery by Australian artist Laura Jones. Deborah Mailman in Maara Collective Photo: Sitthixay Ditthavong



If you’re going to make a statement, a custom sequined tuxedo is the way to go. For the occasion of becoming the first Indigenous inductee to the Logies Hall of Fame, Deborah Mailman wore a striking custom Maara Collective tuxedo suit, designed by Yuwaalaraay creative director Julie Shaw. “Deb really wanted to wear an Indigenous designer this year and we both love sequins,” stylist Donny Galella explains. “We were so excited to create this custom look for her to receive her special honour,” Shaw adds. “We wanted Deb to feel empowered and glamorous up on that stage.” See the rest of the red carpet moments

World.title: ‘I’ve fallen in love with the trade’: The AI-proof job that 30,000 more Australians took up last year
World.content:
Exclusive NationalJobs ‘I’ve fallen in love with the trade’: The AI-proof job that 30,000 more Australians took up last year Sally Rawsthorne August 16, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Extremely early starts on frigid days, crawling in roof cavities, and bad-tempered dogs – according to the hundreds of Day in My Life videos that populate the internet, these are common realities in the workplace for Australia’s electricians. Despite the hazards (which also include risk of electrocution or severe burns from live wires, breathing in toxic building materials, and falls from dangerous heights), being an electrician has never been more popular. Electrical apprentice Kaitlyn McMahon at BlueScope Steel, Australia’s largest crude steel production plant. Martin Feld Government datasets analysed by KPMG show that after a stable period of about 150,000 sparkies nationwide, the number of electricians across the country exploded to 184,000 in 2025. This is playing out locally – more than 11,000 apprentices were enrolled at TAFE NSW to become electricians last year, an increase of 4.5 per cent since 2021.



“The number of electrical apprentices waiting more than six months to commence training is falling – from almost 1000 in 2022 to none this year,” NSW Skills Minister Steve Whan said. Kaitlyn McMahon, 31, is among the largest cohort of electricians in Australia’s history. Inspired by her father, McMahon has a history of working on heavy machinery – including Victoria’s iconic Puffing Billy train, and later trucks. She then moved to the rail at Port Kembla’s steelworks, where she now works as a fourth-year apprentice electrician with BlueScope. “I really wanted to challenge myself … I’ve just fallen in love with the trade,” she said.



KPMG economist Terry Rawnsley said several factors were behind the large jump in numbers since 2022. Related Article Exclusive

Graduates AI is cutting graduate jobs. These are the skills young people will need “One is that during that period, we’ve seen heaps of demand for residential construction – new builds, a big surge of renovations and knockdown-rebuilds,” he said. “The sector provided people with a certainty: there’s going to be jobs for me over the next two or three years. That’s also lined up with Free TAFE. Those things help to shift people’s perceptions that a trade is a good way to earn a wage and get ahead.” Beyond construction, there is demand for electricians in mining, solar farming, data centres and upgrading electrical networks.



It is also work that cannot – yet – be done by AI. “It’s at far less risk of being disrupted than your traditional white-collar job. The robots can’t get in there and rewire a house just yet,” Rawnsley said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Swans secure two home finals, Gulden picks up 47 touches in Dons demolition
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Sydney are guaranteed two home finals with their likely qualifying opponent being Brisbane Lions.

Melbourne’s premiership aspirations have been dealt a major blow after star forward Jacob van Rooyen was suspended for three matches for an ugly hit. Sydney already looked secure in second spot ahead of their clash with Essendon but they made sure even Harry Houdini could not break their lock on their ladder position with a 36-point win at the MCG. They sit two games clear of third place with one game remaining and are guaranteed two home finals with their likely qualifying opponent being the reigning back-to-back premiers, the Brisbane Lions. A blistering open quarter was the difference between the two teams as Sydney piled on nine goals to Essendon’s three to lead by 37 points at the first break. Cop that: An Essendon player feels the brunt of Sydney’s Chat Warner. Getty Images



At that point it looked like a massacre was in play as Charlie Curnow had added three goals to his Coleman Medal-winning tally and Chad Warner had chimed in for three majors himself. The ball was criss-crossing the MCG as Sydney moved the ball with ruthless efficiency in front of a low crowd (not unexpected) of 24,767 spectators and Errol Gulden looked in the mood to break his career best disposal tally of 42. Whether it was a case of Sydney dropping their foot off the accelerator or Essendon finding the brakes the game changed in the second quarter. Essendon began creating forward half turnovers as Zach Merrett and Will Setterfield made their Sydney opponents rush. Their efforts were admirable given the quality of the opposition and in the end the Bombers won the quarter by 13 points to get a sniff. When Will Setterfield kicked Essendon’s second goal in the second half, they had dragged the margin back to 11 points. It was built on the back of hard work with defender Zach Reid restricting Curnow and Vigo Visentini laying two of the biggest tackles an Essendon ruckman has laid in the one game for some time.



The 20-year-old, who also kicked his first AFL goal, humbled Sydney stars Tom Papley and Warner in the second and third quarters as the Bombers forced the harbour town team to wake up. Logan McDonald was the man who steadied the team with two score involvements that stretched the lead to 23 points. He handballed to Jai Serong who kicked a walk-in goal and then kicked a long goal from the boundary. With the threat extinguished the main interest became whether Gulden would break the metres gained record he holds and also lift his career best disposal tally above 42. He finished with 47 touches and the Swans are at the SCG for the next month at least, hoping to return to the MCG on the last Saturday in September. Star midfielder Isaac Heeney said he was excited at the prospect of having another crack at a grand final if they made it. “I think our game style suits [the MCG],” Isaac Heeney said on Fox Footy. “We have done a lot of work to make sure if we get back here on that last day, we will make sure we are mentally ready and physically really prepared.”



MRO verdict is in, and it’s not good news for the Dees Jon Pierik Melbourne’s premiership aspirations have been dealt a major blow after star forward Jacob van Rooyen was suspended for three matches for an ugly hit that ended Aliir Aliir’s 200th game celebrations prematurely. The Demons’ clinical 76-point demolition of Port Adelaide was overshadowed by the van Rooyen incident in which he leapt in the air, took his eye off the ball and carelessly made heavy contact with his hand to Aliir’s head in the second quarter. In trouble: Melbourne forward Jacob van Rooyen clashed with Port Adelaide’s Aliir Aliir. Fox Footy



Aliir lay on the ground for some time before being slowly helped to his feet and to the Power dugout shortly before half-time. Match review officer Michael Christian on Sunday graded the incident as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact, handing van Rooyen a major ban. With one game remaining in the home-and-away season, he appears likely to miss Melbourne’s first final since 2023. Related Article AFL 2026 Why the Hawks and Pies both won out of their historic draw The Demons have until Monday lunchtime to decide if the club will challenge the ban at the tribunal this week. The club was contacted for comment. “Jacob’s one of the nicest blokes you’ll meet in footy,” said van Rooyen’s teammate Bayley Fritsch, who booted four goals in the rout.



“I saw him go up to Aliir after the game to say sorry. Obviously, he didn’t mean it at all.” Van Rooyen, who was roundly booed for the remainder of the contest, apologised to Aliir twice – immediately for his spoil gone wrong, then again one-on-one after the game. Demons coach Steven King didn’t witness the collision real time, but it appears likely he’ll have to prepare for next Saturday’s clash with the Western Bulldogs and at least the start of the finals without the man who leads the Dees’ goalkicking leaderboard this season (42). “I haven’t really seen it, to be honest,” King said on Saturday night. “Obviously, Aliir went down, and it was really unfortunate for him, being such a brave intercept player.”



Big hit: Jacob Wehr and Balyn O’Brien rush to the aid of Aliir Aliir after the latter was hit. AFL Photos via Getty Images Power counterpart Josh Carr noticed Aliir wasn’t his usual ebullient self in the home rooms after the game. “He’s OK. He’s, obviously, a little bit flat and a bit quiet, but Aliir’s Aliir,” Carr said. “He’ll find a way to get himself up. This is the honest truth, but I haven’t looked at it (incident) closely, but at first thought I can see how it happens. “It didn’t look great, but I didn’t think it was overly (with) malice either.”



Meanwhile, Collingwood’s Beau McCreery has been fined $5000 for careless umpire contact for the third time this season. It is the Magpies’ fifth offence, putting them at risk of a big fine from the AFL. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Private school validates division and prejudice
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Private school validates division and prejudice August 16, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. EDUCATION Your correspondent posits that by sending their children to private schools (Letters, ″⁣Private benefits″⁣, 15/8) parents are alleviating ″⁣strain″⁣ on state schools.

I have a family member who has taught in government schools for 25 years, so I am well aware of ″⁣strains″⁣ of a different kind resulting from long-standing inequitable underfunding of facilities, resources and salaries.

Our society is becoming increasingly divided between the haves and have-nots, exacerbated by odious comments from public figures glibly dismissing the needs of those who have less.

The appalling mismatch of grossly inequitable education funding is a blatant example of one sector of society seeing itself as more worthy than others.

Thus, we are ripe for the picking by populist politics.

Jane Ross, San Remo State school parents provide for private school luxury

Re Letters, ″⁣Private benefits″⁣, 15/8: I have zero sympathy, let alone any thanks to offer, to parents who think they make a ″⁣considerable sacrifice″⁣ to supposedly ease the burden on public schools by sending their offspring to schools with all the bells and whistles and everything that opens and shuts.

Whole families have to live on what they spend to send one child to a private school. Through their taxes, parents of government school children contribute not only to the basic education of all children but also to the state-of-the-art facilities at private schools – without their children receiving any benefit from the latter.

There would be no need for those enclaves of conspicuous wealth if even half of that ″⁣considerable sacrifice″⁣ went to government schools which already do a remarkable job in spite of their conspicuous under-resourcing.

Margaret Callinan, Hawthorn



If only public schools were better funded

Is your correspondent aware that many parents who send their children to private schools do so because public schools are underfunded? (Letters, 15/8). According to research commissioned by The Australia Institute, around one-third of parents with children at private schools would have chosen public schools if they were better funded.

James Proctor, Brown Hill Private school is social segregation

The latest scandals of elite private school boys highlight the problems that we are building for ourselves in the future in deepening divisions and prejudice in our community.

If nearly 30 per cent of young people attend these ethnic, religious, gender or class divided schools, how can we then imagine that this will not carry on into the future?

What we experience in our youth goes deep into our psyche in ways we are hardly aware of.

Our schools should be places where young people from all backgrounds get to know, tolerate and value each other.

Schools in Finland have a global reputation for quality and performance. Private schools are virtually unknown there. The clincher is that their public schools are properly funded and respected.

David Scott, Eltham Applaud protesting school students

Your correspondent (Letters, 15/8) suggested that parents should be ashamed that their under voting-aged children took part in a protest.

I would be as proud as punch if my children felt so strongly about an issue, affecting the society in which they live, to go out and protest whether they are old enough to vote or not.

Julian Guy, Mt Eliza THE FORUM Toll cap promise

Re ″⁣Road tolls to be capped at $50 weekly under Coalition commuter plan″⁣, 16/8. The Coalition plan to replicate Sydney’s $50 weekly toll cap in Melbourne is an uninspired piece of policy copying that misunderstands Melbourne’s road transport system.

Sydney’s cap responds to geographic barriers that funnel drivers into unavoidable tollways. Melbourne is fundamentally different. Our road network offers far stronger arterials and freeway alternatives, and toll roads provide convenience rather than essentiality.

Additionally, there are fundamental issues relating to problematic transport engineering and transport economics distortions, coupled with the absurdity of taxpayers subsidising Transurban.

Carlo Ursida, Kensington



Toll companies’ benefit

Perhaps it’s unsurprising that the Coalition is pledging to reimburse drivers who use Melbourne’s toll roads up to $3000 per year. Not only will this effectively transfer public money into the coffers of the highly profitable private toll road companies, but it will encourage more drivers to hit the road and away from public transport, thereby increasing traffic congestion and increasing petrol and diesel fuel usage.

Noting the level of donations to the Coalition parties by both the tolling companies and those that sell such liquid fuel, the cynic in me cannot help thinking that this is a factor in the Coalition’s policy.

Kevin Bailey, Croydon A stupid idea

No state Liberal Party, you do not need to spend $90 million a year (that Victoria cannot afford) to subsidise toll road users. If the example of ″⁣office worker from Glen Iris″⁣ in The Age report (16/8) chooses to drive to the CBD instead of spending half the cost of that on a train or tram fare, why should other taxpayers pay for that?

Stupid ideas like that show that you’re really not ready to take the reins in November.

Greg Smith, Caulfield South Culture clutch

My late mother was a third-generation Australian. Her Anglo-Celtic ancestors arrived by boat in the 1850s and became pioneering farmers. Two of her Australian uncles died in France and Belgium during the Great War. She joined the Women’s Auxiliary Australian Air Force during WWII where she became a sergeant. Her Australian patriotism could never be questioned. However, even as late as the 1970s, when required to nominate her (and my) nationality on official forms, she wrote ″⁣British Subject″⁣ in firm capital letters. One Nation’s requirement that newly arrived Australians ″⁣adapt to one cultural identity″⁣ may require some patience.

Graeme Betts, Shepparton One-eyed Hughes

Re ″⁣Dave Hughes to campaign for Liberals in Victorian election″⁣, (16/8). While I understand Dave Hughes’ view about Labor’s mistake, I also think he’s being one-eyed about it. Both the Labor and Liberal parties are fearful of being seen as cowardly in the face of our powerful business and union lobbies.

It’s not just a Labor or Liberal problem. Even the Greens seem to be caught in this. Hence, a good reason to look to independents and non-partisan politicians of which we thankfully do have a few.

Teresa Martin-Lim, Brighton Not funny, Dave

I am dismayed to learn that life-long Labor supporter and talented comedian Dave Hughes has become so disgruntled with Labor policies that he has, not only “flipped” over to the Liberal side of politics, but decided to help open the Liberal state election campaign, for free.

For a so-called, long-time supporter of social democratic values to make such an emphatic statement and perform such a public backflip to embrace the other side does not compute. It is unfathomable, especially as Liberal Party policies are those of yesteryear, formed from its close relationship with multinational mining corporations, big business and developers.

I must say Dave Hughes’ own values espoused over many years now count for nothing and he will be now known as the Mark Latham of comedy.

Derek Costello, Belmont



Allan’s achievement

In discussion of whether Jacinta Allan ″⁣leaves the electorate in a better or worse condition than she found it″⁣ (15/8), little mention has been made of what, for my part, is a fine achievement of her government. Victorian Labor has stood above all other state governments for its response to the invitation to Australians made in the gracious and dignified Uluru Statement from the Heart in 2017.

The statement, so beautifully worded and ″⁣from the heart″⁣ sought constitutional recognition and Voice, Treaty and Truth in order that our ″⁣children walk together in two worlds″⁣.

The First Peoples’ Assembly (2019) is the voice, representing the Victorian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in negotiations with the Victorian government. The Yoorook Justice Commission heard heartfelt truths from both Indigenous and settlers about the consequences of colonisation. These two laid the groundwork for Treaty (2025), the first between an Australian government and First Peoples.

Anyone who has paid close attention to these steps would surely be impressed by the quiet, patient, exemplary democratic processes that have characterised negotiations on the parts of all involved. Leaders of the First Peoples’ Assembly, Commissioners of Yoorook Justice Commission, Minister for Treaty and First Peoples, Natalie Hutchins and Jacinta Allan deserve the thanks of all for leading us towards a richer and reconciled future.

Prue Gill, North Carlton Too much trivia

Who the heck is this podcaster Nikki Osborne who seems hell-bent on throwing our PM under a bus? Let’s get back to the serious press who want to discuss policy. Enough with the trivia.

Wendy Baker, Lilydale Ley not disingenuous

Your correspondent (Letters, 16/8) comments that Sussan Ley’s Greyhound bus trip through America was ″⁣disingenuous″⁣, is a failure to acknowledge that her trip was to observe, to empathise, to listen to the heartbeat of America without judging.

Ley could have sat in plush surroundings in New York conversing with those of her political persuasion. However, in ethnographic style, she immersed herself in the humble world of her fellow travellers – sometimes prisoners, veterans or nuns with minimal possessions; she walked a distance to the bus in the cold; she travelled light; as a sole woman she went into bars; at times she experienced loneliness.

Her trip encapsulated the ethnographer’s role, to understand the other from their point of view, from their experience of getting through the day. That’s not disingenuous.

David Hickey, Heidelberg Republic question

Is it time that we, as a proud nation, restarted debate surrounding the ‘R’ word? Surely, we are mature enough to stand on our own feet and have a head of state elected from within our own people and with our own interests at the forefront of all decisions.

Ken O’Brien, Mentone Legal system adapts

Re ″⁣A man lied about paying this worker for sex. He is now going to jail for rape”, 16/8). Put to the legal test – Victorian affirmative consent law reforms introduced in July 2023 has confirmed that there is no delineation of the core principle of ″⁣informed consent″⁣ based on vocation and gender.

That the same legal system that once criminalised sex workers for their job has produced the aforementioned ruling is positive progress in another important way. The delineation of labelling a woman a ″⁣damned whores or God’s police″⁣ (a bad or good woman) as a justification to abuse her, is no longer plausible or socially and morally acceptable.

So, bravo to the judiciary for drawing a clear line in the sand whereby any person who “makes false or misleading representations to induce consent” – whether from a sex worker or not – will be said to have committed a “serious violation of bodily autonomy” (ie a basic human right) and will be punished accordingly.

Jelena Rosic, Mornington



Flanagan’s comments

Following controversies, including regarding this year’s Adelaide Writers’ Week, Richard Flanagan (″⁣Lunch with ...″⁣ 15/8) criticises the widely adopted International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism.

It should be pointed out that in her remarks at the commencement of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, Commissioner Virginia Bell stated that the commission would apply the IHRA definition, stating that its critics overlook that it does allow for criticism of the policies of the Israeli government, and that it requires consideration of ″⁣the overall context in which conduct occurs before making any determination that the conduct is antisemitic″⁣.

Geoff Feren, St Kilda East Hornet’s nest

Pedants cop a lot of flak for their interventions, but I suppose somebody has to police our language. Your Letters correspondent, (16/8) admonishes Nikki Barrowclough for apparently confusing style with grammar. He states that she is reacting to ″⁣a trend″⁣ that many find disagreeable. He then adds that ″⁣none seem to be ungrammatical″⁣.

But as ″⁣none]″⁣ is a contraction of’ ″⁣no one″⁣, and as he has made ″⁣trend″⁣ the subject, according to the subject-verb-agreement rule, he should have written ″⁣none seems″⁣. Or is that being too pedantic?

Owen Hugh, Kensington AND ANOTHER THING Politics

Re ″⁣Coalition pledges to cap Melbourne’s road tolls at $50 per week″⁣ 16/8. Motorists to be subsidised by taxpayers to use Melbourne’s profitable privately operated toll ways. The $90 million could be better used to fill in potholes on public country roads.

Jim McLeod, Sale Re ″⁣Dave Hughes to campaign for Liberals in Victorian election″⁣, 16/8. Is there anybody who actually cares what Dave Hughes thinks?

Keith Fletcher, Glenlyon



Dave Hughes, a comedian? Jess Wilson and the clown!

Peter O’Brien, Newport Let’s put Andrew Bragg into one of his recommended, substandard houses for six months in the height of hot summer and see if he has the same opinion regarding solving the housing crisis. (″⁣Taylor rebukes Coalition frontbencher after Bragg goes rogue on housing, migration, tax″⁣, 14/8).

Doug Springall, Yarragon It was great to see so many young folk protesting against Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. Bravo, students.

Merle Mitchell, Mt Eliza Furthermore

There should be weekly rubbish removals across the state. The reason is to avoid health hazards. It is appalling that some councils do not collect garbage weekly. It should be legally required to do so.

Doris LeRoy, Altona Re your correspondent’s question (Letters, 14/8) ″⁣Would you be able to understand the reports if Shakespeare was reading the news on television?″⁣.

I would love to hear Shakespeare reading the news, but it would mean putting up with Pauline Hanson saying ″⁣Please explain″⁣ at the end of each line.

Claude Miller, Castlemaine



Finally

It’s refreshing to hear one of my artistic heroes saying out loud what has become totally evident to me: our fascination with cancelling and self-censoring our discourse on big issues stifles discussion of the human condition in all its forms. Thank you, Richard Flanagan (″⁣Lunch with″⁣, 15/8).

Rupert Steiner, Balnarring Beach The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: The knock on the door: 57 years on, a Vietnam War widow tells her story
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life The knock on the door: 57 years on, a Vietnam War widow tells her story Carolyn Webb August 16, 2026 — 7:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To this day, Lynne Moore can’t stand to watch images from July 20, 1969, of the first humans walking on the moon. Her husband, Private Ray Moore, was killed in action in the Vietnam War that week. Never forgotten: Lynne Moore, with her son Craig Moore, lays roses in memory of her husband, Ray Moore, at Croydon war memorial on Sunday. Chris Hopkins And so rather than evoking a sense of wonder, the moon landing reminds her of army officials arriving to break the bad news at her mother’s house in Kilsyth, in Melbourne’s east, which she was visiting. “It brings back the knock on the door,” Lynne says. “I have to walk away.”



War widows, she says, were expected to get on with their lives, but now at age 80, she is telling her story. The Ray Moore she loved was fun-loving, a hard worker and could talk to anyone. Ray Moore visited his children Rhonda, Craig and Gary at Holsworthy army base in Sydney two months before he died in 1969. She said it felt very emotional laying a bunch of roses – “Ray’s favourite flower” – with their son Craig and grandson Brendan at the Croydon war memorial on Sunday, at a ceremony for Vietnam Veterans’ Day. The family features in a new book, Vietnam – Long Hard Years Not Forgotten, about Lilydale region residents’ Vietnam War experiences.



“It’s nice to know Ray is going to be remembered now, for generations to come,” said Lynne, now a great-grandmother of eight, on Sunday. “He died for his country, and they should be proud of that.” On active duty: Moore posing in Vietnam with a Florida flag belonging to US soldiers. The book’s author, Lilydale RSL secretary Anthony McAleer told the service how in the early 1960s, Ray Moore and Michael Hannaford were teenage apprentices together in the same Croydon butcher shop. Years later Moore joined the army while Hannaford was conscripted. Hannaford, 21, was killed on December 14, 1968, when the tank he was driving hit a mine. He left a young wife, Margaret. Moore, 23, was shot dead by a Viet Cong sentry on July 24, 1969.



Ray and Lynne Moore had three children – Rhonda, aged three at the time, Craig, 2 and Gary, six months. Historian Anthony McAleer addresses the crowd at the Croydon service. Chris Hopkins Both widows suffered indignities, McAleer said, which was “a sad indictment” of institutions at the time. Before Moore’s burial, the army evicted Lynne from their house at Holsworthy army base in Sydney. She was ignored by older war widows, and even parents at her children’s school were hostile. How did she get through it?



“I think you put one foot in front of the other,” she said. “I had three children to look after. It was just something you did.” Margaret Hannaford, who attended Sunday’s service, tells in the book how someone from the army said Michael should be buried in a war cemetery in Vietnam, and so not ruin people’s Christmas in Australia. Vietnam War veterans marching from Croydon Oval to the service at the war memorial on Sunday. Chris Hopkins Margaret refused, and Michael’s funeral was held on Christmas Eve 1968 in a Croydon church. McAleer said it was important to remember the widows who were among the victims of the Vietnam War.



RSL Victoria senior vice-president Des Callaghan pointed out Tuesday is the 60th anniversary of the Battle of Long Tan, in which Australian soldiers bravely fought an overwhelming enemy force. It was a time to remember the 523 Australians who died on active duty in Vietnam, the 2400 who were wounded and service people who returned to an Australia that was divided about the war, Callaghan said. Australia had matured in its treatment of veterans. “We have learnt the vital truth that one can disagree with the politics of war without diminishing respect for the men and women who put on the uniform,” he said.
